stem: A technician reports that two upper complete dentures made from the same acrylic batch have developed different defects. Denture A was processed with an abbreviated heat-curing cycle, shows internal voids in its thickest palatal section and has a persistent monomer odour. Denture B was repaired with a high monomer-to-powder ratio in a chairside cold-cure resin and has developed a fine crack line from the midline repair into the thin palatal region. Both dentures are stressed in flexure during function. The dentist asks which explanation best links the processing decisions to the observed material behaviour.
lead: Which interpretation provides the most coherent cause-and-effect account?

options.A: Attribute the midline crack exclusively to differential cooling stresses because only heat-cure acrylic can develop fatigue cracks
options.B: Attribute both failures predominantly to porosity from excessive exothermic heat and recommend longer curing without evaluating monomer ratio or flexural stresses
options.C: Residual monomer and inadequate conversion can weaken the acrylic; porosity and repeated flexural stress can favour crack initiation and propagation
options.D: Attribute the voids chiefly to inadequate packing pressure, while assuming that residual monomer and degree of cure are clinically unimportant
options.E: Attribute the fractures to cyclical denture flexure and an intrinsically thin palatal section, leaving the laboratory polymerisation cycle unchanged

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Residual monomer and inadequate conversion can weaken the acrylic; porosity and repeated flexural stress can favour crack initiation and propagation

DECISIVE FEATURE: Although processing and geometry interact, neither one should be assumed the only cause without reviewing the laboratory cycle and clinical loading.

RATIONALE: An incomplete polymerisation cycle can leave residual monomer and compromised material properties, while exothermic heat, processing conditions and thick sections contribute to void formation. Excess monomer in a repair mix may increase residual monomer, shrinkage and weakening; cyclic tensile/flexural stresses can initiate and propagate cracks at defects and thin sections. Processing must be corrected alongside fit and flexure.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: Repeated flexure and the cold-cure repair conditions also plausibly contribute.
B: Thermal porosity may contribute but cannot account alone for repair-material composition and fatigue loading.
D: Packing pressure may affect voids but residual monomer and incomplete conversion also weaken acrylic.
E: Clinical loading is important, but the reported voids and residual monomer also require correction.

stem: A 12-year-old presents 50 minutes after avulsion of UR1 during a football match. The tooth was held dry for about 15 minutes, then placed in milk. The apex is open radiographically and the socket wall appears intact. The child is medically well, tetanus status will be verified, and there is no additional facial injury. The parent asks whether it is better to postpone replantation until the next morning to allow specialist pulp revascularisation planning, because the tooth has not been cleaned with an antiseptic.
lead: Which immediate management is most appropriate?

options.A: Replant promptly, stabilise flexibly and arrange age- and apex-appropriate trauma follow-up
options.B: Delay replantation for 24 hours because an open apex is expected to revascularise more readily after prolonged storage
options.C: Gently clean the tooth in saline, complete extra-oral endodontic instrumentation, then replant and splint
options.D: Defer replantation for a planned specialist assessment later that day while maintaining the tooth in milk
options.E: Provide flexible splinting only after radiographic confirmation of pulpal revascularisation

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Replant promptly, stabilise flexibly and arrange age- and apex-appropriate trauma follow-up

DECISIVE FEATURE: Extra-oral root instrumentation and delay would reduce viability. Endodontic management depends on vitality and subsequent course, particularly in immature teeth.

RATIONALE: The tooth is permanent and the total dry time is relatively short with subsequent milk storage. Immediate replantation preserves options for periodontal healing and potential revascularisation of an immature tooth. A passive flexible splint, clinical and radiographic checks, supportive care and follow-up are required.

ALTERNATIVES:
B: The extra delay worsens PDL viability and does not confer an immature-pulp benefit.
C: Immediate extra-oral root-canal treatment is not the preferred strategy for a potentially revascularising immature tooth.
D: Replantation should not be needlessly delayed once urgent assessment and suitable care are available.
E: Splinting is part of initial replantation care, whereas pulpal response is monitored over time.

theme: Dahl concept, occlusal space and alternative management
stem: A patient has significant localised anterior wear with reduced space for restorative material. The posterior occlusal support, mobility, periodontal health, pulpal status, parafunctional load and willingness to accept a reversible adaptive phase are established. One heavily restored anterior tooth lacks clinical height for a retentive crown and localized periodontal and aesthetic effects of lengthening are acceptable.

options.D: Use selective crown lengthening only after evaluating root support, smile line and periodontal consequences
options.E: Offer an alternative restorative design that preserves pulpal and periodontal tissues without increasing full-arch vertical dimension

stem: A specialist reviewing a referral must decide how an investigation or published estimate should influence prosthodontic management. A particular metal-framework component is identified by its described position, and its principal biomechanical purpose is being tested. The identified component is an auxiliary rest positioned anterior to the fulcrum line on an appropriately prepared contralateral premolar.
lead: Which primary function best describes the named component?

options.A: Provide indirect retention resisting rotational lifting of the distal extension
options.B: Provide direct retention through a retentive clasp tip
options.C: Provide cross-arch stabilisation through the rigid major connector
options.D: Provide vertical support via the mesial occlusal rest on the terminal abutment
options.E: Provide a tissue stop that replaces the need for an altered-cast impression

solution:

DECISIVE FINDING: The identified component is an auxiliary rest positioned anterior to the fulcrum line on an appropriately prepared contralateral premolar.

theme: Diagnostic uncertainty in a painful posterior tooth
stem: A previously restored molar has intermittent pain on chewing. Cold sensibility, percussion, six-point periodontal probing, bite testing and an intra-oral radiograph are available. The clinician needs to distinguish a fractured cusp, pulpal disease, a vertical root fracture and non-odontogenic pain without committing prematurely to irreversible care. A recently traumatised tooth tests negative to cold but has normal periapical imaging, uncertain pulpal status and no swelling. The referral includes a clear account of the principal problem; the patient asks which option should be prioritised before further treatment.
lead: What is the best next clinical decision?

options.A: Assess the isolated deep periodontal defect and root-level fracture evidence before attempting reconstruction
options.B: Treat the confirmed symptomatic irreversible pulpitis before planning definitive cuspal coverage
options.C: Remove the existing restoration under magnification, assess the crack, and protect the cusp provisionally
options.D: Reassess the occlusion and muscular pain source before removing a technically sound restoration
options.E: Obtain targeted additional investigation because the initial tests are conflicting and the management choice would change

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Obtain targeted additional investigation because the initial tests are conflicting and the management choice would change

DECISIVE FEATURE: A recently traumatised tooth tests negative to cold but has normal periapical imaging, uncertain pulpal status and no swelling.

RATIONALE: Transient neural non-response after trauma requires review and repeated tests rather than immediate root filling.

ALTERNATIVES:

stem: A new mandibular RPD is planned with a mobile distal-extension saddle. The patient has two strategically placed crowns that could be modified before denture construction. The dentist has an opportunity to prepare the prospective abutment crowns as surveyed restorations rather than cementing them as independent units. A diagnostic survey shows that rest and guide-plane positions may control both insertion and rotational stress. The laboratory has not received a proposed path of insertion.
lead: Which instruction to the referring clinician is most appropriate?

options.A: Complete definitive crowns and perform any adjustments to guiding planes after the framework is cast
options.B: Select retentive clasp positions from the laboratory survey after the crowns are cemented
options.C: Plan resin-bonded retentive wings on the abutment crowns and minimise occlusal rest-seat preparation
options.D: Use broad tissue-borne acrylic saddles to compensate for an absence of designed rests and guide planes
options.E: Plan guiding surfaces, rests and surveyed crown contours before definitive impressions

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Plan guiding surfaces, rests and surveyed crown contours before definitive impressions

DECISIVE FEATURE: A new mandibular RPD is planned with a mobile distal-extension saddle. The patient has two strategically placed crowns that could be modified before denture construction. The dentist has an opportunity to prepare the prospective abutment crowns as surveyed restorations rather than cementing them as independent units. A diagnostic survey shows that rest and guide-plane positions may control both insertion and rotational stress. The laboratory has not received a proposed path of insertion.

RATIONALE: Surveyed crowns are useful precisely because rest seats, guiding surfaces, reciprocal contours and undercuts can be incorporated prospectively. stem: A partial denture has an onlay rest producing a marked premature contact and anterior slide into maximum intercuspation. The patient has begun avoiding the prosthesis. options.A: Provide selective adjustment of the cobalt-chromium onlay rest before confirming the prepared rest-seat form
options.B: Relieve the denture-base intaglio to allow the occlusal rest to move apically under contact
options.C: Reduce the opposing tooth to remove the anterior deflection while preserving framework contour
options.D: Rest seating, occlusal clearance and the intended static/dynamic scheme before adjusting opposing teeth
options.E: Add a clinical remount and balance both arches before checking whether the rest is fully seated

solution:

DECISIVE FEATURE: A partial denture has an onlay rest producing a marked premature contact and anterior slide into maximum intercuspation. The patient has begun avoiding the prosthesis. stem: An anterior prosthodontic patient is dissatisfied with the gingival contour and crown emergence. stem: A 73-year-old receiving monthly high-dose intravenous antiresorptive treatment for metastatic malignancy has a restorable molar with irreversible pulpitis. Extraction is requested because the crown has fractured. The root is periodontally stable, the tooth can be isolated and endodontically treated, and there is adequate tissue for a direct core and later cuspal protection. The oncology team reports no urgent need to alter the antiresorptive schedule. Several technically possible interventions have differing osteonecrosis risks and functional consequences.
lead: What should be prioritised before choosing extraction?

options.A: Extract the tooth with local measures once the patient accepts the elevated MRONJ risk
options.B: Assess restorability and consider tooth-preserving endodontic management because MRONJ risk is elevated
options.C: Provide a long-term provisional crown without endodontic assessment until antiresorptive treatment has ended
options.D: Delay extraction until the next scheduled antiresorptive infusion has been omitted, without changing the prosthetic plan
options.E: Plan extraction and delayed implant restoration after routine socket healing if the medical team confirms remission

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Assess restorability and consider tooth-preserving endodontic management because MRONJ risk is elevated

DECISIVE FEATURE: A 73-year-old receiving monthly high-dose intravenous antiresorptive treatment for metastatic malignancy has a restorable molar with irreversible pulpitis. Extraction is requested because the crown has fractured. stem: An 11-year-old presents three hours after fracturing a permanent maxillary incisor. There is a 2-mm traumatic pulp exposure, a positive vitality response, an open apex and no displacement or root fracture. The child can cooperate with rubber dam treatment.
lead: What treatment best protects future root development?

options.A: Immediate complete root canal treatment regardless of pulp status
options.B: Partial pulpotomy using a suitable biocompatible pulp dressing, with follow-up
options.C: Bleach the exposed pulp before composite restoration
options.D: Extract the permanent incisor and replace it with an implant now
options.E: Observe the exposed pulp without sealing it

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Partial pulpotomy using a suitable biocompatible pulp dressing, with follow-up

RATIONALE: Vital pulp therapy, commonly a partial pulpotomy, seeks to maintain vitality and permit apexogenesis in immature permanent teeth. Traumatically exposed vital pulps should not be left exposed, and definitive RCT is not the routine first choice in this scenario.

theme: Treatment sequencing in a failing dentition
stem: A patient is referred for rehabilitation of multiple failing restorations, missing posterior support and an aesthetic complaint. Diagnostic records show several risks that could change after initial treatment. The specialist must sequence care to prevent premature commitment to an expensive irreversible plan. lead: What is the most defensible recommendation at this stage?

options.A: Obtain a structured multidisciplinary prognosis assessment for teeth and implants before choosing extractions

options.D: Provide provisional restorations that test function, appearance and vertical dimension before definitive work

The patient has a complex eccentric interference pattern that the current virtual system cannot reliably capture or simulate.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Accept a validated digital workflow for a limited conformative restoration without unnecessary extra acquisition
options.B: Use digital wax-up and a conservative prototype to communicate and test intended anatomy
options.C: Select conventional clinical verification when virtual articulation cannot represent the patient's complex functional pattern
options.D: Verify the clinical jaw relation before relying on any digitally generated occlusal design
options.E: Correct inaccurate scan registration or occlusal-contact capture before milling definitive units

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Select conventional clinical verification when virtual articulation cannot represent the patient's complex functional pattern

DECISIVE FEATURE: The patient has a complex eccentric interference pattern that the current virtual system cannot reliably capture or simulate.

RATIONALE: Clinical checking remains essential when software assumptions are not met.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A single posterior crown is conformative, records and margins are accurate and a validated CAD/CAM workflow is available. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A stable record exists but the patient and technician need to evaluate smile line, phonetics and an increased vertical design before preparation. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Full-arch reconstruction is proposed but centric records are inconsistent and mounted diagnostic casts cannot be reproduced. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The virtual interocclusal contacts appear unilateral because the maxillary scan was stitched to the wrong bite record. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A complex prosthodontic patient needs an accurate working record. Moisture control, preparation margin accessibility, span length, material interaction, patient comfort and laboratory timing affect selection between elastomeric and digital techniques. A reflective wet subgingival margin is not captured consistently by the intraoral scanner despite a good short-span scan elsewhere.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Use a physical verification record where full-arch scan stitching uncertainty could compromise passive fit
options.B: Provide a rigid custom tray and appropriate wash/space control when deformable bulk would distort the record
options.C: Use an alternative material or approach when chemical contamination could inhibit the planned setting reaction
options.D: Use addition silicone with correct tray support and careful moisture control for a conventional precise impression
options.E: Repeat a digital scan after exposing the margin and managing reflective or contaminated surfaces

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Repeat a digital scan after exposing the margin and managing reflective or contaminated surfaces

DECISIVE FEATURE: A reflective wet subgingival margin is not captured consistently by the intraoral scanner despite a good short-span scan elsewhere.

RATIONALE: Improved exposure and surface control must precede reacquisition.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A full-arch implant model shows inconsistent interimplant distances on repeat intraoral scans. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A long impression has thin unsupported bulk and flexes on removal, creating systematic arch distortion. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The operator is using a vinyl polysiloxane material after handling latex gloves and the material fails to polymerise locally. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A full crown margin is clearly accessible, conventional impressions have worked reliably and stable addition silicone is available. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

theme: Behavioural and interdisciplinary control of tooth wear
stem: A complex tooth-wear patient has received dental preventive advice, but the exposure pattern involves lifestyle, systemic illness or medications. The dentist must set a feasible pathway that the patient can implement and monitor over time. A patient worries about continuing rapid wear but has no comparative photographs, models or serial BEWE scores. Both a staged and a direct approach have been discussed, and neither is excluded solely by cost or operator access.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Coordinate ongoing repairable restorative protection when risk control is partial but functional symptoms are significant
options.B: Refer suspected uncontrolled reflux or eating-disorder-related acid exposure for appropriate medical evaluation
options.C: Address frequent acidic drinks with timing, substitution and post-exposure advice
options.D: Record objective baseline scores and repeat intervals before concluding that wear is rapidly progressive
options.E: Review xerogenic medication burden and salivary management with the prescriber where feasible

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Record objective baseline scores and repeat intervals before concluding that wear is rapidly progressive

DECISIVE FEATURE: A patient worries about continuing rapid wear but has no comparative photographs, models or serial BEWE scores.

RATIONALE: Serial evidence is needed to quantify progression.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Dentine sensitivity prevents eating and speaking despite appropriate preventive measures, while full-mouth crowns would cause major tissue loss. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Severe palatal wear accompanies repeated unexplained vomiting and psychological distress. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Training involves six acidic isotonic-drink episodes daily despite normal saliva and a previously healthy dentition. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: An older patient has dry mouth following antidepressant and antimuscarinic therapy with rapidly increasing root exposure. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A patient with a mandibular implant bridge has had no reported problems since loading three years earlier. At recall, probing is 5 mm at one implant with bleeding on gentle probing; baseline charts recorded 3 mm at the same surface and a current standardised periapical shows possible additional crestal bone loss of 1 mm. There is also a fractured veneering composite repair, but the framework remains stable. The patient was scheduled for a two-yearly review because the implant prosthesis was considered definitive.
lead: Which recall response is most appropriate?

options.A: Continue two-yearly recalls because the patient has no pain
options.B: Remove the bridge permanently at the first sign of bleeding
options.C: Review and compare probing and radiographs with baseline data, assess inflammation and cleansability, manage identified disease and shorten recall according to risk
options.D: Order CBCT immediately for every implant with a pocket deeper than 4 mm
options.E: Repeat only the porcelain repair and omit biological reassessment

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Review and compare probing and radiographs with baseline data, assess inflammation and cleansability, manage identified disease and shorten recall according to risk

DECISIVE FEATURE: A patient with a mandibular implant bridge has had no reported problems since loading three years earlier. There is also a fractured veneering composite repair, but the framework remains stable. The patient was scheduled for a two-yearly review because the implant prosthesis was considered definitive.

RATIONALE: A change from baseline in probing and possible bone loss warrants focused biological assessment and risk-based maintenance; technical and biological complications must be addressed together.

theme: Occlusal records and complete denture instability
stem: A patient complains that a newly made complete denture tips during chewing. Both dentures are examined for support, borders, tooth position and centric and eccentric contacts; the clinician must avoid treating a prosthesis design problem as a simple retention deficiency. The denture seats well but is immediately lifted by the cheek when the masseter contracts against an overextended distobuccal flange.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Re-record jaw relations when centric records are inconsistent and the vertical dimension is unverified
options.B: Correct peripheral extension and functional polished-surface contours that dislodge the denture
options.C: Eliminate a reproducible premature centric contact and re-evaluate balance
options.D: Consider a new prosthesis design when the basal seat and jaw relationship have changed fundamentally
options.E: Correct the occlusal plane and posterior tooth position over the effective support area

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Correct peripheral extension and functional polished-surface contours that dislodge the denture

DECISIVE FEATURE: The denture seats well but is immediately lifted by the cheek when the masseter contracts against an overextended distobuccal flange.

RATIONALE: The peripheral functional extension is the mechanism of displacement.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The record base was unstable during registration and there is no reproducible centric relation, with excess vertical dimension and speech difficulty. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The upper denture lifts consistently on closure against a prominent lower molar contact despite satisfactory extension. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Severe post-extraction ridge remodelling has occurred since the impression, and a prosthesis now has global poor fit and support. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Posterior teeth are arranged far buccal to the lower support area and the denture tips with chewing even when static contacts are balanced. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

theme: Restoration survival and maintenance after erosive wear
stem: A patient has undergone rehabilitation for erosive wear and now requires evaluation of complications, material choices and maintenance. The clinician knows the initial aetiology, bonded substrate, occlusal scheme and baseline photographs. One palatal composite edge has chipped with otherwise stable function and sound remaining restoration. Both a staged and a direct approach have been discussed, and neither is excluded solely by cost or operator access.
lead: Which course of action provides the strongest patient-specific justification among these alternatives?

options.A: Assess periodontal effects of deep margins before extending preparation
options.B: Repair local direct composite defects and reassess loading and acid exposure
options.C: Investigate unexplained post-treatment pulpal sensitivity and exclude irreversible pulpal pathology
options.D: Review the adhesive substrate and restorative thickness before changing to an indirect material
options.E: Use longitudinal wear measurements and preventive review to distinguish stable repair needs from active disease

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Repair local direct composite defects and reassess loading and acid exposure

DECISIVE FEATURE: One palatal composite edge has chipped with otherwise stable function and sound remaining restoration.

RATIONALE: Local repair is usually more conservative than wholesale replacement.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Gingival inflammation persists around overdeep crown margins despite good hygiene and no supragingival plaque source. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Spontaneous thermal pain develops after extensive preparation and persists well beyond expected short postoperative sensitivity. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Repeated widespread fracture occurs at thin unsupported ceramic margins and much bonding is to sclerotic dentine. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The patient reports continued erosion, but paired scans show no measurable loss since prevention was introduced. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A 52-year-old completed a minimally invasive composite rehabilitation for erosive tooth wear two years ago. The intraoral photographs show generally satisfactory aesthetics, but the patient describes gradually increasing sensitivity and several small restoration repairs. Serial BEWE scores are recorded at the same sites, calibrated photographs are available and current dietary review suggests a renewed pattern of frequent acidic beverages. The patient asks whether an increased restoration survival rate alone would demonstrate that treatment had succeeded, as chewing efficiency is acceptable.
lead: Which outcome set most appropriately evaluates clinical success?

options.A: A fixed review interval with no reassessment of risk factors once the original rehabilitation has been completed
options.B: Use radiographic marginal integrity and maintenance cost as the principal quantitative indicators, adding subjective symptom scoring
options.C: Restoration survival only, because acid exposure does not affect the long-term health of restored teeth
options.D: Patient-rated aesthetics only, because subjective satisfaction is more important than recurrent tooth wear
options.E: Measure wear progression, tissue health, function, restoration maintenance, patient experience and acid control together

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Measure wear progression, tissue health, function, restoration maintenance, patient experience and acid control together

DECISIVE FEATURE: Using restoration survival as one endpoint is valid but insufficient to establish control of the disease or long-term biological success.

RATIONALE: Wear rehabilitation is a chronic-care pathway. Outcome assessment includes the disease process, restorative maintenance and patient-reported benefit, not just short-term survival of composite restorations. Recurrence of acid exposure is clinically significant.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: The newly reported risk exposure requires reassessment.
B: The combination omits direct assessment of disease progression, tissue health and causative exposure.
C: Restoration survival says little about continued acid disease or pulpal impact.
D: Aesthetics alone cannot show that wear has stabilised.

stem: A mandibular Kennedy Class I patient has an otherwise stable cast cobalt–chromium framework with mesial rests and RPI clasp assemblies on both premolars. Under a static fit check the rests are fully seated, but during mastication the posterior saddles rotate tissueward and the premolars exhibit increasing distal inclination. Both ridges are severely resorbed and the denture bases were made from a single mucostatic impression. Occlusal records are acceptable, and there is no infection or active periodontitis. A laboratory technician recommends making the retentive clasps deeper to stop the saddles moving.
lead: Which modification best addresses the primary biomechanical mismatch?

options.A: Add a rigid lingual bar extension to prevent all rotational movement
options.B: Reassess extension and loaded tissue support, and use functional impression principles without increasing abutment torque
options.C: Change both abutments to distal occlusal rests and wrought-wire circumferential clasps while keeping the present base impression
options.D: Shorten the distal saddle to keep the base away from mobile mucosa and reduce lever-arm length
options.E: Increase clasp undercut engagement on the premolar abutments

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Reassess extension and loaded tissue support, and use functional impression principles without increasing abutment torque

DECISIVE FEATURE: Implant assistance could also improve support if appropriate, but that is a different treatment burden and not the best initial correction to the described RPD mechanism.

RATIONALE: The two support systems—periodontal ligament and resilient distal ridge—displace differently under load. Functional impression/altered cast and proper base extension aim to support the distal extension without turning premolar abutments into levers. Deeper clasping would worsen potentially harmful torque.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: Connector rigidity cannot replace distal tissue support.
C: This may alter retention but does not remedy differential tissue settlement; distal rests can increase torque.
D: Reduced extension can increase pressure on the remaining tissue and worsen support.
E: More retentive clasping does not prevent ridge settlement and may increase abutment torque.

stem: A 69-year-old is edentulous in the maxilla and retains the mandibular six anterior teeth and bilateral first premolars. The maxillary complete denture has repeatedly become loose despite apparently appropriate borders and a satisfactory posterior palatal seal. On examination there is marked anterior maxillary flabby ridge tissue, over-erupted mandibular anterior teeth, a broad anterior contact with no posterior occluding support, and enlarged maxillary tuberosities. The patient has declined implant treatment and reports that previous relines improve retention for only a few weeks. The remaining mandibular teeth have a guarded but stabilisable periodontal prognosis.
lead: Which rehabilitation principle should most strongly guide planning?

options.A: Extract mandibular incisors and provide a lower complete denture to eliminate anterior contacts
options.B: Use a selective-pressure impression for the flabby anterior ridge and a stronger posterior palatal seal without reviewing the opposing arch
options.C: Repeat the maxillary denture reline and omit occlusal reassessment because the seal is satisfactory
options.D: Remake the maxillary denture in crossbite to improve posterior contacts while preserving the same upper-ridge impression protocol
options.E: Address the combination-syndrome load pattern by re-establishing appropriate posterior support and managing the denture-bearing tissues and opposing occlusion

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Address the combination-syndrome load pattern by re-establishing appropriate posterior support and managing the denture-bearing tissues and opposing occlusion

DECISIVE FEATURE: Posterior occlusal support could be re-established with various tooth-supported or removable options; the best strategy is the one that addresses load distribution and is maintainable within patient constraints.

RATIONALE: This is a classic anterior-loading pattern associated with combination syndrome. Prosthetic instability arises from multiple interacting factors, including support distribution, occlusal relationships and altered tissues; recurrent reline alone does not correct the functional cause. The remaining lower dentition deserves prognosis-led management rather than automatic extraction.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: Extraction might become justified by prognosis but is not routine while viable teeth remain.
B: Better impression management may improve fit but cannot correct the unbalanced anterior loading pattern.
C: Relining does not correct the pathological anterior-loading mechanism.
D: Posterior occlusion must be re-established in a coordinated plan, not by tooth arrangement alone.

stem: A previously crowned upper premolar has a persistent sinus and an apical radiolucency. The crown is intact but there is extensive subgingival caries under one margin and no predictable ferrule. The patient has no acute facial swelling and is willing to undergo further endodontic investigation if the tooth has a reasonable prognosis. Periodontal charting identifies a deep isolated defect adjacent to the carious margin, and the dentist is considering crown lengthening for additional ferrule. Technical retreatment success alone would not establish whether definitive rehabilitation is justified.
lead: What should primarily determine whether retreatment is worthwhile?

options.A: Whether the patient prefers a white post
options.B: Restorability and combined endodontic-periodontal prognosis before choosing retreatment or extraction
options.C: Size of the apical radiolucency in isolation
options.D: An assumption that every apical lesion heals after retreatment
options.E: The cost of a new zirconia crown alone

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Restorability and combined endodontic-periodontal prognosis before choosing retreatment or extraction

DECISIVE FEATURE: A previously crowned upper premolar has a persistent sinus and an apical radiolucency. RATIONALE: Endodontic success cannot salvage a structurally non-restorable tooth. The complete prognosis must precede a technically complex retreatment.

stem: An adolescent has translucent blue-grey to amber teeth, severe incisal wear and hypersensitivity. Radiographs demonstrate bulbous crowns, cervical constriction, short roots and early obliteration of pulp spaces. Multiple posterior teeth have lost occlusal anatomy and restorative height; the patient is growing.
lead: Which overall strategy is most defensible?

options.A: Prepare every tooth for irreversible full crowns immediately without growth assessment
options.B: Extract all teeth because pulp chambers are obliterated
options.C: Bleach all teeth as the sole treatment
options.D: Use enamel microabrasion alone for the structural defects
options.E: Stage protective restoration of compromised teeth to preserve function and vertical dimension, with growth-aware planning

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Stage protective restoration of compromised teeth to preserve function and vertical dimension, with growth-aware planning

RATIONALE: The combination is characteristic of dentinogenesis imperfecta. Where progressive structural wear is severe, management aims to protect remaining tissues, function and appearance with age-appropriate restorations; conservative measures alone will not address extensive dentine structural weakness.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Prepare every tooth for irreversible full crowns immediately without growth assessment B. Extract all teeth because pulp chambers are obliterated C. Bleach all teeth as the sole treatment D. Use enamel microabrasion alone for the structural defects

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

EVIDENCE / SOURCE: Developmental dental anomalies literature; DSFE ES 10.1

theme: Treatment sequencing in a failing dentition
stem: A patient is referred for rehabilitation of multiple failing restorations, missing posterior support and an aesthetic complaint. Diagnostic records show several risks that could change after initial treatment. The specialist must sequence care to prevent premature commitment to an expensive irreversible plan. Multiple active lesions, a draining sinus and uncontrolled bleeding on probing remain, and the patient requests immediate veneers. Both a staged and a direct approach have been discussed, and neither is excluded solely by cost or operator access.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Provide provisional restorations that test function, appearance and vertical dimension before definitive work
options.B: Stabilise active endodontic, periodontal and caries disease before definitively choosing prostheses
options.C: Proceed with definitive rehabilitation once prerequisites and patient agreement are verified
options.D: Obtain a structured multidisciplinary prognosis assessment for teeth and implants before choosing extractions
options.E: Offer a staged lower-cost strategy with maintenance rather than full-mouth definitive reconstruction at one visit

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Stabilise active endodontic, periodontal and caries disease before definitively choosing prostheses

DECISIVE FEATURE: Multiple active lesions, a draining sinus and uncontrolled bleeding on probing remain, and the patient requests immediate veneers.

RATIONALE: Active disease is an immediate prognostic threat to definitive restorations.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The proposed vertical change is substantial and speech, phonetics and muscular adaptation have not been tested. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A complex fixed or implant prosthesis is planned using an intraoral scanner and a three-dimensional dataset. The team must decide when the recorded geometry is trustworthy, when another acquisition is justified and when an analogue verification step adds information. A large metallic restoration produces streak artefact adjacent to a canal and the interpreted border changes with reconstruction settings. The patient wishes to preserve future options where possible but would accept a more extensive treatment if demonstrably necessary.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Use an alternative impression or verification index to control long-span stitching error
options.B: Perform a new scan only after hardware or material artefact has been reduced or interpreted appropriately
options.C: Repeat the intraoral scan with a changed acquisition path and improved surface management
options.D: Re-register the CBCT and optical surface datasets using stable landmarks before final planning

stem: A 39-year-old presents with bilateral masseter tenderness, pain on chewing and clicking on opening. Maximum unassisted opening is 43 mm, the click is reproducible and the pain is familiar on palpation. The patient reports prolonged stressful work shifts and frequent daytime clenching. There are no red flags or systemic symptoms.

theme: TMD: acute closed lock after reducing clicking
stem: A 29-year-old reports years of painless right TMJ clicking. This morning the click stopped, and mouth opening became limited to 24 mm with deviation to the right. A firm end feel is present, with no fever, facial swelling or recent trauma.
lead: What is the leading working diagnosis and initial management approach?

options.A: Trigeminal neuralgia; remove the high crown
options.B: Disc displacement with reduction; immediate irreversible equilibration
options.C: Disc displacement without reduction with limited opening; conservative care and appropriate review
options.D: Myofascial pain only; prescribe full arch crowns
options.E: Bilateral TMJ ankylosis requiring immediate joint replacement

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Disc displacement without reduction with limited opening; conservative care and appropriate review

RATIONALE: An abruptly disappearing click accompanied by restricted opening and deviation suggests disc displacement without reduction (closed lock). Early management is conservative and function-focused; irreversible occlusal alteration is not indicated solely for TMD symptoms.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Trigeminal neuralgia; remove the high crown B. Disc displacement with reduction; immediate irreversible equilibration D. Myofascial pain only; prescribe full arch crowns E. Bilateral TMJ ankylosis requiring immediate joint replacement

theme: Timing of crown after completed RCT
stem: A symptom-free mandibular first molar has completed root canal therapy and has a secure bonded core. Both marginal ridges are lost and cuspal coverage is planned. No swelling or sinus tract remains. A trainee cites Pratt et al. and suggests waiting exactly four months before crown preparation.
lead: Which interpretation best reflects the evidence?

options.A: Place definitive cuspal coverage promptly when infection, symptoms and restorability have been addressed
options.B: Never crown a root-filled molar
options.C: Use a post in every root to strengthen the crown
options.D: Wait four months so radiographic bone healing can always be demonstrated
options.E: Delay at least a year to check endodontic success

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Place definitive cuspal coverage promptly when infection, symptoms and restorability have been addressed

RATIONALE: Pratt et al. retrospectively associated crown placement AFTER four months with poorer survival than placement WITHIN four months. The study does not prescribe a four-month waiting period. Complete a sound definitive coronal seal and indicated cuspal coverage promptly when the tooth is clinically suitable.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: B. Never crown a root-filled molar C. Use a post in every root to strengthen the crown D. Wait four months so radiographic bone healing can always be demonstrated E. Delay at least a year to check endodontic success

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

EVIDENCE / SOURCE: Pratt et al., J Endod 2016; doi:10.1016/j.joen.2016.08.006

theme: Dental trauma: pulp status and root maturity
stem: An adult attends two hours after fracturing the incisal enamel and dentine of UR1. There is no pulp exposure, displacement, root fracture or other trauma. The tooth responds to sensibility tests and can be restored immediately.
lead: Which immediate plan best accounts for pulp exposure, root maturity and injury mechanism?

options.A: Restore an uncomplicated enamel-dentine fracture, document baseline and arrange injury-specific follow-up
options.B: Perform vital pulp therapy in an immature permanent tooth with recent traumatic pulp exposure
options.C: Commence routine root-canal treatment for every traumatized tooth immediately
options.D: Use a provisional restoration only and discharge without follow-up
options.E: Assess repositioning and risk-based endodontic follow-up for a mature intruded tooth

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Restore an uncomplicated enamel-dentine fracture, document baseline and arrange injury-specific follow-up

CLINICAL REASONING: Restore exposed dentine and arrange trauma-specific clinical and radiographic review, often at 6–8 weeks and 1 year for an uncomplicated crown fracture.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
B. Perform vital pulp therapy in an immature permanent tooth with recent traumatic pulp exposure — Favours maintaining vitality in a recently injured immature tooth with exposed pulp; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. Commence routine root-canal treatment for every traumatized tooth immediately — Not routinely indicated for simple uncomplicated injuries or all immature teeth; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Use a provisional restoration only and discharge without follow-up — Trauma requires follow-up for pulpal/periodontal sequelae; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. Assess repositioning and risk-based endodontic follow-up for a mature intruded tooth — Intrusion of a mature tooth requires specific repositioning and endodontic planning; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

stem: A 61-year-old who needs replacement of UL6 by an implant has a recent, technically acceptable panoramic radiograph showing limited residual height beneath the maxillary sinus. stem: A patient requests replacement of a missing maxillary anterior tooth. A full periodontal record, radiographs, diagnostic wax-up and cost discussion are available. stem: A 45-year-old teacher has bilateral temporalis pain, poor sleep, a history of tension headaches and intermittent pain on wide opening. A review reveals significant stress, widespread sensitivity and psychosocial interference with daily activities.
lead: Which management strategy is best supported?

options.A: Provide a full-coverage crown rehabilitation to reposition the mandible
options.B: Refer for arthrocentesis after excluding dental causes because maximum opening is 39 mm
options.C: Proceed with selective grinding until all lateral excursive contacts are eliminated, because splint failure proves an occlusal cause
options.D: Change the stabilisation splint to anterior repositioning and monitor headache frequency as the main endpoint
options.E: Reassess the chronic pain phenotype and provide reversible, multidisciplinary biopsychosocial management

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Reassess the chronic pain phenotype and provide reversible, multidisciplinary biopsychosocial management

DECISIVE FEATURE: Splint review remains reasonable for dental protection and comfort, but failure to abolish chronic pain is not evidence that grinding or extensive restoration will succeed.

RATIONALE: The clinical pattern is predominantly myogenous and biopsychosocial, not established surgically treatable intracapsular disease. In a chronic case without structural red flags, reversible treatment, education, physical rehabilitation and psychosocial pain management are more appropriate than irreversible occlusal changes.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: Full-crown rehabilitation would expose healthy teeth to irreversible harm.
B: Mildly limited opening without locking or structural evidence does not support arthrocentesis.
C: Splint non-response is not proof of a dental interference cause.
D: Anterior repositioning does not address the broader myogenous/psychosocial contributors.

stem: A posterior three-unit zirconia FDP debonded after only nine months. At removal the crown interiors show a glossy, uncontaminated zirconia surface, while substantial cement remains on the tooth preparations. Retention form is borderline but not grossly deficient; preparation height could be improved conservatively. The original laboratory had no documented airborne-particle abrasion or phosphate-monomer priming, and the dentist proposes treating zirconia with hydrofluoric acid and silane, as would be done for a glass ceramic. The patient seeks a durable remake without elective endodontics.
lead: Which corrective strategy best addresses the suspected interfacial failure?

options.A: Reassess fit and retention, control surface contamination and condition zirconia using appropriate abrasion and MDP chemistry
options.B: Use an MDP-containing primer without assessing surface cleanliness, contamination or macro-retention
options.C: Use the laboratory’s standard HF/silane protocol after airborne-particle abrasion to improve zirconia bonding
options.D: Replace the zirconia restoration with a lithium-disilicate crown to allow HF and silane bonding while retaining the current preparation form
options.E: Re-cement the zirconia restoration with a higher compressive-strength adhesive cement after cleaning both interfaces

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Reassess fit and retention, control surface contamination and condition zirconia using appropriate abrasion and MDP chemistry

DECISIVE FEATURE: Re-preparation to improve conventional retention may be reasonable, but surface chemistry cannot be ignored when the failure pattern points to the restoration–cement interface.

RATIONALE: Zirconia is not a glass-containing silica ceramic and is not routinely HF-etchable for durable bonding. Mechanical microroughening within manufacturer limits and phosphate monomer chemistry improve zirconia interaction. Retention, fit, contamination control and cement selection must also be reassessed.

ALTERNATIVES:
B: MDP chemistry helps but retention and surface control still need review.
C: HF/silane is appropriate for glass-containing ceramic, but not a reliable primary conditioning protocol for zirconia.
D: Changing the material solely to permit HF etching ignores connector suitability, occlusal load and existing zirconia retention conditions.
E: Cement strength alone does not address a glossy, poorly conditioned zirconia interface.

stem: A 39-year-old patient has localised palatal erosion affecting all six maxillary anterior teeth, exposing dentine and causing sensitivity with acidic drinks. stem: A 64-year-old wears a new mandibular RPD replacing both posterior segments. options.D: Polish the metal clasps and reduce their retentive undercuts without establishing whether inflammation is hygiene-related
options.E: Routinely substitute a more flexible acrylic framework to facilitate daily cleaning around the abutment

PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Target abutment and denture cleaning, reassess retainer cleanability and provide risk-based supportive review

DECISIVE FEATURE: Temporary antimicrobial use does not replace mechanical plaque removal, and automatic replacement of the prosthesis is not necessary when a local correction will do.

RATIONALE: Excellent prosthesis fit does not eliminate plaque retention or the need for maintenance. A specialist plan includes abutment risk assessment, personal hygiene support, review intervals and modification of plaque-retentive features where required.

B: Short-term antiseptic therapy may be useful but cannot substitute for mechanical hygiene and design assessment.

theme: Metal ceramic interface and framework mechanics
stem: A metal-ceramic prosthesis has fractured or delaminated. lead: Which course of action provides the strongest patient-specific justification among these alternatives?

options.A: Evaluate coefficient of thermal expansion compatibility and residual thermal stress
options.B: Control alloy oxidation and oxide-layer thickness to maintain the intended chemical bond
options.C: Improve framework and connector support beneath vulnerable porcelain
options.D: Correct an occlusal contact that repeatedly loads unsupported ceramic in shear
options.E: Investigate porosity, casting defect or contamination before committing to a material change

solution:

RATIONALE: Lateral contact and shear loading are the predominant failure drivers.

stem: A 58-year-old is planned for a guided posterior mandibular implant adjacent to a root-filled first premolar. CBCT and optical scans have been registered, and the virtual prosthesis has an acceptable crown axis. The surgical software reports a 2-mm clearance from the adjacent root, but metallic artefact affects the segmentation at that site and visual overlays disagree by nearly 1 mm in the area of the contact point. A printed guide appears to seat on the diagnostic cast, and the surgeon is tempted to proceed without independent verification because the plan is computer-generated.
lead: Which action most directly reduces the potentially preventable error?

options.A: Verify the CBCT–scan fusion and guide fit before revising implant position and maintaining anatomical safety
options.B: Increase the apparent virtual clearance to 3 mm without revisiting the fusion, because error will then be absorbed
options.C: Decrease the clearance allowance because the adjacent tooth is root-filled
options.D: Change from a fully guided to a pilot-guided technique but preserve the same digital registration and implant plan
options.E: Proceed because digital planning eliminates registration and guide-transfer error once the overlay is accepted by the software

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Verify the CBCT–scan fusion and guide fit before revising implant position and maintaining anatomical safety

DECISIVE FEATURE: Repeating CBCT may be needed if the volume is inadequate but simply resampling without checking registration does not address the immediate source of uncertainty.

RATIONALE: Guided surgery accumulates uncertainty from scan quality, segmentation, surface-to-volume fusion, guide manufacturing and transfer. The apparent 2-mm root clearance cannot be trusted when disagreement approaches 1 mm in the critical direction. Independent verification and plan correction take precedence.

ALTERNATIVES:
B: An unverified fusion can invalidate a nominal 3-mm buffer.
C: Endodontic status does not lower the safety margin needed for an adjacent root.
D: Reducing guide constraint does not correct uncertain fusion or anatomical relationship.
E: Software acceptance does not prove accurate registration or guide transfer.

theme: Hypodontia: timing of implants in a growing patient
stem: A 15-year-old with a congenitally absent maxillary lateral incisor has a harmonious smile after orthodontics. A definitive single implant is requested immediately. Serial facial and dental growth records suggest vertical dentoalveolar development is still ongoing.
lead: What is the most appropriate planning recommendation?

options.A: Avoid any temporary replacement until age 30
options.B: Place an implant immediately because osseointegration always tracks eruption
options.C: Provide a reversible or tooth-preserving provisional replacement and defer implant timing until growth is adequately complete
options.D: Extract the contralateral lateral incisor for symmetry
options.E: Increase implant diameter to prevent infra-occlusion

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Provide a reversible or tooth-preserving provisional replacement and defer implant timing until growth is adequately complete

RATIONALE: An implant behaves like an ankylosed unit rather than erupting with neighbouring teeth, so placement during residual vertical growth risks infra-occlusion. Interim options should be considered without a universal age cut-off.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Avoid any temporary replacement until age 30 B. Place an implant immediately because osseointegration always tracks eruption D. Extract the contralateral lateral incisor for symmetry E. Increase implant diameter to prevent infra-occlusion

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

EVIDENCE / SOURCE: Hypodontia interdisciplinary planning and implant timing

stem: A 65-year-old has four parallel posterior implants and is scheduled for a screw-retained splinted prosthesis. theme: AI versus fluorosis: minimally invasive treatment
stem: An 18-year-old reports diffuse fine white horizontal striations on corresponding anterior teeth since eruption. Enamel thickness is normal, the surface is smooth and hard, there is no hypersensitivity or attrition, and exposure history is compatible with mild dental fluorosis. The patient wants a small aesthetic improvement.
lead: What is the most reasonable initial treatment discussion?

options.A: Porcelain veneers on every tooth without evaluating minimal interventions
options.B: Extensive full coverage crowns as mandatory first-line care
options.C: Initial conservative counselling and consideration of supervised microabrasion or related low-invasive approaches based on lesion depth
options.D: Routine root canal treatment on all affected teeth
options.E: Immediate extraction and implants

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Initial conservative counselling and consideration of supervised microabrasion or related low-invasive approaches based on lesion depth

RATIONALE: Mild fluorosis with intact enamel should initially be approached conservatively. Non-operative options, microabrasion and/or infiltration can be considered selectively; treatment choice depends on lesion depth, risk and preference.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Porcelain veneers on every tooth without evaluating minimal interventions B. Extensive full coverage crowns as mandatory first-line care D. Routine root canal treatment on all affected teeth E. Immediate extraction and implants

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

EVIDENCE / SOURCE: Enamel defect aesthetic management; DSFE ES 10.3

stem: A root-filled premolar is considered for definitive restoration. The clinical crown has been dismantled sufficiently to assess the remaining dentine. Post type, ferrule, periodontal support and crown-root ratio are documented, along with any implications of crown lengthening or orthodontic extrusion. A strategic root lacks coronal ferrule but has a long favourable root, healthy periodontium and suitable orthodontic extrusion potential.

options.A: Use orthodontic extrusion to establish ferrule while preserving supporting tissues
options.B: Avoid repeated post enlargement when the remaining root is structurally nonrestorable
options.C: Reconsider crown lengthening if the required bone removal would sacrifice attachment on the tooth and neighbours
options.D: Use a post only to retain a core where insufficient coronal tooth tissue remains
options.E: Preserve a sound circumferential ferrule and restore without adding an unnecessary post

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Use orthodontic extrusion to establish ferrule while preserving supporting tissues

DECISIVE FEATURE: A strategic root lacks coronal ferrule but has a long favourable root, healthy periodontium and suitable orthodontic extrusion potential.

RATIONALE: Extrusion can expose sound tooth structure without excessive periodontal sacrifice.

stem: A young adult with a developmental dental anomaly seeks an attractive, durable restorative solution. Orthodontic records, tooth vitality, enamel quality, jaw growth and periodontal support have been assessed. The treatment must address long-term reparability and avoid unnecessary loss of otherwise sound tissue. The lateral incisor space is too narrow for a properly proportioned restoration and roots converge despite visible crown spacing. Both a staged and a direct approach have been discussed, and neither is excluded solely by cost or operator access.
lead: Which course of action provides the strongest patient-specific justification among these alternatives?

options.A: Retain a suitable primary tooth temporarily with monitoring while definitive timing is reconsidered
options.B: Plan a multidisciplinary stage of orthodontic redistribution before selecting prosthesis form
options.C: Consider conventional full coverage only where severe structural deficiency limits reliable additive solutions
options.D: Offer additive direct composite with maintenance and potential later modification
options.E: Plan adhesive indirect restorations only after assessing the quality and amount of bondable enamel

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Plan a multidisciplinary stage of orthodontic redistribution before selecting prosthesis form

DECISIVE FEATURE: The lateral incisor space is too narrow for a properly proportioned restoration and roots converge despite visible crown spacing.

RATIONALE: Root and restorative-space correction should precede fixed prosthesis selection.

ALTERNATIVES:

E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Hypoplastic amelogenesis imperfecta has created adequate but thin, reasonably mineralised enamel on vital teeth and the patient wants definitive indirect colour stability. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A specialist reviewing a referral must decide how an investigation or published estimate should influence prosthodontic management. Test reliability, validity, prevalence, effect size and clinical benefit are kept distinct; routine intervention is not justified simply because a reported p-value is small. options.A: Prefer an additional independent test when the first test does not adequately rule out disease
options.B: Recognise high repeatability without assuming the observations are accurate
options.C: Revise the clinical plan when the investigation is technically compromised rather than interpreting it as definitive
options.D: Distinguish statistical significance from a clinically useful effect and check confidence intervals
options.E: Interpret a positive result in light of the pre-test probability and the test likelihood ratio

RATIONALE: A negative imperfect test cannot be used alone to exclude a condition with high pre-test probability.

theme: Risk-based fixed versus implant versus removable
stem: A patient requests replacement of a missing maxillary anterior tooth. A full periodontal record, radiographs, diagnostic wax-up and cost discussion are available. The plan must balance neighbouring tooth preservation, ridge morphology, aesthetic risk, age and long-term maintenance. Both neighbours are intact and enamel-rich, the occlusal scheme permits a single retainer and the patient favours reversibility. Two options have been discussed at the referral visit;
lead: Which management strategy best addresses the dominant limitation in this patient?

options.A: Provide a removable prosthesis when the patient prioritises reversibility and cannot undertake invasive care
options.B: Plan a delayed implant crown after correcting ridge and soft-tissue limitations
options.C: Offer an enamel-retained cantilever resin-bonded bridge as a conservative definitive or interim option
options.D: Use a conventional tooth-supported bridge when adjacent teeth already require full-coverage reconstruction
options.E: Observe without replacement after discussing function, aesthetics, spacing and longer-term consequences

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Offer an enamel-retained cantilever resin-bonded bridge as a conservative definitive or interim option

DECISIVE FEATURE: Both neighbours are intact and enamel-rich, the occlusal scheme permits a single retainer and the patient favours reversibility.

RATIONALE: Preserving intact teeth with adhesive cantilever design gives a favourable risk-benefit balance.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Medical complexity and inability to attend staged treatment make grafting and implant placement unacceptable; the patient accepts a removable device. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: An adult with a high smile line requests implant treatment but has a thin buccal ridge and inadequate restorative space that needs correction. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Both adjacent teeth have failing crowns and require replacement independently; the pontic span is short and periodontal support is stable. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A low-demand patient is comfortable with the space, occlusal contacts are stable and treatment would bring little patient-centred benefit. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A patient with a severely resorbed edentulous arch remains dissatisfied with removable treatment. theme: Behavioural and interdisciplinary control of tooth wear
stem: A complex tooth-wear patient has received dental preventive advice, but the exposure pattern involves lifestyle, systemic illness or medications. The dentist must set a feasible pathway that the patient can implement and monitor over time. An older patient has dry mouth following antidepressant and antimuscarinic therapy with rapidly increasing root exposure.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Coordinate ongoing repairable restorative protection when risk control is partial but functional symptoms are significant
options.B: Review xerogenic medication burden and salivary management with the prescriber where feasible

options.D: Address frequent acidic drinks with timing, substitution and post-exposure advice
options.E: Refer suspected uncontrolled reflux or eating-disorder-related acid exposure for appropriate medical evaluation

solution:

RATIONALE: Saliva and medications alter erosive and cariogenic risks.

stem: A partially covered tooth requires an indirect restoration with adhesive retention. stem: A patient with an implant-supported prosthesis presents for treatment planning or review. The prosthesis has been assessed for passivity, component fit, access-channel location, tissue support, occlusion, plaque access and the anticipated need for maintenance or future modification. A multiunit bridge has a gap on the one-screw test and one cylinder does not fully seat until the distal screw is tightened. The patient returns to discuss a definitive plan after the diagnostic appointment; the clinician now has to reconcile the clinical evidence with expected maintenance and prognosis. The referral includes a clear account of the principal problem; the patient asks which option should be prioritised before further treatment.
lead: What is the best next clinical decision?

options.A: Reassess implant angulation or use a suitable angulated component only if a safe retrievable restoration can be designed
options.B: Develop peri-implant soft tissues with an appropriately shaped provisional restoration before final crown fabrication
options.C: Verify framework passivity and fit before tightening or loading across multiple implants
options.D: Correct excessive emergence contour and allow hygiene access before treating inflammation as refractory disease
options.E: Use a retrievable screw-retained design when access emerges favourably and prosthetic support is adequate

RATIONALE: Tightening must not be used to force a misfitting prosthesis onto fixtures.

stem: A young adult with a developmental dental anomaly seeks an attractive, durable restorative solution. Orthodontic records, tooth vitality, enamel quality, jaw growth and periodontal support have been assessed. stem: A patient requests extensive fixed prosthodontic reconstruction. A charted medical history, current medication list, caries record and periodontal measurements are provided. options.B: Consider a cleansable removable or simplified treatment plan when self-care and adaptation are limiting

theme: Peri-implant tissue inflammation and emergence contour
stem: A cement-retained posterior implant crown has increasing bleeding and probing depths. Radiographs show early crestal change. The crown is markedly overcontoured submucosally, cement is suspected below the margin and floss cannot enter the embrasure.
lead: Which is the most appropriate first-line restorative contribution?

options.A: Assess and manage possible excess cement and correct inaccessible emergence contours while diagnosing and treating peri-implant disease
options.B: Grind the occlusal surface only and close the case
options.C: Increase gingival bulk with a wider overcontoured crown
options.D: Place a second implant in the same pocket
options.E: Ignore the crown and prescribe antiseptics indefinitely

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Assess and manage possible excess cement and correct inaccessible emergence contours while diagnosing and treating peri-implant disease

RATIONALE: Residual cement and uncleanable emergence contours may perpetuate inflammation. A coordinated peri-implant assessment and correction of local prosthetic risk factors is needed, not symptomatic care alone.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: B. Grind the occlusal surface only and close the case C. Increase gingival bulk with a wider overcontoured crown D. Place a second implant in the same pocket E. Ignore the crown and prescribe antiseptics indefinitely

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

stem: A 28-year-old sustains a complicated crown-root fracture of UL1. The fracture extends palatally below the gingival margin, while the facial tooth structure appears nearly intact. CBCT excludes a vertical root fracture; the root is long enough for potential restoration but the palatal margin approaches the crestal bone and the periodontal support is otherwise good. The patient has a high smile line, and both surgical crown lengthening and orthodontic extrusion are being discussed. The adjacent incisors have intact interdental papillae and favourable bone levels.
lead: Which consideration most strongly guides the restorability plan?

options.A: Whether a post can be made longer than the clinical crown regardless of the final margin location
options.B: Whether an adequate ferrule and maintainable supracrestal tissue attachment can be established without unacceptable aesthetic or periodontal consequences
options.C: Whether a custom cast post can achieve at least two-thirds root engagement after endodontic treatment
options.D: Attempt adhesive fragment reattachment first while postponing evaluation of the subcrestal palatal margin
options.E: Whether the provisional crown can maintain the pre-injury incisal relationship without needing orthodontic space creation

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Whether an adequate ferrule and maintainable supracrestal tissue attachment can be established without unacceptable aesthetic or periodontal consequences

DECISIVE FEATURE: Post selection cannot overcome a biologically inaccessible fracture margin or absent ferrule; definitive restorability is a periodontal–restorative decision.

RATIONALE: The treatment is constrained by the relationship of the fracture margin to bone, the ability to create a ferrule and the periodontal/aesthetic consequences of exposing the margin. Orthodontic extrusion may preserve papillae better than extensive anterior crown lengthening, but requires time and sufficient remaining root length.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: Post dimensions alone cannot resolve a subcrestal margin.
C: Post retention may matter but does not overcome the inaccessible fracture margin and missing ferrule.
D: A temporary attachment may be possible, but cannot establish long-term restorability without margin and ferrule assessment.
E: Occlusal space matters, but the subcrestal margin and ferrule are primary determinants of restorability.

stem: A root-filled premolar is considered for definitive restoration. The clinical crown has been dismantled sufficiently to assess the remaining dentine. stem: A patient has undergone rehabilitation for erosive wear and now requires evaluation of complications, material choices and maintenance. The clinician knows the initial aetiology, bonded substrate, occlusal scheme and baseline photographs. The patient reports continued erosion, but paired scans show no measurable loss since prevention was introduced. The patient wishes to preserve future options where possible but would accept a more extensive treatment if demonstrably necessary.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Assess periodontal effects of deep margins before extending preparation
options.B: Investigate unexplained post-treatment pulpal sensitivity and exclude irreversible pulpal pathology
options.C: Use longitudinal wear measurements and preventive review to distinguish stable repair needs from active disease
options.D: Repair local direct composite defects and reassess loading and acid exposure
options.E: Review the adhesive substrate and restorative thickness before changing to an indirect material

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Use longitudinal wear measurements and preventive review to distinguish stable repair needs from active disease

DECISIVE FEATURE: The patient reports continued erosion, but paired scans show no measurable loss since prevention was introduced.

RATIONALE: Serial monitoring avoids premature extensive re-treatment.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Gingival inflammation persists around overdeep crown margins despite good hygiene and no supragingival plaque source. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

theme: Root caries: xerostomia and active lesions
stem: A dependent 78-year-old takes several xerogenic medications and has three soft active cervical/root lesions on strategic RPD abutments. Salivary flow is low, plaque control is limited and the carer can assist with daily care.
lead: What should the initial treatment plan prioritise?

options.A: Use occlusal equilibration to arrest root lesions
options.B: Cosmetic tooth whitening only
options.C: Individualised high-caries-risk prevention including appropriate high-fluoride treatment, salivary review and carer-assisted plaque control
options.D: Delay all prevention until the lesions cavitate widely
options.E: Remove all RPD clasps and leave the lesions untreated

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Individualised high-caries-risk prevention including appropriate high-fluoride treatment, salivary review and carer-assisted plaque control

RATIONALE: Active root caries in xerostomia is an elevated disease-risk scenario. Caries arrest and prevention require fluoride exposure, plaque/diet/medication review, and practical support; cavitated lesions may also need operative repair.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Use occlusal equilibration to arrest root lesions B. Cosmetic tooth whitening only D. Delay all prevention until the lesions cavitate widely E. Remove all RPD clasps and leave the lesions untreated

theme: Bridge design: span and abutment loading
stem: A 46-year-old has a long maxillary posterior edentulous span. The proposed tooth-supported bridge would join a periodontally stable premolar to a molar with a short clinical crown. Diagnostic casts show a steep lateral interference on the molar and anticipated high connector loading. The patient asks the dentist to proceed without additional assessment.
lead: Which is the strongest planning response?

options.A: Assess span mechanics, abutment retention and excursions before selecting a bridge or alternative
options.B: Add a cantilever pontic without changing load assessment
options.C: Prepare the short molar more conically to increase retention
options.D: Proceed because periodontal stability alone ensures bridge success
options.E: Shorten the pontic occlusogingivally and ignore the terminal abutment

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Assess span mechanics, abutment retention and excursions before selecting a bridge or alternative

RATIONALE: Long spans flex more, loading is affected by occlusal scheme and abutment geometry, and a short molar may have poor resistance form. The correct choice is to reassess whether a fixed tooth-supported design is predictable before irreversible preparation.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: B. Add a cantilever pontic without changing load assessment C. Prepare the short molar more conically to increase retention D. Proceed because periodontal stability alone ensures bridge success E. Shorten the pontic occlusogingivally and ignore the terminal abutment

theme: Anterior tooth proportions and gingival architecture
stem: A patient with anterior aesthetic dissatisfaction is evaluated with frontal and dynamic smile photographs, diagnostic casts, clinical crown proportions and gingival level assessment. The definitive plan should distinguish tooth-shape errors from gingival architecture and altered tooth position. A large defective labio-incisal composite has failed repeatedly, abundant enamel remains and the patient accepts a conservative indirect restoration. options.B: Use additive reshaping to correct an isolated tooth-proportion discrepancy without destructive preparation

options.D: Evaluate gingival-margin correction where altered passive eruption or crown-length discrepancy is the dominant concern

RATIONALE: An enamel-bonded indirect solution can balance durability and tissue preservation.
