theme: Systemic and oral disease before rehabilitation
stem: A patient requests extensive fixed prosthodontic reconstruction. A charted medical history, current medication list, caries record and periodontal measurements are provided. Moderate dementia, declining dexterity and recurrent plaque-associated mucositis make a complex connector system unrealistic despite the patient’s idealised aesthetic request. The patient returns to discuss a definitive plan after the diagnostic appointment; the clinician now has to reconcile the clinical evidence with expected maintenance and prognosis. Both a staged and a direct approach have been discussed, and neither is excluded solely by cost or operator access.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Consider a cleansable removable or simplified treatment plan when self-care and adaptation are limiting
options.B: Coordinate with the medical team to assess medication-related surgical risk before proposing extractions or implants
options.C: Provide staged direct repairs while assessing salivary function and instituting intensive prevention
options.D: First control active disease and modifiable risk factors, then re-evaluate the definitive restorative plan
options.E: Proceed to definitive fixed restoration after documenting periodontal stability and appropriate long-term maintenance

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Consider a cleansable removable or simplified treatment plan when self-care and adaptation are limiting

DECISIVE FEATURE: Moderate dementia, declining dexterity and recurrent plaque-associated mucositis make a complex connector system unrealistic despite the patient’s idealised aesthetic request.

RATIONALE: A prosthesis is unsuccessful if its hygiene, function and maintenance exceed the patient’s capabilities.

ALTERNATIVES:
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Oncological-dose antiresorptive treatment is current, a strategic tooth is painful but potentially restorable and extractions have been proposed solely to simplify implant planning. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Radiotherapy has produced profound xerostomia and multiple new cervical lesions, but most teeth remain restorable and the patient has not received salivary or fluoride intervention. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Several teeth have active cavitated root caries and bleeding pockets despite acceptable radiographic root lengths; the patient wants an immediate full-arch bridge. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Periodontal therapy is complete, plaque scores are low, pocketing has resolved, crown margins can be cleansed and the patient accepts recalls. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A mandibular Kennedy Class II RPD is planned for a unilateral distal-extension saddle. A mesial rest on the terminal abutment, a suitable clasp assembly and a rigid major connector are provided. The practitioner wants to improve resistance to rotation of the free-end base away from the tissues.
lead: Where is an indirect retainer best placed?

options.A: On a tissue-covered flange with no tooth support
options.B: Only on the same terminal abutment as the saddle rest
options.C: As an occlusal interference on the opposing arch
options.D: On the distal extension acrylic directly adjacent to the last molar
options.E: As an appropriately prepared rest on a suitable tooth as far anterior to the fulcrum line as practical

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — As an appropriately prepared rest on a suitable tooth as far anterior to the fulcrum line as practical

RATIONALE: The distal extension can rotate about a fulcrum through primary rests. An indirect retainer placed anterior to that fulcrum, with sound tooth support and appropriate connector rigidity, resists lifting of the base.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. On a tissue-covered flange with no tooth support B. Only on the same terminal abutment as the saddle rest C. As an occlusal interference on the opposing arch D. On the distal extension acrylic directly adjacent to the last molar

stem: A specialist reviewing a referral must decide how an investigation or published estimate should influence prosthodontic management. Test reliability, validity, prevalence, effect size and clinical benefit are kept distinct; routine intervention is not justified simply because a reported p-value is small. Two examiners classify lesions almost identically, yet both consistently miss lesions confirmed by an independent reference method. The patient returns to discuss a definitive plan after the diagnostic appointment; the clinician now has to reconcile the clinical evidence with expected maintenance and prognosis.
lead: Which course of action provides the strongest patient-specific justification among these alternatives?

options.A: Prefer an additional independent test when the first test does not adequately rule out disease
options.B: Interpret a positive result in light of the pre-test probability and the test likelihood ratio
options.C: Distinguish statistical significance from a clinically useful effect and check confidence intervals
options.D: Revise the clinical plan when the investigation is technically compromised rather than interpreting it as definitive
options.E: Recognise high repeatability without assuming the observations are accurate

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Recognise high repeatability without assuming the observations are accurate

DECISIVE FEATURE: Two examiners classify lesions almost identically, yet both consistently miss lesions confirmed by an independent reference method.

RATIONALE: Agreement establishes reliability, not diagnostic validity.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Clinical suspicion for a cracked tooth is high but one transillumination test is negative and the test sensitivity is imperfect. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: An apparently accurate caries detection test is positive in a very low-prevalence asymptomatic group; the finding conflicts with clinical inspection. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A 58-year-old receives a new metal–ceramic crown on UR4, but the soft-tissue margin becomes inflamed in the weeks after cementation. The crown has a slightly over-contoured emergence profile and an interproximal finish line 1.5 mm subgingivally; a small amount of residual cement is visible on bitewing imaging. Periodontal tissues were healthy before treatment, and the patient has good plaque-control skills. The impression and try-in records show that a more supragingival finish line would have been aesthetically acceptable. The referring clinician asks whether repeated chlorhexidine courses are likely to resolve the problem.
lead: What correction best addresses the likely cause while conserving future periodontal health?

options.A: Provide crown lengthening surgery to move the margin supragingivally before checking cement residue or contours
options.B: Remove cement, correct contour and margin problems, and remake the crown if local modification cannot achieve cleanability
options.C: Perform full-thickness periodontal flap surgery before evaluating the crown contour
options.D: Prescribe chlorhexidine indefinitely and leave the contour unchanged
options.E: Introduce a longer proximal contact so that plaque is excluded from the papilla

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Remove cement, correct contour and margin problems, and remake the crown if local modification cannot achieve cleanability

DECISIVE FEATURE: Periodontal surgery may occasionally be needed for restorative margin access, but it would be premature before eliminating removable local irritants.

RATIONALE: An accessible, cleansable contour and biologically appropriate margin are integral to gingival health. Residual cement and over-contouring are modifiable local factors; anti-plaque drugs are not a substitute for their correction. The need for remaking should be determined by whether the current crown can be made cleansable without compromising fit.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: Surgery is premature before correcting local prosthesis-related irritants.
C: Surgery is unnecessary before removing direct irritants and re-evaluating.
D: Chemical plaque reduction cannot permanently neutralise retained cement or over-contour.
E: A longer contact does not correct an over-contoured subgingival margin.

stem: An anterior ceramic crown is judged an excellent match beside the contralateral tooth in daylight and in the dental surgery. Under the warm restaurant lighting at dinner, the crown looks conspicuously brighter. When the same teeth are checked under the original daylight source the mismatch vanishes.
lead: Which optical phenomenon best accounts for the observation?

options.A: Metamerism due to differences in spectral reflectance
options.B: Increased chroma independent of illumination
options.C: A vertical dimension error
options.D: A change in ceramic surface roughness occurring only after dark
options.E: A stable excess of value under all light sources

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Metamerism due to differences in spectral reflectance

RATIONALE: The match depends on the illuminant: two objects can appear alike under one light but different under another (metamerism). If all environments showed a consistently lighter crown, a value mismatch would be a better description.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: B. Increased chroma independent of illumination C. A vertical dimension error D. A change in ceramic surface roughness occurring only after dark E. A stable excess of value under all light sources

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

EVIDENCE / SOURCE: Colour science in prosthodontics; DSFE ES 10.1

stem: A dentist is planning a missing posterior tooth replacement. Existing periapical and panoramic imaging, proposed restorative emergence and adjacent anatomical structures are reviewed. theme: Diagnostic uncertainty in a painful posterior tooth
stem: A previously restored molar has intermittent pain on chewing. Cold sensibility, percussion, six-point periodontal probing, bite testing and an intra-oral radiograph are available. The clinician needs to distinguish a fractured cusp, pulpal disease, a vertical root fracture and non-odontogenic pain without committing prematurely to irreversible care. Spontaneous pain lasts hours, cold provokes prolonged lingering pain, and a protected cusp no longer explains the symptoms.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Remove the existing restoration under magnification, assess the crack, and protect the cusp provisionally
options.B: Assess the isolated deep periodontal defect and root-level fracture evidence before attempting reconstruction
options.C: Treat the confirmed symptomatic irreversible pulpitis before planning definitive cuspal coverage
options.D: Obtain targeted additional investigation because the initial tests are conflicting and the management choice would change
options.E: Reassess the occlusion and muscular pain source before removing a technically sound restoration

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Treat the confirmed symptomatic irreversible pulpitis before planning definitive cuspal coverage

DECISIVE FEATURE: Spontaneous pain lasts hours, cold provokes prolonged lingering pain, and a protected cusp no longer explains the symptoms.

RATIONALE: The pulpal diagnosis has advanced beyond an uncomplicated cracked vital cusp.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A sharp pain occurs specifically on release of pressure over the distolingual cusp, cold response is short and six-point probing is 2–3 mm throughout. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: There is a narrow isolated 10-mm pocket next to a root-filled tooth and a J-shaped radiolucency after repeated post debonding. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A recently traumatised tooth tests negative to cold but has normal periapical imaging, uncertain pulpal status and no swelling. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The tooth has no localised bite-test response and reproducible pain follows masseter loading, with matched nocturnal clenching and normal dental investigations. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

theme: TMD muscular pain versus neuropathic pain
stem: A 43-year-old describes episodic unilateral facial discomfort and requests occlusal adjustment because a previous crown feels high. The clinician assesses jaw function, familiar pain reproduction on muscle palpation, opening pattern, neurological triggers and potential red flags before selecting reversible versus irreversible care. Pain consists of seconds-long electric-shock episodes triggered by light touch to the cheek and brushing, separated by pain-free periods, without muscular familiar-pain reproduction.
lead: Which is the most appropriate next management approach?

options.A: Education and conservative management of clinically supported myalgia
options.B: Permanent selective grinding of multiple tooth surfaces
options.C: Assess and refer for a trigeminal-neuralgia-type neuropathic pattern
options.D: Start irreversible TMJ surgery without an established joint diagnosis
options.E: Provide full-mouth rehabilitation to eliminate occlusal interferences

stem: A maxillary first premolar pontic lies within the patient's full smile and normal speech display. The edentulous ridge is moderately convex, with healthy keratinised tissue and enough clearance for cleaning devices. The patient needs an attractive facial emergence without an uncleanable full saddle.
lead: Which design provides a reasonable aesthetic-hygiene balance?

options.A: Deep concave pontic wrapping round the ridge
options.B: A cantilever connector touching the mucosa without a pontic
options.C: Broad full ridge-lap pontic
options.D: Modified ridge-lap with convex cleansable lingual tissue surface
options.E: Sanitary pontic 4 mm above the visible ridge

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Modified ridge-lap with convex cleansable lingual tissue surface

RATIONALE: A modified ridge-lap achieves facial resemblance to a natural tooth while limiting ridge contact and making the lingual surface convex and cleansable. A full ridge-lap traps plaque and is generally undesirable.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Deep concave pontic wrapping round the ridge B. A cantilever connector touching the mucosa without a pontic C. Broad full ridge-lap pontic E. Sanitary pontic 4 mm above the visible ridge

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

EVIDENCE / SOURCE: Fixed prosthodontic pontic morphology

stem: A posterior or anterior restoration has failed and an indirect replacement is proposed. Clinical examination describes the available clearance, enamel distribution, bonding substrate, occlusal loading and aesthetic zone. The vital premolar has predominantly sound enamel, adequate occlusal thickness for a bonded onlay and a moderate aesthetic requirement. Two options have been discussed at the referral visit;
lead: Which management strategy best addresses the dominant limitation in this patient?

options.A: Use additive direct composite when minimal intervention, reversibility and future repair are dominant
options.B: Gain additional restorative clearance or revise the preparation design before choosing a material
options.C: Use a monolithic zirconia restoration with manufacturer-specified thickness and suitable conditioning for a high-load site
options.D: Prefer a metal restoration where clearance and load make a thin, durable restoration advantageous
options.E: Choose an adhesively retained lithium disilicate partial-coverage restoration where supported by enamel and adequate clearance

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Choose an adhesively retained lithium disilicate partial-coverage restoration where supported by enamel and adequate clearance.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: The vital premolar has predominantly sound enamel, adequate occlusal thickness for a bonded onlay and a moderate aesthetic requirement.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Enamel-rich adhesive partial coverage offers tissue conservation with adequate ceramic support.

theme: Adhesive surface treatment: glass ceramic versus zirconia
stem: A monolithic zirconia crown with adequate preparation form is intended for adhesive cementation. The laboratory confirms that its internal surface has not been conditioned. The clinician must select zirconia-compatible pretreatment.
lead: Which surface-conditioning strategy is best matched to the identified ceramic?

options.A: Use a material-specific hydrofluoric acid etch and silane before adhesive resin luting
options.B: Use controlled airborne-particle abrasion and an MDP-containing primer/cement
options.C: Use phosphoric acid alone as the sole bonding strategy for all ceramics
options.D: Treat both glass ceramic and zirconia with the same routine hydrofluoric acid sequence
options.E: Lute without surface treatment solely because the crown is accurately fitting

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Use controlled airborne-particle abrasion and an MDP-containing primer/cement

CLINICAL REASONING: Zirconia bonding is optimised by appropriate controlled surface roughening plus phosphate-containing chemistry.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
A. Use a material-specific hydrofluoric acid etch and silane before adhesive resin luting — For silica-based etchable glass ceramics, following the specific manufacturer instructions; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. Use phosphoric acid alone as the sole bonding strategy for all ceramics — Phosphoric acid alone does not replace material-specific treatment; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Treat both glass ceramic and zirconia with the same routine hydrofluoric acid sequence — Zirconia is not a glass ceramic and is not treated by standard HF etching; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. Lute without surface treatment solely because the crown is accurately fitting — Mechanical fit does not remove need to evaluate adhesion; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

theme: Kennedy Class II: indirect retention versus cross-arch stability
stem: The technician proposes a broad, rigid lingual bar/plate connector uniting the tooth-supported and extension sides of a Kennedy Class II design. The question concerns resistance to horizontal rocking across the arch, not disengagement from the ridge.
lead: What is the principal mechanical purpose of the described RPD feature?

options.A: Indirect retention resisting lifting of a distal-extension base
options.B: Cross-arch stabilisation by a rigid major connector and reciprocal components
options.C: Direct clasp retention resisting removal along the path of insertion
options.D: Tissue support provided solely by a posterior acrylic saddle
options.E: Tooth-supported occlusal rest preventing vertical settling

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Cross-arch stabilisation by a rigid major connector and reciprocal components

CLINICAL REASONING: Rigid major connectors and bracing components provide cross-arch stability.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
A. Indirect retention resisting lifting of a distal-extension base — A rest anterior to the fulcrum line can resist distal-base rotation away from the ridge; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. Direct clasp retention resisting removal along the path of insertion — Clasp engages an appropriate undercut against withdrawal; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Tissue support provided solely by a posterior acrylic saddle — Soft tissue may support extension base but does not describe the stated metal feature; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. Tooth-supported occlusal rest preventing vertical settling — Rest limits movement toward tissue, not indirect lifting; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

stem: A well-maintained anterior maxillary implant has 4 mm of keratinised mucosa but a thin buccal contour and aesthetic show-through of the grey abutment. There is no brushing discomfort or inflammation.
lead: Which soft-tissue intervention addresses the actual peri-implant problem?

options.A: Non-surgical plaque control and site-specific hygiene instruction
options.B: Increase the width of keratinised mucosa with a free gingival graft
options.C: Increase mucosal thickness for contour using connective tissue grafting
options.D: Remove the healthy implant and graft the ridge
options.E: Reduce the crown emergence contour without assessing the soft tissue

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Increase mucosal thickness for contour using connective tissue grafting

CLINICAL REASONING: The problem is a thin tissue phenotype and contour, for which connective-tissue augmentation is more targeted.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
A. Non-surgical plaque control and site-specific hygiene instruction — First line for plaque-associated inflammation with sufficient keratinised tissue; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

D. Remove the healthy implant and graft the ridge — Not justified for a healthy osseointegrated implant; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

theme: Localised tooth wear and the Dahl concept
stem: A 42-year-old has moderate anterior erosive wear, but records show no progression over four years. The patient has neither sensitivity nor aesthetic concern and posterior support is unchanged. Diet and reflux factors are being managed.
lead: Which management plan best balances symptoms, interocclusal space and preservation?

options.A: Continue prevention and monitor without restoration
options.B: Use localised additive direct composite with a monitored Dahl approach
options.C: Prepare the entire dentition for immediate full-coverage crowns
options.D: Plan a staged full-arch rehabilitation with a diagnostic provisional occlusal trial
options.E: Extract the most worn teeth and replace them with implants

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Continue prevention and monitor without restoration

CLINICAL REASONING: Stable asymptomatic wear alone does not mandate operative treatment.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
B. Use localised additive direct composite with a monitored Dahl approach — Appropriate to localised symptomatic anterior wear and reduced space with posterior support; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. Prepare the entire dentition for immediate full-coverage crowns — More invasive than needed for localised wear; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Plan a staged full-arch rehabilitation with a diagnostic provisional occlusal trial — Indicated for generalised complex wear after diagnosis, a functional provisional trial and informed consent; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

theme: Dental trauma: pulp status and root maturity
stem: A 9-year-old sustains a crown fracture of a permanent incisor with a small traumatic pulp exposure. The root has an open apex, the tooth can be isolated, and the child presents within hours. There are no signs of pulp necrosis.
lead: Which immediate plan best accounts for pulp exposure, root maturity and injury mechanism?

options.A: Restore an uncomplicated enamel-dentine fracture, document baseline and arrange injury-specific follow-up
options.B: Perform vital pulp therapy in an immature permanent tooth with recent traumatic pulp exposure
options.C: Commence routine root-canal treatment for every traumatized tooth immediately
options.D: Use a provisional restoration only and discharge without follow-up
options.E: Assess repositioning and risk-based endodontic follow-up for a mature intruded tooth

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Perform vital pulp therapy in an immature permanent tooth with recent traumatic pulp exposure

CLINICAL REASONING: Conservative vital pulp therapy supports continuing root development in an immature permanent tooth.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
A. Restore an uncomplicated enamel-dentine fracture, document baseline and arrange injury-specific follow-up — Appropriate when no pulp exposure or additional injury is identified; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. Commence routine root-canal treatment for every traumatized tooth immediately — Not routinely indicated for simple uncomplicated injuries or all immature teeth; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Use a provisional restoration only and discharge without follow-up — Trauma requires follow-up for pulpal/periodontal sequelae; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. Assess repositioning and risk-based endodontic follow-up for a mature intruded tooth — Intrusion of a mature tooth requires specific repositioning and endodontic planning; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

theme: Cracked tooth, irreversible pulpitis and vertical root fracture
stem: A 56-year-old has severe lingering pain for minutes after cold stimulation, spontaneous nocturnal pain and no isolated periodontal defects. A deep carious lesion is present; there is no bite-release pain or radiographic evidence of root fracture.

options.C: Cracked tooth with likely vital pulp
options.D: Vertical root fracture

stem: A 31-year-old has peg-shaped lateral incisors already restored repeatedly with substantial composite veneers that now fail mechanically. The gingivae are healthy, enamel is extensive and a diagnostic mock-up confirms a minimal bonded indirect design can achieve the desired shape.

options.E: Treat active periodontal disease before any elective aesthetic restoration

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Definitive ceramic veneers with bonded enamel preparation

CLINICAL REASONING: A conservative ceramic veneer is reasonable after recurrent direct failure, with adequate enamel and stable adult dentition.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
A. Direct additive composite build-ups using a wax-up index — Ideal for growing patients with sound enamel and feasible no-preparation reshaping; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. Full-coverage ceramic crowns on the lateral incisors — Usually unnecessarily destructive for sound peg-shaped teeth; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Defer cosmetic restorations until growth ceases irrespective of patient concerns — May be appropriate only when the patient genuinely does not need interim treatment; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. Treat active periodontal disease before any elective aesthetic restoration — A necessary first step in active periodontal instability; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

stem: During a supervised adjustment of a recently fitted posterior crown, a working-side excursion produces an isolated contact between the buccal cusp of the maxillary crown and the buccal cusp of the opposing mandibular molar. Centric stops are correct. The maxillary buccal cusp is non-supporting, and the mandibular buccal cusp is supporting.
lead: Which adjustment follows the BULL principle while preserving the centric stop?

options.A: Adjust the upper palatal supporting cusp instead
options.B: Apply DUML regardless of the excursion
options.C: Reduce the lower buccal supporting cusp tip
options.D: Reduce the relevant incline of the upper buccal non-supporting cusp selectively
options.E: Flatten both opposing cusp tips until contact disappears

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Reduce the relevant incline of the upper buccal non-supporting cusp selectively

RATIONALE: BULL means Buccal of Upper, Lingual of Lower for working-side contacts, favouring selective modification of non-supporting inclines while preserving supporting cusp height. Confirm actual incline and excursion before irreversible adjustment.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Adjust the upper palatal supporting cusp instead B. Apply DUML regardless of the excursion C. Reduce the lower buccal supporting cusp tip E. Flatten both opposing cusp tips until contact disappears

theme: Bruxism with extensive MOD: restoration decision
stem: A 50-year-old bruxist has an extensive MOD cavity in a vital mandibular first molar. Both marginal ridges are lost, a functional cusp is undermined and cracks stop in coronal dentine. No symptoms of irreversible pulpitis are present; good isolation can be obtained.
lead: Which strategy best addresses structure and loading?

options.A: An adhesively retained cuspal-coverage restoration with material and thickness selected for load, preservation and space
options.B: Full root canal treatment before any restorative assessment
options.C: Extraction solely because the patient bruxes
options.D: Microabrasion of the occlusal surface
options.E: A small intracoronal filling without cuspal protection

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — An adhesively retained cuspal-coverage restoration with material and thickness selected for load, preservation and space

theme: Selective imaging and dynamic implant navigation
stem: A single posterior maxillary implant is planned near the sinus floor. Existing intraoral and panoramic imaging do not establish the three-dimensional bone envelope. The clinician needs focused cross-sectional measurement while limiting dose and field size.
lead: Which imaging or digital technique is justified by the specific question being asked?

options.A: Obtain an intraoral periapical radiograph for a localised dental question
options.B: Use a justified limited-field CBCT for three-dimensional anatomical assessment
options.C: Use real-time dynamic surgical navigation with verified registration
options.D: Acquire a routine full-head CBCT before every single implant
options.E: Use panoramic imaging alone to control drill-to-nerve distance intraoperatively

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Use a justified limited-field CBCT for three-dimensional anatomical assessment

CLINICAL REASONING: A justified limited-FOV CBCT answers the 3D anatomy question with a smaller irradiated volume.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:

stem: A patient has significant localised anterior wear with reduced space for restorative material. The posterior occlusal support, mobility, periodontal health, pulpal status, parafunctional load and willingness to accept a reversible adaptive phase are established. Wear is localised to palatal anterior teeth, posterior support is intact, teeth are periodontally stable and the patient wants a lower-cost repairable option. The patient wishes to preserve future options where possible but would accept a more extensive treatment if demonstrably necessary.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Defer restoration and manage aetiology when wear is stable and symptom-free
options.B: Offer an alternative restorative design that preserves pulpal and periodontal tissues without increasing full-arch vertical dimension
options.C: Use selective crown lengthening only after evaluating root support, smile line and periodontal consequences
options.D: Use localised additive anterior composite using the Dahl concept with planned review of posterior contact re-establishment
options.E: Plan a provisional reorganised occlusion when generalised wear requires a full-arch change

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Use localised additive anterior composite using the Dahl concept with planned review of posterior contact re-establishment.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: Wear is localised to palatal anterior teeth, posterior support is intact, teeth are periodontally stable and the patient wants a lower-cost repairable option.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: The additive Dahl approach can create space through relative axial adaptation while conserving tooth tissue.

A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The tooth wear is old, has not progressed and does not cause discomfort or aesthetic concern. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: One heavily restored anterior tooth lacks clinical height for a retentive crown and localized periodontal and aesthetic effects of lengthening are acceptable. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: There is generalised destructive wear, several collapsed posterior units and no stable interarch relationship for isolated anterior Dahl treatment. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

theme: MIH incisor opacity: depth-dependent aesthetic choice
stem: A healthy 19-year-old with known MIH has a stable superficial creamy opacity on a maxillary incisor. The enamel is hard and intact, no caries is present and the lesion appears shallow on wet-dry examination. The patient requests a minimally invasive aesthetic improvement.
lead: Which option is reasonable after discussing uncertain response and alternatives?

options.A: Non-vital bleaching despite a vital tooth and no root filling
options.B: Immediate aggressive deep enamel removal
options.C: Mandatory full crown preparation
options.D: Conservative supervised microabrasion for a superficial opacity
options.E: Extraction of the incisor

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Conservative supervised microabrasion for a superficial opacity

stem: A patient complains that a newly made complete denture tips during chewing. options.B: Eliminate a reproducible premature centric contact and re-evaluate balance

stem: A single implant scan repeatedly positions the virtual implant 0.8 mm too deeply despite an apparently complete digital arch scan. A postoperative radiograph indicates the scan body has not fully seated because peri-implant tissue obstructs the interface.

stem: A 59-year-old asks for implants to replace a short bounded space but has untreated active periodontitis. The patient believes implants cannot develop periodontal-type problems and wants immediate surgery.
lead: What is the best next step in this patient-centred treatment plan?

options.A: Explain options and consequences, check understanding and document the patient’s informed preference
options.B: Extract all requested teeth without checking whether extraction is clinically indicated
options.C: Proceed with a comprehensive fixed reconstruction before caries control
options.D: Defer all care indefinitely without discussion
options.E: Refuse to discuss prosthodontic options because the patient has strong preferences

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Explain options and consequences, check understanding and document the patient’s informed preference

CLINICAL REASONING: Clarify disease control, implant maintenance risks and conventional alternatives before consent to any irreversible plan.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:

options.D: Full-coverage ceramic veneers for every affected tooth

solution:

theme: Retention versus resistance: short wide crown
stem: A short, broad mandibular second molar has well-controlled total occlusal convergence but only 2 mm of effective axial height. The crown resists removal along its path but readily tips under lateral loading on the mounted cast.
lead: Which feature is most critically deficient?

options.A: Occlusal value and hue
options.B: Resistance form against oblique/tipping forces
options.C: Pulp sensibility
options.D: Pontic emergence profile
options.E: Gingival shade matching

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Resistance form against oblique/tipping forces

RATIONALE: Resistance form prevents dislodgement under lateral/oblique forces. Short wide preparations may lack adequate resistance even when axial walls are nearly parallel. Judicious grooves/boxes or alternative restorative design may improve resistance without unnecessary taper.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Occlusal value and hue C. Pulp sensibility D. Pontic emergence profile E. Gingival shade matching

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

EVIDENCE / SOURCE: Fixed prosthodontic retention and resistance principles

theme: Incisal restoration: remaining enamel and failure pattern
stem: A 19-year-old presents with a small uncomplicated incisal chip on UL1 after minor trauma. The pulp is sensibly responsive, no occlusal interference is detected and the surrounding enamel is intact. The tooth has never been restored and the patient values reversibility.
lead: Which definitive restoration best matches the remaining tissue, previous failures and occlusal risk?

options.A: Replace the direct composite with an additive, repairable restoration
options.B: Provide a minimal-preparation bonded labio-incisal ceramic veneer
options.C: Provide a circumferential full-coverage ceramic crown
options.D: Provide a palatal ceramic onlay without treating the labial deficiency
options.E: Extract and replace the tooth with an implant-supported crown

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Replace the direct composite with an additive, repairable restoration

theme: Consent and request for total extraction
stem: A capable 49-year-old requests extraction of all remaining teeth despite several being restorable. The dentist has discussed the likely effects of complete dentures, implant options, functional and psychological consequences, and alternatives. The patient remains insistent, but no immediate irreversible procedure has begun. Good consent requires more than obtaining a signature. The patient demonstrates full understanding and has consistent preferences, but the clinician considers the proposed non-indicated extractions to be harmful and outside acceptable professional practice.
lead: Which next action best meets professional decision-making standards?

options.A: Extract every asymptomatic tooth as a matter of patient autonomy
options.B: Proceed immediately once the patient signs a printed consent form
options.C: Declare the patient lacks capacity solely because the request seems unusual
options.D: Explore goals and alternatives, assess understanding and voluntariness, and make a proportionate treatment recommendation
options.E: Decline a clinically unjustified extraction plan while explaining reasons and offering appropriate alternatives or a second opinion

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Decline a clinically unjustified extraction plan while explaining reasons and offering appropriate alternatives or a second opinion

DECISIVE FINDING: The patient demonstrates full understanding and has consistent preferences, but the clinician considers the proposed non-indicated extractions to be harmful and outside acceptable professional practice.

WHY IT WINS: The clinician is not obliged to deliver clinically inappropriate care; option B is refined below to counselling/referral rather than dismissing.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: Closest alternative: Autonomy does not mandate providing clinically inappropriate treatment.
B: This option does not resolve the decisive finding or carries a less favourable risk/benefit for the stated patient; verify the applicable clinical indication before selecting it.
C: This option does not resolve the decisive finding or carries a less favourable risk/benefit for the stated patient; verify the applicable clinical indication before selecting it.

theme: Digital impression: short span versus full arch
stem: A dentist obtains repeatable accurate intraoral scans for a short tooth-supported bridge with clearly visible margins. The same scanner produces visibly differing distal implant coordinates when scanning six implants across a fully edentulous maxillary arch without reliable anatomical landmarks.
lead: Which conclusion is best supported?

options.A: A passive framework on a printed model proves the scan is true
options.B: All digital impressions are necessarily less accurate than conventional impressions
options.C: Scan accuracy is indication- and protocol-dependent; a full-arch implant case may need additional verification or an alternative validated workflow
options.D: Single crowns must always be fabricated from conventional alginate impressions
options.E: Optical stitching cannot produce cumulative error

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Scan accuracy is indication- and protocol-dependent; a full-arch implant case may need additional verification or an alternative validated workflow

RATIONALE: Short-span tooth scans can be reliable under suitable conditions. Full-arch edentulous implant scans can accumulate stitching error and may need verification or a more suitable workflow; no single impression modality is universally superior.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. A passive framework on a printed model proves the scan is true B. All digital impressions are necessarily less accurate than conventional impressions D. Single crowns must always be fabricated from conventional alginate impressions E. Optical stitching cannot produce cumulative error

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

EVIDENCE / SOURCE: Digital versus conventional impression evidence, full-arch implant accuracy

stem: A posterior or anterior restoration has failed and an indirect replacement is proposed. Clinical examination describes the available clearance, enamel distribution, bonding substrate, occlusal loading and aesthetic zone. A small functional cusp defect has ample sound enamel and the patient wants an inexpensive reversible treatment with future repair potential. Two options have been discussed at the referral visit;
lead: What is the most defensible recommendation at this stage?

options.A: Gain additional restorative clearance or revise the preparation design before choosing a material
options.B: Prefer a metal restoration where clearance and load make a thin, durable restoration advantageous
options.C: Use a monolithic zirconia restoration with manufacturer-specified thickness and suitable conditioning for a high-load site
options.D: Use additive direct composite when minimal intervention, reversibility and future repair are dominant
options.E: Choose an adhesively retained lithium disilicate partial-coverage restoration where supported by enamel and adequate clearance

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Use additive direct composite when minimal intervention, reversibility and future repair are dominant.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A small functional cusp defect has ample sound enamel and the patient wants an inexpensive reversible treatment with future repair potential.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Additive composite can address a limited defect without unnecessary preparation.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A tooth has only 0.3 mm occlusal space at the load-bearing cusp and all proposed ceramics would be below recommended thickness. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: An upper second molar has very limited clearance, low aesthetic visibility and a stable, retentive preparation that can accommodate a thin cast-metal onlay. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A heavily loaded molar has acceptable preparation height and adequate clearance for the specified monolithic zirconia design. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The vital premolar has predominantly sound enamel, adequate occlusal thickness for a bonded onlay and a moderate aesthetic requirement. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

theme: Dental trauma: isolated crown fracture or luxation
stem: A 16-year-old has an injured permanent maxillary central incisor after a sports collision. Enamel and dentine were fractured and restored with composite after clinical and radiographic examination. The dentist records pulp sensibility, mobility, percussion and possible periodontal injuries, then selects a follow-up interval that reflects the complete injury pattern. The crown fracture accompanies clear extrusion and increased mobility with a widened periodontal ligament space.
lead: Which follow-up plan is most appropriate?

options.A: Clinical and radiographic review at 6–8 weeks and one year
options.B: Use the additional luxation-injury review schedule when a luxation is present
options.C: Discharge without further review once the composite is polished
options.D: Review only after five years unless pain develops
options.E: Routine root canal treatment irrespective of pulp diagnosis

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Use the additional luxation-injury review schedule when a luxation is present

DECISIVE FINDING: The crown fracture accompanies clear extrusion and increased mobility with a widened periodontal ligament space.

WHY IT WINS: The associated extrusive luxation determines a more intensive management and review schedule than crown fracture alone.

ALTERNATIVES:
A: Closest alternative: A fracture-only schedule would not monitor the injured periodontal ligament adequately.

theme: Implant anatomy near IAN and guidance accuracy
stem: A patient needs an implant in the posterior mandible, where a narrow vertical bone envelope lies above the inferior alveolar canal. A prosthetically planned implant has been superimposed on cross-sectional images. The surgeon considers static guides, dynamic navigation, shorter implants and an alternative prosthesis. All safety margins must be judged using the full surgical and imaging uncertainty. The residual ridge has insufficient height for any clinically justified implant without encroaching on the canal, and a tooth-supported fixed option is readily available.
lead: Which planning action is most appropriate?

options.A: Choose a tooth-supported alternative when no safe, maintainable implant trajectory exists
options.B: Assume dynamic navigation eliminates registration and drill-tip errors
options.C: Select a validated prosthetic and surgical plan with sufficient anatomical clearance, considering shorter implants or another treatment
options.D: Use a panoramic measurement alone to avoid 3D assessment
options.E: Proceed with a long implant if the navigation screen displays a 2-mm margin

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Choose a tooth-supported alternative when no safe, maintainable implant trajectory exists

DECISIVE FINDING: The residual ridge has insufficient height for any clinically justified implant without encroaching on the canal, and a tooth-supported fixed option is readily available.

WHY IT WINS: Decline an unsafe implant trajectory when a maintainable tooth-supported alternative is available.

stem: A technician and prosthodontist review an acrylic denture base that has cracked or distorted after processing. The original mould, resin mixture, curing history, occlusal loading and repair materials are known. Several processing changes might affect different failure mechanisms. Numerous internal voids arise when too much liquid was added and the mix was packed too early in the sandy stage. Two options have been discussed at the referral visit;
lead: Which management strategy best addresses the dominant limitation in this patient?

options.A: Repeat processing with the specified time–temperature cycle and adequate monomer conversion
options.B: Improve bonding and material matching at a repair interface rather than relying on bulk cold-cure acrylic
options.C: Correct the polymer-to-monomer ratio and packing stage to limit porosity and dimensional error
options.D: Reduce stress concentration through base design, thickness, contour and fit
options.E: Check polymerisation shrinkage and cooling procedure before assuming a jaw-relation error

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Correct the polymer-to-monomer ratio and packing stage to limit porosity and dimensional error.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: Numerous internal voids arise when too much liquid was added and the mix was packed too early in the sandy stage.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Wrong mixing and packing conditions impair integrity and dimensional consistency.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The denture has persistent monomer odour and poor strength after a markedly shortened heat-cure cycle. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: An old heat-cured base has been repaired with a broad cold-cure joint that repeatedly separates along the original interface. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A repeated midline fracture initiates at an anterior notch in a thin base, directly beneath a heavy incisal contact. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The newly processed base fits its casts poorly after rapid cooling and uneven dimensional contraction, despite acceptable curing duration. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A patient with a partially dentate arch is considering a tooth-supported reconstruction. The candidate abutments have been charted for ferrule, clinical crown height, periodontal attachment, endodontic health and load distribution; treatment cost and possible future failure are important. A root-filled premolar has approximately 2 mm circumferential ferrule, stable attachment and favourable crown-root proportions. The referral includes a clear account of the principal problem; the patient asks which option should be prioritised before further treatment.
lead: Which management option is most appropriate on the information given?

options.A: Gain coronal tooth structure by appropriate orthodontic extrusion before reassessing restorability
options.B: Avoid relying on a structurally hopeless root and redesign the span or replacement strategy
options.C: Preserve and restore an abutment with sound ferrule and maintainable periodontal support
options.D: Stage periodontal therapy and reassess support rather than judging prognosis from bone loss percentage alone
options.E: Choose a removable design that allows independent replacement of future failing teeth

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Preserve and restore an abutment with sound ferrule and maintainable periodontal support.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A root-filled premolar has approximately 2 mm circumferential ferrule, stable attachment and favourable crown-root proportions.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: The ferrule and support make retention plausible with appropriate protection.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A strategically valuable root has insufficient coronal dentine but orthodontic extrusion can create ferrule without losing necessary root support. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A long root-supported bridge would depend on a vertically fractured distal abutment with repeated post loosening. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A periodontally reduced tooth has resolved inflammation and stable attachment after active treatment, with no root fracture or active mobility. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Several abutments have fluctuating prognosis, the patient expects future tooth losses and seeks a repairable low-cost option. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A patient is undergoing complex prosthodontic reconstruction with suspected instability of jaw relations. Articulator records, clinical contacts and mandibular movement are compared. There is extensive posterior support loss, multiple proposed units and no consistent mandibular record across appointments. Both a staged and a direct approach have been discussed, and neither is excluded solely by cost or operator access.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Use a repeatable clinical intercuspal position when the existing scheme is stable and unchanged
options.B: Evaluate mandibular joint and muscle symptoms before inferring that an occlusal discrepancy is the pain source
options.C: Repeat the facebow transfer and verify cast mounting after a demonstrable transfer error
options.D: Use a provisional diagnostic arrangement to test altered occlusion and patient adaptation
options.E: Confirm a reproducible reference jaw relation before extensive alteration of vertical dimension or guidance

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Confirm a reproducible reference jaw relation before extensive alteration of vertical dimension or guidance.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: There is extensive posterior support loss, multiple proposed units and no consistent mandibular record across appointments.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: The reference jaw relation must be reproducible before a reorganised plan is implemented.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The patient has stable bilateral contacts and a conformative single crown is planned with no functional change. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A patient attributes chronic facial pain to a small retruded-contact slide, but muscle palpation reproduces the characteristic pain. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The mounted casts show a unilateral premature contact not reproducible in the mouth and the facebow jig moved during recording. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: An increase in occlusal vertical dimension is proposed for generalised wear but adaptation and speech effects remain uncertain. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A dentist requests a restorative plan for discoloured or malformed anterior teeth. Tooth vitality, intrinsic and extrinsic staining, existing restorations, enamel quantity, age and the ability to maintain the result are documented. A root-filled incisor has substantial coronal tissue loss, an established ferrule and recurrent fracture of large direct restorations.
lead: Which course of action provides the strongest patient-specific justification among these alternatives?

options.A: Use direct composite addition where shape and repairability matter more than long-term ceramic colour stability
options.B: Reserve full coverage for teeth with extensive structural compromise or inadequate conservative options
options.C: Select an enamel-bonded partial-coverage veneer for an appropriate mature patient with persistent shape and colour concerns
options.D: Investigate non-vital tooth discolouration and endodontic status before attempting internal bleaching or definitive coverage
options.E: Begin with professional cleaning or whitening when tooth structure is intact and colour is the principal complaint

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Reserve full coverage for teeth with extensive structural compromise or inadequate conservative options.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A root-filled incisor has substantial coronal tissue loss, an established ferrule and recurrent fracture of large direct restorations.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Structural restoration needs may justify coverage beyond an aesthetic veneer.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A growing teenager has peg-shaped lateral incisors with a successful no-preparation wax-up and wants reversible adjustment. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A mature patient has a small persistent labio-incisal defect and repeated composite cohesive failure, with abundant enamel available for an adhesive veneer. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: One central incisor is discoloured after trauma, gives no response to sensibility tests and has a periapical radiolucency. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A vital tooth is uniformly yellow, unrestored and has adequate enamel; the patient dislikes the colour but not the shape. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: Posterior maxillary implant rehabilitation is considered in a patient with limited residual bone and radiographic sinus findings. Restorative space, sinus ostial patency, anatomy and alternatives to grafting are evaluated; the surgeon asks whether augmentation should proceed or be modified. There is minimal residual bone, insufficient primary stability and a large volume of reconstruction needed for the restorative plan. The patient understands that several technically feasible options differ in biological burden, retrievability, and long-term maintenance. The consultant is asked to prioritise the evidence that most changes prognosis.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Proceed with the planned approach when an asymptomatic benign sinus-floor finding does not obstruct drainage
options.B: Refer for sinus assessment before augmentation when symptoms or ostial obstruction suggest active disease
options.C: Obtain or re-interpret limited-field three-dimensional imaging where anatomy materially affects the chosen surgical path
options.D: Consider a short implant or prosthetic alternative when dimensions and risk-benefit support avoiding major augmentation
options.E: Plan staged augmentation when graft volume, primary stability and restorative position cannot be achieved simultaneously

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Plan staged augmentation when graft volume, primary stability and restorative position cannot be achieved simultaneously.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: There is minimal residual bone, insufficient primary stability and a large volume of reconstruction needed for the restorative plan.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Staging may provide a safer foundation before implant placement.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A small dome-shaped sinus-floor opacity is asymptomatic, the ostium is patent and a suitable lateral window can avoid relevant structures. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The patient has unilateral discharge, sinus pain and imaging showing occluded drainage with diffuse mucosal disease. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Panoramic imaging does not define buccopalatal width or the relation of the sinus septum to the intended implant site. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Residual vertical bone permits a validated short-implant strategy for the planned crown, and the patient wishes to avoid complex grafting. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A 72-year-old takes rivaroxaban every morning and needs flap-based surgical removal of two adjacent molars. Renal function is stable, and no recent high-risk thromboembolic event is reported. The elective procedure will be early in the day with local haemostasis.
lead: Which periprocedural medication advice follows a risk-based dental approach?

options.A: Continue the prescribed DOAC and use local haemostatic measures
options.B: Delay the scheduled morning rivaroxaban dose for a higher-bleeding-risk procedure
options.C: Stop rivaroxaban for several days without medical agreement
options.D: Change rivaroxaban to warfarin solely for a dental procedure
options.E: Omit all postoperative doses until every suture has been removed

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Delay the scheduled morning rivaroxaban dose for a higher-bleeding-risk procedure

CLINICAL REASONING: For higher-bleeding-risk surgery, SDCEP advises delaying the morning rivaroxaban dose; restart no sooner than 4 h after haemostasis.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
A. Continue the prescribed DOAC and use local haemostatic measures — Recommended for low-risk bleeding procedures where medication change is unnecessary; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. Stop rivaroxaban for several days without medical agreement — Unsupervised multiday cessation creates avoidable thrombotic risk; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Change rivaroxaban to warfarin solely for a dental procedure — Routine conversion is not indicated; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. Omit all postoperative doses until every suture has been removed — Prolonged interruption is not supported by routine dental guidance; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

stem: A restored implant is reviewed because of discomfort, bleeding, tissue change or a cosmetic complaint. Baseline probing and imaging are available or their absence is recognised; mucosal inflammation must be distinguished from progressive loss of supporting bone. An otherwise healthy posterior implant has less than 1 mm of buccal keratinised tissue and recurrent painful toothbrushing despite careful plaque control. Two options have been discussed at the referral visit;
lead: Which management strategy best addresses the dominant limitation in this patient?

options.A: Improve plaque control and prosthetic cleanability, then reassess peri-implant mucositis
options.B: Consider increasing keratinised mucosa when brushing discomfort persists despite health and suitable hygiene measures
options.C: Investigate peri-implantitis with baseline comparison and provide cause-focused nonsurgical care before considering further treatment
options.D: Assess prosthetic contours and residual cement as removable inflammatory drivers
options.E: Return to risk-based maintenance when probing, tissues and bone are stable

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Consider increasing keratinised mucosa when brushing discomfort persists despite health and suitable hygiene measures.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: An otherwise healthy posterior implant has less than 1 mm of buccal keratinised tissue and recurrent painful toothbrushing despite careful plaque control.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Symptomatic keratinised mucosa deficiency may justify an augmentation discussion.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Bleeding occurs with plaque accumulation but no progressive bone loss beyond expected remodelling, and the patient struggles to clean a bulky contour. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: There is new deep probing, suppuration and radiographic bone loss compared with the restoration baseline. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A cement-retained crown has submucosal excess cement visible after careful examination and inflammation localised to that area. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Probing is unchanged from baseline, no bleeding or suppuration exists, and radiographs show no progression. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

theme: Resin-bonded bridge: cantilever and abutment risk
stem: A 16-year-old with congenitally missing UR2 has stable orthodontic space and favourable enamel on UR3. Facial growth is continuing, and an interim fixed aesthetic replacement is sought.
lead: Which fixed replacement design best limits unnecessary abutment preparation and debonding risk?

options.A: A single-retainer cantilever resin-bonded prosthesis to sound enamel
options.B: A two-retainer fixed–fixed resin-bonded prosthesis across independent abutments
options.C: A full-coverage conventional three-unit fixed prosthesis
options.D: Immediate implant placement before confirming growth and site anatomy
options.E: No replacement without discussing the patient’s concerns

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — A single-retainer cantilever resin-bonded prosthesis to sound enamel

CLINICAL REASONING: An additive single-retainer RBB can be considered during growth rather than preparing adjacent sound teeth.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
B. A two-retainer fixed–fixed resin-bonded prosthesis across independent abutments — Can carry differential movement and debonding risks in certain designs; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. A full-coverage conventional three-unit fixed prosthesis — Requires much more preparation when teeth are otherwise sound; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Immediate implant placement before confirming growth and site anatomy — Implant selection requires completion of growth and adequate planning; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. No replacement without discussing the patient’s concerns — Reasonable only where no replacement is acceptable to the informed patient; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

stem: Two clinicians repeatedly agree when categorising a clinical photograph, but subsequent independent reference-standard assessment shows that both consistently misclassify the lesion.
lead: Which interpretation is correct?

options.A: The test is reliable but not necessarily valid or accurate
options.B: Inter-rater reliability proves that the diagnostic classification is correct
options.C: Specificity is always 100% when examiners agree
options.D: No reference standard is required if the examiners are specialists
options.E: The prevalence of disease must be zero

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — The test is reliable but not necessarily valid or accurate

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Agreement and repeatability describe reliability; validity concerns whether the result corresponds to the true condition.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
B. Inter-rater reliability proves that the diagnostic classification is correct — Agreement alone cannot confirm the truth of the diagnosis.
C. Specificity is always 100% when examiners agree — Specificity cannot be inferred from inter-examiner agreement.
D. No reference standard is required if the examiners are specialists — An independent reference standard is relevant to assessing validity.
E. The prevalence of disease must be zero — Agreement does not determine condition prevalence.

stem: A root-filled maxillary premolar has lost both marginal ridges and most cuspal tissue. After caries removal, 2 mm of sound circumferential coronal dentine remains above the proposed finish line; periodontal prognosis is favourable.
lead: Which restorative choice best reflects remaining tooth structure and ferrule?

options.A: Conservative bonded onlay without unnecessary full coverage
options.B: Full-coverage crown when adequate ferrule and tooth structure allow it
options.C: Post-and-core alone as the definitive coronal restoration
options.D: Elective extraction without assessing restorability
options.E: Crown lengthening/orthodontic extrusion assessment before an irreversible restoration

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Full-coverage crown when adequate ferrule and tooth structure allow it

CLINICAL REASONING: A crown may be justified with adequate ferrule and cuspal loss; a post is not automatically required.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
A. Conservative bonded onlay without unnecessary full coverage — Appropriate for vital or endodontically treated teeth with sufficient cuspal structure, depending on load; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. Post-and-core alone as the definitive coronal restoration — A post does not itself provide a durable coronal restoration or increase root strength; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Elective extraction without assessing restorability — Reserved for nonrestorable or hopeless prognosis after assessment; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. Crown lengthening/orthodontic extrusion assessment before an irreversible restoration — Appropriate when ferrule is absent and restoration would violate tissue attachment, if feasible; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

stem: A restored implant is reviewed because of discomfort, bleeding, tissue change or a cosmetic complaint. Baseline probing and imaging are available or their absence is recognised; mucosal inflammation must be distinguished from progressive loss of supporting bone. Probing is unchanged from baseline, no bleeding or suppuration exists, and radiographs show no progression. Both a staged and a direct approach have been discussed, and neither is excluded solely by cost or operator access.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Return to risk-based maintenance when probing, tissues and bone are stable
options.B: Consider increasing keratinised mucosa when brushing discomfort persists despite health and suitable hygiene measures
options.C: Improve plaque control and prosthetic cleanability, then reassess peri-implant mucositis
options.D: Assess prosthetic contours and residual cement as removable inflammatory drivers
options.E: Investigate peri-implantitis with baseline comparison and provide cause-focused nonsurgical care before considering further treatment

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Return to risk-based maintenance when probing, tissues and bone are stable.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: Probing is unchanged from baseline, no bleeding or suppuration exists, and radiographs show no progression.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Stable peri-implant health calls for continuing tailored supportive care.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: An otherwise healthy posterior implant has less than 1 mm of buccal keratinised tissue and recurrent painful toothbrushing despite careful plaque control. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Bleeding occurs with plaque accumulation but no progressive bone loss beyond expected remodelling, and the patient struggles to clean a bulky contour. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A cement-retained crown has submucosal excess cement visible after careful examination and inflammation localised to that area. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: There is new deep probing, suppuration and radiographic bone loss compared with the restoration baseline. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A fully edentulous patient needs a screw-retained complete-arch prosthesis on six implants. The record must accurately relate implant positions across the entire arch; the local scanner workflow has not been validated for this span.
lead: Which recording approach best addresses this case’s principal accuracy limitation?

options.A: Validated intraoral scan for a short-span tooth-supported restoration
options.B: Verified conventional implant-level impression with passive-fit assessment
options.C: Conventional functional impression with border moulding for mobile edentulous tissues
options.D: Unverified full-arch scan stitched across mobile mucosa only
options.E: Select the fastest method regardless of restoration span or tissue mobility

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Verified conventional implant-level impression with passive-fit assessment

CLINICAL REASONING: Use a verified implant-level workflow and passive-fit assessment rather than relying on an unverified long-span scan.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
A. Validated intraoral scan for a short-span tooth-supported restoration — Works well for routine short-span tooth-supported work with visible margins; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. Conventional functional impression with border moulding for mobile edentulous tissues — Captures functional support and extension of highly mobile edentulous tissues; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Unverified full-arch scan stitched across mobile mucosa only — Prone to stitching/tissue-displacement limitations in stated scenarios; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. Select the fastest method regardless of restoration span or tissue mobility — Speed alone is not a substitute for accuracy; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

stem: A dentist is planning a missing posterior tooth replacement. Existing periapical and panoramic imaging, proposed restorative emergence and adjacent anatomical structures are reviewed. Radiographic benefit must be proportionate to exposure, and a scan must answer a decision that conventional imaging cannot resolve. A single-tooth crown is planned, available imaging clearly shows healthy adjacent structures and ridge geometry has been reliably assessed for the chosen simple procedure.
lead: Which management option is most appropriate on the information given?

options.A: Use an existing diagnostically adequate two-dimensional study without further radiation
options.B: Correct the prosthetic wax-up and implant position planning before choosing the imaging field
options.C: Defer the implant proposal and investigate unexplained relevant pathology before surgery
options.D: Justify a restricted-field CBCT where three-dimensional anatomy will change implant safety or augmentation decisions
options.E: Request a new periapical image with appropriate projection to clarify local teeth and periodontal status

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Use an existing diagnostically adequate two-dimensional study without further radiation.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A single-tooth crown is planned, available imaging clearly shows healthy adjacent structures and ridge geometry has been reliably assessed for the chosen simple procedure.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Additional CBCT is not justified when it does not change management.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The surgical plan places the implant through the buccal crown contour and no definitive restorative contour or screw-access corridor has been agreed. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The lower molar canal position is uncertain buccolingually and implant length versus nerve safety cannot be resolved on panoramic imaging. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A heavily restored adjacent premolar is tender with suspected apical pathology, while existing local imaging is blurred by movement. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

theme: TMD: myalgia versus joint disorder versus neuralgia
stem: A 29-year-old has an intermittent preauricular click during opening and again on closing, with 44-mm opening and little pain. There is no familiar masseter pain on palpation and no episodes of prolonged locking.
lead: Which diagnosis is most consistent with the symptoms and reproducible examination findings?

options.A: Masticatory myalgia
options.B: Disc displacement with reduction
options.C: Trigeminal neuralgia pattern requiring referral
options.D: Temporomandibular joint ankylosis
options.E: Irreversible occlusal interference causing all symptoms

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Disc displacement with reduction

CLINICAL REASONING: Reciprocal joint clicks with maintained opening are consistent with disc displacement with reduction.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
A. Masticatory myalgia — Familiar pain reproduced by muscle palpation or movement; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. Trigeminal neuralgia pattern requiring referral — Brief unilateral electric-shock attacks from innocuous tactile triggers; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Temporomandibular joint ankylosis — Marked chronic limitation with clinical and imaging evidence of ankylosis; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. Irreversible occlusal interference causing all symptoms — Occlusal contacts alone do not establish a pain diagnosis; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
