theme: Nonhereditary enamel defect from systemic insult
stem: A 17-year-old has well-demarcated horizontal hypoplastic bands on canines and premolars, at corresponding developmental positions. Medical records document a prolonged severe childhood illness during formation of those crowns. No close relatives have similar defects; other teeth are normally formed.
lead: Which explanation is more likely than a hereditary generalised amelogenesis imperfecta?

options.A: Dentinogenesis imperfecta with pulp obliteration
options.B: Post-eruptive erosion by a current acidic diet
options.C: A cracked tooth syndrome affecting all four teeth
options.D: Generalised enamel wear from nocturnal bruxism
options.E: Chronological enamel hypoplasia after a systemic disturbance during development

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Chronological enamel hypoplasia after a systemic disturbance during development

RATIONALE: Band-like defects affecting teeth mineralising at the same time, with an appropriate timing history, suggest systemic/chronological enamel hypoplasia rather than a generalised Mendelian AI phenotype.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Dentinogenesis imperfecta with pulp obliteration B. Post-eruptive erosion by a current acidic diet C. A cracked tooth syndrome affecting all four teeth D. Generalised enamel wear from nocturnal bruxism

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

EVIDENCE / SOURCE: Developmental enamel defect differential diagnosis

theme: Selective occlusal adjustment and restoration design
stem: In an otherwise stable planned reorganised occlusion, a posterior deflective contact is identified only in protrusive movement. The team asks which traditional incline mnemonic applies to distal upper and mesial lower incline modification.
lead: Which occlusal management principle is most appropriate given the described contact?

options.A: Use the BULL principle when eliminating an identified working-side deflective incline interference
options.B: Use the DUML principle for the appropriate protrusive incline adjustment
options.C: Avoid irreversible selective grinding until a reproducible functional diagnosis is established
options.D: Remove all supporting cusp contacts irrespective of their role in vertical support
options.E: Increase every posterior occlusal table width to eliminate excursion contacts

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Use the DUML principle for the appropriate protrusive incline adjustment

CLINICAL REASONING: DUML is the conventional mnemonic for protrusive interference on distal upper and mesial lower inclines.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:
A. Use the BULL principle when eliminating an identified working-side deflective incline interference — Buccal inclines of upper lingual cusps / lingual inclines of lower buccal cusps may be adjusted in working-side interferences; preserve holding contacts; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
C. Avoid irreversible selective grinding until a reproducible functional diagnosis is established — Necessary when pain or articulating paper marks do not establish the cause of symptoms; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
D. Remove all supporting cusp contacts irrespective of their role in vertical support — Destroying centric stops is not a routine adjustment goal; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. Increase every posterior occlusal table width to eliminate excursion contacts — Generally increases interference risk instead of treating it; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.

stem: A 16-year-old recently completed orthodontic treatment. Several matte, chalky, rough white areas surround previous bracket sites and plaque accumulates over them. The patient drinks sugary beverages frequently and asks for resin infiltration at the first appointment.
lead: What is the most appropriate initial priority?

options.A: Aggressive microabrasion of every lesion immediately
options.B: Full veneers on the affected anterior teeth
options.C: Caries-risk control with plaque/diet measures and appropriate topical fluoride before cosmetic intervention
options.D: Bleach the teeth first without discussing lesion activity
options.E: Root canal treatment of all white lesions

stem: A patient with a partially dentate arch is considering a tooth-supported reconstruction. The candidate abutments have been charted for ferrule, clinical crown height, periodontal attachment, endodontic health and load distribution; treatment cost and possible future failure are important. A long root-supported bridge would depend on a vertically fractured distal abutment with repeated post loosening. The patient wishes to preserve future options where possible but would accept a more extensive treatment if demonstrably necessary.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Preserve and restore an abutment with sound ferrule and maintainable periodontal support
options.B: Choose a removable design that allows independent replacement of future failing teeth
options.C: Stage periodontal therapy and reassess support rather than judging prognosis from bone loss percentage alone
options.D: Avoid relying on a structurally hopeless root and redesign the span or replacement strategy
options.E: Gain coronal tooth structure by appropriate orthodontic extrusion before reassessing restorability

stem: A patient returns after delivery of a new removable prosthesis with discomfort or poor tolerance. The pattern of symptoms, mucosal findings, occlusal examination and functional movements are recorded before any intervention. Generalised palatal erythema accompanies nocturnal denture wear and heavy biofilm without an identifiable mechanical fault. stem: A young adult with a developmental dental anomaly seeks an attractive, durable restorative solution. Orthodontic records, tooth vitality, enamel quality, jaw growth and periodontal support have been assessed. The treatment must address long-term reparability and avoid unnecessary loss of otherwise sound tissue. A primary canine remains sound and stable with an acceptable root; the permanent successor is absent and the patient is still growing. The patient understands that several technically feasible options differ in biological burden, retrievability, and long-term maintenance. The consultant is asked to prioritise the evidence that most changes prognosis.
lead: Which course of action provides the strongest patient-specific justification among these alternatives?

options.A: Retain a suitable primary tooth temporarily with monitoring while definitive timing is reconsidered
options.B: Consider conventional full coverage only where severe structural deficiency limits reliable additive solutions
options.C: Offer additive direct composite with maintenance and potential later modification
options.D: Plan adhesive indirect restorations only after assessing the quality and amount of bondable enamel
options.E: Plan a multidisciplinary stage of orthodontic redistribution before selecting prosthesis form

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Retain a suitable primary tooth temporarily with monitoring while definitive timing is reconsidered.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A primary canine remains sound and stable with an acceptable root; the permanent successor is absent and the patient is still growing.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Conservative retention can preserve bone and choices until long-term planning is mature.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Hypocalcified enamel is friable and breaks down under normal use over most functional surfaces, with poor predictable bonding. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Bilateral small peg lateral incisors are vital, growing jaw relationships are not yet stable and a no-preparation wax-up looks acceptable. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Hypoplastic amelogenesis imperfecta has created adequate but thin, reasonably mineralised enamel on vital teeth and the patient wants definitive indirect colour stability. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The lateral incisor space is too narrow for a properly proportioned restoration and roots converge despite visible crown spacing. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

options.B: Temporary cuspal splinting followed by assessment of crack extent and definitive cuspal coverage if restorable

stem: A 22-year-old with genetically confirmed dentinogenesis imperfecta has opalescent anterior teeth but only mild localized wear, no pain and stable posterior support. There is no significant loss of vertical dimension, and the patient wants limited aesthetic improvement.
lead: Which plan is most biologically conservative?

options.A: Place posts prophylactically in every obliterated pulp
options.B: Offer bleaching as a cure for the dentine defect
options.C: Prepare all teeth for full coverage irrespective of tooth loss
options.D: Remove all sound crowns and insert implants
options.E: Careful risk assessment and selective adhesive additions if indicated, with monitoring and preventive protection

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Careful risk assessment and selective adhesive additions if indicated, with monitoring and preventive protection

RATIONALE: Management is severity-dependent. Mild phenotypes may be monitored or managed with limited adhesive restorations; severe structural breakdown warrants staged protective coverage. Pulp obliteration does not mean routine prophylactic endodontics.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Place posts prophylactically in every obliterated pulp B. Offer bleaching as a cure for the dentine defect C. Prepare all teeth for full coverage irrespective of tooth loss D. Remove all sound crowns and insert implants

stem: A patient has periodontal treatment complexity code 2, root canal treatment code 3 and fixed prosthodontic complexity code 1 on the original RDITN worksheet. All modifying factors have already been considered in those component scores.
lead: What overall RDITN complexity code should be recorded?

options.A: 1, the lowest component score
options.B: 2, the most frequently encountered code
options.C: 3, the highest component code
options.D: 6, the sum of the three component scores
options.E: An arithmetic average rounded to the nearest integer

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — 3, the highest component code

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: The original RDITN overall complexity is the highest applicable component score, not a sum, average or majority vote.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. 1, the lowest component score — The overall index is not set to the least complex component.
B. 2, the most frequently encountered code — Component scores are not combined by their frequency.
D. 6, the sum of the three component scores — The separate complexity scores are not added.
E. An arithmetic average rounded to the nearest integer — The arithmetic mean is not used for this index.

stem: A 38-year-old reports a tender localized swelling of the interdental papilla after lodging popcorn husk between two teeth. Probing elsewhere is 2-3 mm, no deep pocket exists at the site, teeth respond normally to cold, and periapical radiographs show no apical pathology.
lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Vertical root fracture
options.B: Peri-implant abscess
options.C: Acute apical abscess
options.D: Periodontal abscess arising from advanced pocketing
options.E: Gingival abscess associated with a local foreign-body insult

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Gingival abscess associated with a local foreign-body insult

RATIONALE: A gingival abscess involves marginal/interdental gingiva, often after local foreign-body impaction, and does not require a pre-existing periodontal pocket. A periodontal abscess arises in supporting tissues and is often associated with a deep pocket; an apical abscess typically has a necrotic pulp.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Vertical root fracture B. Peri-implant abscess C. Acute apical abscess D. Periodontal abscess arising from advanced pocketing

stem: A patient reports unilateral brief electric-shock facial pains triggered by light touch to the cheek or toothbrushing, with pain-free intervals. Jaw movement and palpation do not reproduce familiar muscular pain.
lead: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic pathway?

options.A: Irreversible occlusal grinding of all posterior teeth
options.B: Consider neuropathic facial pain including trigeminal neuralgia and refer for appropriate assessment
options.C: Diagnose myalgia solely because the face hurts
options.D: Provide crown replacement as first-line pain therapy
options.E: Confirm disc displacement without reduction based on cheek sensitivity alone

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Consider neuropathic facial pain including trigeminal neuralgia and refer for appropriate assessment

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Triggerable brief electric-shock pain with pain-free intervals is atypical for ordinary myalgia and requires neuropathic differential diagnosis.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Irreversible occlusal grinding of all posterior teeth — Irreversible grinding is not indicated without an occlusal cause and diagnosis.
C. Diagnose myalgia solely because the face hurts — Muscular familiar-pain reproduction is absent and the symptom quality is neuropathic.
D. Provide crown replacement as first-line pain therapy — A crown does not treat a demonstrated neuropathic pain pattern.
E. Confirm disc displacement without reduction based on cheek sensitivity alone — Disc displacement does not explain triggerable electric-shock cheek pain alone.

stem: A single central-incisor crown matches the adjacent tooth under daylight-equivalent illumination but appears noticeably different under the surgery fluorescent light. The material and tooth have different spectral reflectance.
lead: What best describes this phenomenon?

options.A: A consistent mismatch in value under all lighting
options.B: Metamerism due to illuminant-dependent colour matching
options.C: An occlusal interference
options.D: Pulp necrosis confirmed by shade alone
options.E: Gingival recession measured as 3 mm

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Metamerism due to illuminant-dependent colour matching

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Metamerism is a colour match under one illumination that fails under another; cross-light assessment helps identify it.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. A consistent mismatch in value under all lighting — A persistent value mismatch would be seen across illuminants.
C. An occlusal interference — Occlusal contact is unrelated to light-dependent colour matching.
D. Pulp necrosis confirmed by shade alone — Crown shade changes under differing lights do not establish pulp necrosis.
E. Gingival recession measured as 3 mm — A periodontal measurement is unrelated to the illumination-specific mismatch.

stem: A previously painful maxillary premolar now has a vestibular swelling. The tooth is non-responsive to cold and EPT, has marked percussion tenderness, a large untreated carious lesion and a periapical radiolucency. Adjacent periodontal probing is 2-3 mm.
lead: Which diagnosis best integrates the findings?

options.B: Acute apical abscess of endodontic origin
options.C: Localized periodontal abscess from a deep pocket
options.D: Lateral periodontal cyst with vital pulp

stem: A patient receives an implant where definitive crown timing is under consideration. Bone quality, insertion stability, occlusal loading, healing conditions and the planned restoration have been assessed; the team must not confuse implant insertion with predictable osseointegration. After several weeks the implant is mobile and tender despite an apparently intact provisional crown. Clinical and technical teams have reviewed the available evidence; the patient asks how the most important diagnostic feature should change the plan.

options.A: Consider immediate provisionalisation only when stability, loading control and case selection support it
options.B: Delay loading when primary stability is inadequate and use a nonloading provisional replacement
options.C: Select components and a passive prosthetic interface that avoid excessive preload or cantilever forces
options.D: Stage implant placement after infection or tissue risks have been controlled
options.E: Manage a suspected early failure by investigating mobility, infection and mechanical causes before definitive restoration

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Manage a suspected early failure by investigating mobility, infection and mechanical causes before definitive restoration.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: After several weeks the implant is mobile and tender despite an apparently intact provisional crown.

stem: A permanent maxillary central incisor has an enamel-dentin fracture, but the tooth is additionally extruded 2 mm and very mobile. The crown fracture is repaired after appropriate repositioning and stabilisation of the luxation injury.
lead: How should the follow-up schedule be chosen?

options.A: Use the luxation-injury follow-up regime because the combined injury increases risk
options.B: No follow-up after composite repair
options.C: Review only if the patient requests whitening
options.D: Obtain mandatory monthly large-field CBCT scans
options.E: Only the isolated uncomplicated crown-fracture schedule, ignoring mobility

stem: A patient has localised anterior tooth wear with palatal dentine exposure and persistent sensitivity despite preventive management. Posterior contacts are stable; there is insufficient interocclusal space for additive anterior restorations at current contact levels.
lead: Which approach most conservatively creates restorative space?

options.A: Prepare all posterior teeth for full-coverage crowns
options.B: Use a localised additive direct composite Dahl approach with informed review and potential posterior contact re-establishment
options.C: Immediate extraction and anterior implants
options.D: Reduce the opposing posterior teeth by 2 mm
options.E: Prepare every maxillary tooth for indirect veneers

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Use a localised additive direct composite Dahl approach with informed review and potential posterior contact re-establishment

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: A Dahl approach can create relative restorative space via controlled anterior additions and dentoalveolar adaptation, while preserving intact posterior tooth tissue.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Prepare all posterior teeth for full-coverage crowns — Routine posterior crown preparation is unnecessarily destructive for localised anterior space needs.
C. Immediate extraction and anterior implants — The teeth are retainable and responsive to conservative treatment.
D. Reduce the opposing posterior teeth by 2 mm — Grinding sound opposing teeth is not a suitable default method of creating space.
E. Prepare every maxillary tooth for indirect veneers — Full arch preparation overtreats a localised problem.

stem: A root-filled mandibular molar has an isolated 11-mm narrow pocket along one root, recurrent sinus tract and a J-shaped periradicular radiolucency. stem: A patient previously experienced reciprocal clicking of one temporomandibular joint. Over the past week the click has disappeared and painful mouth opening is restricted with deflection to the affected side. No red flags are present.

options.B: Normal maturation of joint anatomy
options.C: Trigeminal neuralgia with no jaw limitation
options.D: Irreversible fracture of every restoration
options.E: Dental abscess solely because the jaw hurts

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Disc displacement without reduction causing closed lock

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: A transition from clicking to restricted opening can suggest disc displacement without reduction, while clinical assessment is needed to exclude other diagnoses.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
B. Normal maturation of joint anatomy — The symptomatic onset and restriction are not explained by normal joint maturation.
C. Trigeminal neuralgia with no jaw limitation — Neuralgia alone would not usually account for mechanical opening restriction following reciprocal clicking.
D. Irreversible fracture of every restoration — No restorations are described as fractured.
E. Dental abscess solely because the jaw hurts — A dental abscess requires separate infectious diagnostic findings.

stem: An 11-year-old with an immature permanent maxillary incisor presents immediately after avulsion; the tooth has been kept moist in suitable storage medium. There are no other contraindications to replantation.
lead: Which treatment direction best preserves prognosis?

options.A: Discard the tooth because an immature apex is not treatable
options.B: Replant promptly, provide appropriate flexible splinting and monitor for pulp revascularisation or infection
options.C: Complete extraoral root-canal filling before replantation in every immature tooth
options.D: Wait six months for spontaneous eruption
options.E: Replace with a definitive implant immediately

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Replant promptly, provide appropriate flexible splinting and monitor for pulp revascularisation or infection

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Prompt replantation, appropriate splinting and structured follow-up support periodontal healing, with the possibility of revascularisation in immature permanent teeth.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Discard the tooth because an immature apex is not treatable — An immature permanent tooth should not routinely be discarded when replantation is appropriate.
C. Complete extraoral root-canal filling before replantation in every immature tooth — An immature replanted tooth may revascularise; extraoral obturation is not standard for every case.
D. Wait six months for spontaneous eruption — Six months of delay forfeits periodontal-ligament viability.
E. Replace with a definitive implant immediately — A definitive implant is inappropriate in a growing patient and cannot preserve the avulsed tooth.

stem: A patient complains that a newly made complete denture tips during chewing. Both dentures are examined for support, borders, tooth position and centric and eccentric contacts; the clinician must avoid treating a prosthesis design problem as a simple retention deficiency. options.D: Correct the occlusal plane and posterior tooth position over the effective support area
options.E: Consider a new prosthesis design when the basal seat and jaw relationship have changed fundamentally

stem: A root-filled premolar is considered for definitive restoration. The clinical crown has been dismantled sufficiently to assess the remaining dentine. Post type, ferrule, periodontal support and crown-root ratio are documented, along with any implications of crown lengthening or orthodontic extrusion. options.D: Avoid repeated post enlargement when the remaining root is structurally nonrestorable
options.E: Preserve a sound circumferential ferrule and restore without adding an unnecessary post

stem: An adhesively retained lithium disilicate onlay is planned with adequate enamel and isolation. The laboratory confirms that the restoration is a silica-based glass ceramic.
lead: Which surface treatment is suitable when specified by the material manufacturer?

options.A: Zirconia-only MDP priming without ceramic etch
options.B: Compatible hydrofluoric acid etching followed by silanisation and resin bonding
options.C: No pretreatment because lithium disilicate chemically bonds to water
options.D: Mechanical sandpaper roughening alone
options.E: Repeated chairside grinding without polishing

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Compatible hydrofluoric acid etching followed by silanisation and resin bonding

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Lithium disilicate is silica-based and can be bonded with appropriate manufacturer-specified ceramic etching and silane protocols, unlike zirconia.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Zirconia-only MDP priming without ceramic etch — Zirconia-only priming omits the usual silica-glass conditioning steps.
C. No pretreatment because lithium disilicate chemically bonds to water — Water does not provide chemical bonding of lithium disilicate to resin.
D. Mechanical sandpaper roughening alone — Roughening alone is insufficient for a validated adhesive protocol.
E. Repeated chairside grinding without polishing — Grinding without appropriate finishing can damage the ceramic and does not condition the intaglio surface.

stem: A permanent maxillary central incisor has an uncomplicated enamel-dentine crown fracture with no associated luxation injury. Clinical sensibility and periapical assessments are documented at presentation.
lead: What is the usual follow-up interval under IADT 2020 guidance?

options.A: No review unless the tooth changes colour
options.B: Daily radiographs for a month
options.C: Clinical and radiographic review at 6–8 weeks and one year
options.D: Routine splinting for four months
options.E: Extraction after six months

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Clinical and radiographic review at 6–8 weeks and one year

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: IADT uncomplicated crown-fracture guidance uses 6–8-week and one-year clinical/radiographic follow-up; concomitant luxation changes follow-up.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. No review unless the tooth changes colour — Pulp complications may emerge after the initial injury despite satisfactory first tests.
B. Daily radiographs for a month — Daily radiographs provide no supported routine benefit and unnecessary exposure.
D. Routine splinting for four months — Uncomplicated crown fractures without luxation do not routinely need prolonged splinting.
E. Extraction after six months — Routine extraction is not indicated for an uncomplicated restorable fracture.

theme: Test prevalence and positive predictive value
stem: A screening test has reasonably good sensitivity and specificity, but it is used in a population with very low prevalence of the condition. The positive result conflicts with an otherwise unremarkable clinical examination.
lead: Which statement about the positive result is most accurate?

options.A: Its positive predictive value must be 100%
options.B: Its interpretation depends on pretest probability and likelihood ratios; false positives may predominate in low-prevalence settings
options.C: Specificity is identical to the proportion of positive tests that are true positives
options.D: Prevalence affects analytical sensitivity itself
options.E: A positive result automatically justifies irreversible treatment

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Its interpretation depends on pretest probability and likelihood ratios; false positives may predominate in low-prevalence settings

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: With a low pretest probability, the probability of disease after a positive test may remain modest despite apparently good test performance.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Its positive predictive value must be 100% — Positive predictive value can be low when disease prevalence is low.
C. Specificity is identical to the proportion of positive tests that are true positives — Specificity is a conditional probability among those without disease, not positive predictive value.
D. Prevalence affects analytical sensitivity itself — Prevalence alters predictive probability, not the inherent analytical sensitivity in the usual interpretation.
E. A positive result automatically justifies irreversible treatment — Diagnostic and clinical confirmation is needed before irreversible treatment.

stem: A complex fixed or implant prosthesis is planned using an intraoral scanner and a three-dimensional dataset. The team must decide when the recorded geometry is trustworthy, when another acquisition is justified and when an analogue verification step adds information. A complete-arch implant scan shows progressively different interimplant distances across rescans, although single short segments align well. The dentist has checked the relevant supporting records and asks for a recommendation that avoids unnecessary intervention.
lead: What is the best next clinical decision?

options.A: Use an alternative impression or verification index to control long-span stitching error
options.B: Repeat the intraoral scan with a changed acquisition path and improved surface management
options.C: Accept the scan after a local cross-check shows consistent landmarks and sufficient tissue capture
options.D: Re-register the CBCT and optical surface datasets using stable landmarks before final planning
options.E: Perform a new scan only after hardware or material artefact has been reduced or interpreted appropriately

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Use an alternative impression or verification index to control long-span stitching error.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A complete-arch implant scan shows progressively different interimplant distances across rescans, although single short segments align well.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Long-span stitching and passive-fit concerns justify independent verification.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Saliva and reflective subgingival surfaces obscure one proximal preparation margin and repeated scans show inconsistent finish-line shape. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A short-span preparation has clear margins, stable contacts and repeat scans that agree with clinical measurements. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Implant planning software shows the planned crown shifted away from the actual cast after CBCT and surface models were merged. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A large metallic restoration produces streak artefact adjacent to a canal and the interpreted border changes with reconstruction settings. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A completely edentulous arch is being scanned optically for an implant-supported full-arch framework. Few stable geometric landmarks are present and long-span image stitching may accumulate error.
lead: What is the most appropriate additional control?

options.A: Assume software automatically eliminates drift
options.B: Verify accuracy with a validated independent reference or verification method before definitive manufacture
options.C: Discard all conventional impressions regardless of scanner validation
options.D: Increase occlusal vertical dimension to correct stitching
options.E: Accept the file because individual scan bodies look sharp

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Verify accuracy with a validated independent reference or verification method before definitive manufacture

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Long-span stitching error and absent anatomical features can affect full-arch accuracy; prosthetic fit requires validation beyond screen appearance.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Assume software automatically eliminates drift — The presence of software stitching does not prove cumulative error is absent.
C. Discard all conventional impressions regardless of scanner validation — Conventional workflows remain useful in selected difficult full-arch situations.
D. Increase occlusal vertical dimension to correct stitching — Vertical dimension does not resolve scan-registration drift.
E. Accept the file because individual scan bodies look sharp — Sharp local capture does not guarantee accurate interimplant spatial relationships.

stem: A restored implant is reviewed because of discomfort, bleeding, tissue change or a cosmetic complaint. Baseline probing and imaging are available or their absence is recognised; mucosal inflammation must be distinguished from progressive loss of supporting bone. There is new deep probing, suppuration and radiographic bone loss compared with the restoration baseline. The patient understands that several technically feasible options differ in biological burden, retrievability, and long-term maintenance. The consultant is asked to prioritise the evidence that most changes prognosis.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Assess prosthetic contours and residual cement as removable inflammatory drivers
options.B: Return to risk-based maintenance when probing, tissues and bone are stable
options.C: Improve plaque control and prosthetic cleanability, then reassess peri-implant mucositis
options.D: Consider increasing keratinised mucosa when brushing discomfort persists despite health and suitable hygiene measures
options.E: Investigate peri-implantitis with baseline comparison and provide cause-focused nonsurgical care before considering further treatment

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Investigate peri-implantitis with baseline comparison and provide cause-focused nonsurgical care before considering further treatment.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: There is new deep probing, suppuration and radiographic bone loss compared with the restoration baseline.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Inflammation with progressive support loss requires peri-implantitis assessment and staged intervention.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A cement-retained crown has submucosal excess cement visible after careful examination and inflammation localised to that area. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Probing is unchanged from baseline, no bleeding or suppuration exists, and radiographs show no progression. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Bleeding occurs with plaque accumulation but no progressive bone loss beyond expected remodelling, and the patient struggles to clean a bulky contour. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: An otherwise healthy posterior implant has less than 1 mm of buccal keratinised tissue and recurrent painful toothbrushing despite careful plaque control. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A patient with an implant-supported prosthesis presents for treatment planning or review. The prosthesis has been assessed for passivity, component fit, access-channel location, tissue support, occlusion, plaque access and the anticipated need for maintenance or future modification. A multiunit bridge has a gap on the one-screw test and one cylinder does not fully seat until the distal screw is tightened. The referral includes a clear account of the principal problem; the patient asks which option should be prioritised before further treatment.
lead: Which management option is most appropriate on the information given?

options.B: Reassess implant angulation or use a suitable angulated component only if a safe retrievable restoration can be designed
options.C: Develop peri-implant soft tissues with an appropriately shaped provisional restoration before final crown fabrication
options.D: Use a retrievable screw-retained design when access emerges favourably and prosthetic support is adequate
options.E: Correct excessive emergence contour and allow hygiene access before treating inflammation as refractory disease

stem: A patient with a partially dentate arch is considering a tooth-supported reconstruction. The candidate abutments have been charted for ferrule, clinical crown height, periodontal attachment, endodontic health and load distribution; treatment cost and possible future failure are important. A strategically valuable root has insufficient coronal dentine but orthodontic extrusion can create ferrule without losing necessary root support. The dentist has checked the relevant supporting records and asks for a recommendation that avoids unnecessary intervention.

options.A: Choose a removable design that allows independent replacement of future failing teeth
options.B: Stage periodontal therapy and reassess support rather than judging prognosis from bone loss percentage alone

options.D: Gain coronal tooth structure by appropriate orthodontic extrusion before reassessing restorability
options.E: Avoid relying on a structurally hopeless root and redesign the span or replacement strategy

stem: A patient is referred for rehabilitation of multiple failing restorations, missing posterior support and an aesthetic complaint. Diagnostic records show several risks that could change after initial treatment. The specialist must sequence care to prevent premature commitment to an expensive irreversible plan. stem: A patient has a high technical complexity score for extensive fixed prosthodontics but cannot maintain plaque control and prefers a simpler removable option. The clinician is considering whether the RDITN score mandates the most technically advanced plan.
lead: What is the most defensible interpretation?

options.A: The highest numerical code obliges full-arch fixed reconstruction
options.B: Patient preference is irrelevant once technical complexity is scored
options.C: The score defines complexity, while an informed treatment plan must additionally consider maintainability, patient values and risk
options.D: A technically complex case must always be treated immediately
options.E: The score alone establishes prognosis of each strategic tooth

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — The score defines complexity, while an informed treatment plan must additionally consider maintainability, patient values and risk

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Complexity classification is not consent, indication, prognosis or a prescription for a specific prosthesis.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. The highest numerical code obliges full-arch fixed reconstruction — Technical complexity does not mandate a fixed reconstruction.
B. Patient preference is irrelevant once technical complexity is scored — Patient consent and preferences remain essential to care selection.
D. A technically complex case must always be treated immediately — Disease control and planning may be prerequisites to definitive treatment.
E. The score alone establishes prognosis of each strategic tooth — A complexity score does not establish a tooth-by-tooth prognosis.

stem: After a sporting injury, a maxillary central incisor has tenderness, slight mobility and a subtle radiolucent line on one periapical projection. Two additional angulated periapicals remain equivocal, and knowing whether the fracture is cervical or middle-third would change management.

options.B: A justified small-field CBCT to assess suspected root fracture extent if the result will change management
options.C: No further clinical examination is required

stem: A mandibular complete denture repeatedly dislodges during speech despite acceptable fit of the intaglio surface and reasonable border extension. The polished lingual surface is bulky and impinges on tongue function.

stem: Posterior maxillary implant rehabilitation is considered in a patient with limited residual bone and radiographic sinus findings. Restorative space, sinus ostial patency, anatomy and alternatives to grafting are evaluated; the surgeon asks whether augmentation should proceed or be modified. Residual vertical bone permits a validated short-implant strategy for the planned crown, and the patient wishes to avoid complex grafting. The patient wishes to preserve future options where possible but would accept a more extensive treatment if demonstrably necessary.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Obtain or re-interpret limited-field three-dimensional imaging where anatomy materially affects the chosen surgical path
options.B: Consider a short implant or prosthetic alternative when dimensions and risk-benefit support avoiding major augmentation
options.C: Proceed with the planned approach when an asymptomatic benign sinus-floor finding does not obstruct drainage
options.D: Refer for sinus assessment before augmentation when symptoms or ostial obstruction suggest active disease
options.E: Plan staged augmentation when graft volume, primary stability and restorative position cannot be achieved simultaneously

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Consider a short implant or prosthetic alternative when dimensions and risk-benefit support avoiding major augmentation.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: Residual vertical bone permits a validated short-implant strategy for the planned crown, and the patient wishes to avoid complex grafting.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: A less invasive suitable implant option may outperform augmentation-heavy treatment on total burden.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Panoramic imaging does not define buccopalatal width or the relation of the sinus septum to the intended implant site. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A small dome-shaped sinus-floor opacity is asymptomatic, the ostium is patent and a suitable lateral window can avoid relevant structures. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The patient has unilateral discharge, sinus pain and imaging showing occluded drainage with diffuse mucosal disease. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: There is minimal residual bone, insufficient primary stability and a large volume of reconstruction needed for the restorative plan. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A young adult with a developmental dental anomaly seeks an attractive, durable restorative solution. Orthodontic records, tooth vitality, enamel quality, jaw growth and periodontal support have been assessed. The treatment must address long-term reparability and avoid unnecessary loss of otherwise sound tissue. A primary canine remains sound and stable with an acceptable root; the permanent successor is absent and the patient is still growing. Both a staged and a direct approach have been discussed, and neither is excluded solely by cost or operator access.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Consider conventional full coverage only where severe structural deficiency limits reliable additive solutions
options.B: Plan a multidisciplinary stage of orthodontic redistribution before selecting prosthesis form
options.C: Offer additive direct composite with maintenance and potential later modification
options.D: Retain a suitable primary tooth temporarily with monitoring while definitive timing is reconsidered
options.E: Plan adhesive indirect restorations only after assessing the quality and amount of bondable enamel

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Retain a suitable primary tooth temporarily with monitoring while definitive timing is reconsidered.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A primary canine remains sound and stable with an acceptable root; the permanent successor is absent and the patient is still growing.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Conservative retention can preserve bone and choices until long-term planning is mature.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:

stem: A stable patient takes apixaban twice daily. An elective periodontal flap procedure with higher postoperative bleeding risk is planned for 09:00. There are no additional thrombotic factors requiring specialist variation.
lead: Which medication plan best follows SDCEP recommendations?

options.A: Stop apixaban five days before surgery without liaison
options.B: Miss the morning apixaban dose, use local haemostasis and advise when to resume the evening dose
options.C: Continue the morning apixaban dose because all dental treatments are low risk
options.D: Switch to warfarin for the operation
options.E: Miss all subsequent doses until sutures are removed

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Miss the morning apixaban dose, use local haemostasis and advise when to resume the evening dose

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: For higher-bleeding-risk dental procedures, SDCEP advises missing the morning apixaban dose and taking the evening dose at its usual time if at least four hours after haemostasis.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Stop apixaban five days before surgery without liaison — Unsupervised prolonged cessation increases thrombotic risk.
C. Continue the morning apixaban dose because all dental treatments are low risk — The flap is classified as a higher-risk dental procedure, not a low-risk one.
D. Switch to warfarin for the operation — Routine conversion to warfarin is not recommended for this dental procedure.
E. Miss all subsequent doses until sutures are removed — Withholding later doses until suture removal is excessive and unsupported.

stem: A mandibular removable partial denture is planned for a Kennedy Class I pattern. stem: A patient receives an implant where definitive crown timing is under consideration. theme: RPD Kennedy I: mesial rest and clasp geometry
stem: A mandibular bilateral distal-extension RPD is being designed with one terminal premolar on each side. The clinician wishes to limit potentially damaging distal torque on abutments as the denture bases rotate towards the mucosa under function.
lead: Which design principle is appropriate, assuming adequate surveys and tooth contours?

options.A: Distal occlusal rests with rigid circumferential arms engaging deep mesial undercuts in all cases
options.B: Consider mesial rests with a suitably stress-releasing direct retainer design such as RPI where anatomy permits
options.C: Remove all rests so the saddles are purely mucosa-supported
options.D: Place an indirect retainer only in the distal saddle
options.E: Use a major connector that flexes markedly under load

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Consider mesial rests with a suitably stress-releasing direct retainer design such as RPI where anatomy permits

RATIONALE: A mesial rest and appropriately selected stress-releasing clasp can reduce unfavourable distal torque in many distal-extension situations. RPI is not universal: soft-tissue undercuts, vestibular depth and surveys may necessitate alternatives such as RPA.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Distal occlusal rests with rigid circumferential arms engaging deep mesial undercuts in all cases C. Remove all rests so the saddles are purely mucosa-supported D. Place an indirect retainer only in the distal saddle E. Use a major connector that flexes markedly under load

stem: A root-filled upper central incisor has adequate root length, no evidence of vertical root fracture and a favourable periodontal prognosis. After caries removal, only a small coronal rim remains and a post is being considered.
lead: Which statement best informs restorability?

options.A: A larger post strengthens the root independent of remaining tooth structure
options.B: Ferrule and remaining sound coronal dentine are key considerations; a post primarily retains the core
options.C: Every root-filled tooth requires a post before crown
options.D: A full crown alone makes a vertically fractured root restorable
options.E: Crown lengthening can always be carried out without periodontal or aesthetic cost

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Ferrule and remaining sound coronal dentine are key considerations; a post primarily retains the core

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Posts primarily retain cores; remaining sound tooth structure and adequate ferrule influence fracture resistance and prognosis.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. A larger post strengthens the root independent of remaining tooth structure — Oversized posts may weaken the root rather than reinforce it.
C. Every root-filled tooth requires a post before crown — Posts are indicated by core-retention needs, not by pulp status alone.
D. A full crown alone makes a vertically fractured root restorable — A confirmed vertical root fracture is not corrected by a crown.
E. Crown lengthening can always be carried out without periodontal or aesthetic cost — Crown lengthening may compromise support, crown-root ratio or aesthetics.

stem: A complex fixed or implant prosthesis is planned using an intraoral scanner and a three-dimensional dataset. options.D: Accept the scan after a local cross-check shows consistent landmarks and sufficient tissue capture

stem: A patient has erosive tooth wear that affects future restorative choices. stem: A mandibular removable partial denture is planned for a Kennedy Class I pattern. stem: A 31-year-old has shallow, stable erosive changes restricted to a few posterior teeth. No sensitivity, progressive loss or aesthetic complaint is present. Risk assessment identifies frequent acidic drinks.
lead: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Immediate full-mouth crowns at raised vertical dimension
options.B: Dietary risk reduction, monitoring with repeatable records and prevention
options.C: All anterior teeth restored with indirect palatal ceramics
options.D: Increase occlusal vertical dimension to treat the BEWE score itself
options.E: Extract all posterior teeth and place implants

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Dietary risk reduction, monitoring with repeatable records and prevention

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Wear management must combine cause, activity, symptoms and functional impact; stable limited erosive wear generally starts with prevention and monitoring.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Immediate full-mouth crowns at raised vertical dimension — Conservative stable wear does not justify universal full-coverage reconstruction.
C. All anterior teeth restored with indirect palatal ceramics — There is no anterior restorative indication in this vignette.
D. Increase occlusal vertical dimension to treat the BEWE score itself — BEWE is an assessment tool, not by itself a directive to increase OVD.
E. Extract all posterior teeth and place implants — Extraction is not justified in stable limited erosive wear.

options.E: Provide a rigid custom tray and appropriate wash/space control when deformable bulk would distort the record

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Provide a rigid custom tray and appropriate wash/space control when deformable bulk would distort the record.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A long impression has thin unsupported bulk and flexes on removal, creating systematic arch distortion.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Adequate tray stiffness and controlled wash support are essential.

stem: A posterior all-ceramic bridge has fractured through an undersized connector after one year. The occlusion shows repeated lateral loading; the material and span are otherwise appropriate.
lead: What is the most useful design review before remaking?

options.A: Select a lighter cement shade
options.B: Check connector cross-section and height, occlusal clearance and loading rather than changing surface glaze alone
options.C: Reduce the connector dimensions to increase flexibility
options.D: Polish only the external fracture edge
options.E: Change shade tab under fluorescent light

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Check connector cross-section and height, occlusal clearance and loading rather than changing surface glaze alone

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Connector geometry and tensile stresses are central determinants of all-ceramic FDP fracture risk; surface glaze cannot correct inadequate dimensions.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Select a lighter cement shade — Cement shade does not correct structural connector weakness.
C. Reduce the connector dimensions to increase flexibility — Smaller connector sections increase fracture risk under bending.
D. Polish only the external fracture edge — Surface polishing alone does not restore an undersized structural connector.
E. Change shade tab under fluorescent light — Shade selection cannot correct loading or structural design.

stem: A previously restored molar has intermittent pain on chewing. Cold sensibility, percussion, six-point periodontal probing, bite testing and an intra-oral radiograph are available. The clinician needs to distinguish a fractured cusp, pulpal disease, a vertical root fracture and non-odontogenic pain without committing prematurely to irreversible care. Spontaneous pain lasts hours, cold provokes prolonged lingering pain, and a protected cusp no longer explains the symptoms. The referral includes a clear account of the principal problem; the patient asks which option should be prioritised before further treatment.
lead: Which management option is most appropriate on the information given?

options.A: Assess the isolated deep periodontal defect and root-level fracture evidence before attempting reconstruction
options.B: Remove the existing restoration under magnification, assess the crack, and protect the cusp provisionally
options.C: Reassess the occlusion and muscular pain source before removing a technically sound restoration
options.D: Treat the confirmed symptomatic irreversible pulpitis before planning definitive cuspal coverage
options.E: Obtain targeted additional investigation because the initial tests are conflicting and the management choice would change

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Treat the confirmed symptomatic irreversible pulpitis before planning definitive cuspal coverage.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: Spontaneous pain lasts hours, cold provokes prolonged lingering pain, and a protected cusp no longer explains the symptoms.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: The pulpal diagnosis has advanced beyond an uncomplicated cracked vital cusp.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: There is a narrow isolated 10-mm pocket next to a root-filled tooth and a J-shaped radiolucency after repeated post debonding. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A sharp pain occurs specifically on release of pressure over the distolingual cusp, cold response is short and six-point probing is 2–3 mm throughout. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The tooth has no localised bite-test response and reproducible pain follows masseter loading, with matched nocturnal clenching and normal dental investigations. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A recently traumatised tooth tests negative to cold but has normal periapical imaging, uncertain pulpal status and no swelling. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

The existing prosthesis has been assessed for fit, extension, occlusion, hygiene and adaptation. Implant surgery may improve retention but entails additional financial and maintenance commitments. options.C: Correct the conventional denture first when technical faults explain instability

theme: CBCT-surface scan registration for guided surgery
stem: An implant guide is planned by registering a CBCT dataset to an intraoral surface scan. The patient has metallic restorations producing CBCT artefacts, and the proposed guide appears shifted near adjacent roots.
lead: Which action most directly reduces planning-to-placement risk?

options.A: Accept the scan registration because the planning software displays a green marker
options.B: Recheck the registration against reliable anatomy, verify guide seating and correct the dataset before surgery
options.C: Increase drill speed to reduce deviation
options.D: Skip confirmation radiographs after guide delivery
options.E: Move the implant digitally away from the roots without checking the matched datasets

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Recheck the registration against reliable anatomy, verify guide seating and correct the dataset before surgery

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Registration and seating errors can propagate into guide position; anatomical correspondence and clinical verification must be checked.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Accept the scan registration because the planning software displays a green marker — A software status indicator is not independent anatomical verification.
C. Increase drill speed to reduce deviation — Drill speed does not repair incorrect registration geometry.
D. Skip confirmation radiographs after guide delivery — Verification is more important when image registration is uncertain.
E. Move the implant digitally away from the roots without checking the matched datasets — Moving a virtual implant does not correct underlying dataset mismatch.

stem: A prosthodontist is assessing discrepant clinical findings in a restoration or implant follow-up. A screening test, clinical examination and relevant imaging each have different sensitivities and potential errors; the decision should be based on a coherent synthesis, not an isolated number. Peri-implant probing measurements differ by 3 mm between visits taken by different clinicians with unequal force and angulation. The patient wishes to preserve future options where possible but would accept a more extensive treatment if demonstrably necessary.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Interpret longitudinal change against baseline rather than a single cross-sectional cut-off
options.B: Request an additional targeted test when a negative result conflicts with strong clinical suspicion
options.C: Confirm the positive screening finding with targeted examination when disease prevalence is low
options.D: Proceed with a conservative decision when investigations consistently show low risk and intervention carries greater harm
options.E: Repeat an unreliable measurement using a standardised technique before judging progression

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Repeat an unreliable measurement using a standardised technique before judging progression.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: Peri-implant probing measurements differ by 3 mm between visits taken by different clinicians with unequal force and angulation.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Measurement reproducibility must be established before diagnosing tissue change.

stem: A referral includes an old RDITN code of 3. The clinician is also asked to use the contemporary NHS England Levels 1–3 restorative care framework for pathway planning.
lead: Which statement most accurately distinguishes the frameworks?

options.A: RDITN code 3 automatically guarantees NHS Level 3 treatment
options.B: The frameworks describe complexity, but current pathway allocation requires clinical triage and cannot be inferred from RDITN alone
options.C: The NHS framework replaced the need for any clinical complexity assessment
options.D: Both codes represent exactly the same validated numerical scale
options.E: An RDITN code measures only the number of missing teeth

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — The frameworks describe complexity, but current pathway allocation requires clinical triage and cannot be inferred from RDITN alone

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: RDITN is an older complexity-index framework; NHS levels are service/pathway complexity descriptions requiring assessment of patient and treatment context.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. RDITN code 3 automatically guarantees NHS Level 3 treatment — One index code does not automatically allocate a care pathway.
C. The NHS framework replaced the need for any clinical complexity assessment — Complexity assessment remains important within the current framework.
D. Both codes represent exactly the same validated numerical scale — The numerical labels are not equivalent measurements.
E. An RDITN code measures only the number of missing teeth — RDITN includes periodontal, root-canal, fixed and removable components, not only missing teeth.

stem: A patient complains that a newly made complete denture tips during chewing. Both dentures are examined for support, borders, tooth position and centric and eccentric contacts; the clinician must avoid treating a prosthesis design problem as a simple retention deficiency. Severe post-extraction ridge remodelling has occurred since the impression, and a prosthesis now has global poor fit and support. The referral includes a clear account of the principal problem; the patient asks which option should be prioritised before further treatment.
lead: Which management option is most appropriate on the information given?

options.A: Consider a new prosthesis design when the basal seat and jaw relationship have changed fundamentally
options.B: Eliminate a reproducible premature centric contact and re-evaluate balance
options.C: Correct the occlusal plane and posterior tooth position over the effective support area
options.D: Re-record jaw relations when centric records are inconsistent and the vertical dimension is unverified
options.E: Correct peripheral extension and functional polished-surface contours that dislodge the denture

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Consider a new prosthesis design when the basal seat and jaw relationship have changed fundamentally.

theme: Combination syndrome versus denture tooth wear
stem: A patient has a long-standing maxillary complete denture opposing a mandibular implant overdenture. The upper anterior ridge is significantly more resorbed than the posterior ridge, the anterior tissue is mobile and the maxillary tuberosities are enlarged. The denture has progressively rotated and loses retention.
lead: Which explanation best integrates the clinical pattern?

options.A: Combination syndrome associated with unfavourable anterior loading and tissue changes
options.B: Normal isolated wear of acrylic teeth alone
options.C: An exclusively allergic response to denture cleanser
options.D: A scan-body registration error
options.E: A root fracture in the edentulous maxilla

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Combination syndrome associated with unfavourable anterior loading and tissue changes

RATIONALE: The pattern of anterior maxillary ridge resorption, flabby tissues and posterior compensatory changes is consistent with combination syndrome. Denture instability may have several causes, so assessment of occlusal support and the whole denture system remains essential.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: B. Normal isolated wear of acrylic teeth alone C. An exclusively allergic response to denture cleanser D. A scan-body registration error E. A root fracture in the edentulous maxilla

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

EVIDENCE / SOURCE: Complete denture occlusion and combination syndrome

stem: A specialist provides a care plan for tooth wear after reviewing mounted casts or digital design, clinical photographs, substrate quality and the intended occlusal scheme. stem: A patient returns after delivery of a new removable prosthesis with discomfort or poor tolerance. The pattern of symptoms, mucosal findings, occlusal examination and functional movements are recorded before any intervention. There are widespread tender ridges, no distinct pressure spot and an easily reproducible eccentric balancing error. stem: A maxillary Kennedy Class III bounded saddle is to replace a first molar. Both adjacent abutments have good periodontal support and surveyed contours. The operator plans a clasp but omits rests and guide planes, believing that clasp retention alone will prevent the base from sinking.

options.B: Recommend medical liaison to modify procedural risk without unnecessarily stopping therapy

stem: A patient with an implant crown has bleeding on probing and plaque accumulation. Probing depths are unchanged from baseline, and standardised radiographs show no progressive supporting-bone loss. The implant is stable.
lead: What is the most likely diagnosis and initial approach?

options.A: Peri-implantitis requiring immediate implant removal
options.B: Peri-implant mucositis: improve biofilm control and address plaque-retentive prosthesis features
options.C: Physiological gingival recession: no oral-hygiene change
options.D: Implant fracture requiring replacement
options.E: Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Peri-implant mucositis: improve biofilm control and address plaque-retentive prosthesis features

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Inflammation without progressive supporting-bone loss fits peri-implant mucositis; plaque control and prosthesis cleansability are first priorities.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Peri-implantitis requiring immediate implant removal — Progressive supporting-bone loss defining peri-implantitis is absent.
C. Physiological gingival recession: no oral-hygiene change — Bleeding and plaque are active inflammatory findings, not merely physiological recession.
D. Implant fracture requiring replacement — The implant is stable and there is no evidence of structural fracture.
E. Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw — The described findings do not meet criteria for medication-related jaw osteonecrosis.

stem: Mounted casts show that on protrusion, a posterior interference occurs along the distal-facing incline of a maxillary molar against the mesial-facing incline of a mandibular molar. The patient's anterior guidance is suitable and centric occlusion must remain unchanged.

options.B: MUDL: mesial upper and distal lower

options.D: No adjustment can be considered for protrusive interference

stem: Posterior maxillary implant rehabilitation is considered in a patient with limited residual bone and radiographic sinus findings. Restorative space, sinus ostial patency, anatomy and alternatives to grafting are evaluated; the surgeon asks whether augmentation should proceed or be modified. Residual vertical bone permits a validated short-implant strategy for the planned crown, and the patient wishes to avoid complex grafting. Both a staged and a direct approach have been discussed, and neither is excluded solely by cost or operator access.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Refer for sinus assessment before augmentation when symptoms or ostial obstruction suggest active disease
options.B: Consider a short implant or prosthetic alternative when dimensions and risk-benefit support avoiding major augmentation
options.C: Obtain or re-interpret limited-field three-dimensional imaging where anatomy materially affects the chosen surgical path
options.D: Proceed with the planned approach when an asymptomatic benign sinus-floor finding does not obstruct drainage
options.E: Plan staged augmentation when graft volume, primary stability and restorative position cannot be achieved simultaneously

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Consider a short implant or prosthetic alternative when dimensions and risk-benefit support avoiding major augmentation.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: Residual vertical bone permits a validated short-implant strategy for the planned crown, and the patient wishes to avoid complex grafting.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: A less invasive suitable implant option may outperform augmentation-heavy treatment on total burden.

stem: A root-filled mandibular molar has almost no supragingival peripheral dentine. Obtaining a 2-mm ferrule circumferentially would require crown lengthening into the furcation and create an unacceptable crown-to-root ratio. The tooth has a large periapical lesion and mobility.

stem: A restored implant is reviewed because of discomfort, bleeding, tissue change or a cosmetic complaint. Baseline probing and imaging are available or their absence is recognised; mucosal inflammation must be distinguished from progressive loss of supporting bone. stem: A specialist is counselling a patient about prosthodontic options with different initial and lifetime maintenance burdens. The patient’s values, manual dexterity and capacity for periodic recall are recorded explicitly. An enamel-rich anterior tooth is fractured, the patient values future repair and seeks minimal invasive preparation. options.A: Select a conservative adhesive restoration that is simple to repair and preserves intact teeth
options.B: Offer implant-supported treatment only after explaining component and peri-implant maintenance

options.D: Document non-restoration as a considered informed option when intervention has limited incremental benefit
options.E: Recommend a removable device that is cleanable and affordable with predictable replacement needs

stem: A dentist requests a restorative plan for discoloured or malformed anterior teeth. Tooth vitality, intrinsic and extrinsic staining, existing restorations, enamel quantity, age and the ability to maintain the result are documented. A mature patient has a small persistent labio-incisal defect and repeated composite cohesive failure, with abundant enamel available for an adhesive veneer. options.A: Reserve full coverage for teeth with extensive structural compromise or inadequate conservative options
options.B: Select an enamel-bonded partial-coverage veneer for an appropriate mature patient with persistent shape and colour concerns
options.C: Begin with professional cleaning or whitening when tooth structure is intact and colour is the principal complaint
options.D: Investigate non-vital tooth discolouration and endodontic status before attempting internal bleaching or definitive coverage
options.E: Use direct composite addition where shape and repairability matter more than long-term ceramic colour stability

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A mature patient has a small persistent labio-incisal defect and repeated composite cohesive failure, with abundant enamel available for an adhesive veneer.

stem: A 24-year-old with a missing maxillary lateral incisor has sound enamel on the neighbouring canine, stable occlusion and no need for conventional full-coverage crowns. An adhesive bridge is preferred.
lead: Which option is the most conservative defensible fixed solution?

options.A: Prepare both adjacent sound teeth for complete crowns
options.B: A suitably designed single-retainer cantilever resin-bonded bridge after occlusal assessment
options.C: Extract the sound canine to improve pontic symmetry
options.D: Fixed–fixed adhesive retainers are mandatory for every short span
options.E: Use an implant without assessing ridge maturity and anatomical limits

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — A suitably designed single-retainer cantilever resin-bonded bridge after occlusal assessment

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: A single-retainer cantilever RBB can preserve sound enamel and avoid differential abutment mobility where clinical conditions permit.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Prepare both adjacent sound teeth for complete crowns — Sound adjacent enamel should not be sacrificed without an indication for crowns.
C. Extract the sound canine to improve pontic symmetry — Extraction of a sound abutment is disproportionate.
D. Fixed–fixed adhesive retainers are mandatory for every short span — Two-retainer adhesive designs can introduce differential-abutment movement and are not universally required.
E. Use an implant without assessing ridge maturity and anatomical limits — Implants require growth and site assessment and may not be the least invasive option.

theme: TMD: distinguish headache attributed to TMD
stem: A 45-year-old reports temporal headaches that are consistently modified by jaw movement and parafunction. Palpation of the temporalis reproduces the familiar headache, neurological review is normal and no thunderclap or systemic red flags are present.
lead: Which assessment is most appropriate?

options.A: Diagnose trigeminal neuralgia because pain is near the eye
options.B: Dismiss all symptoms because jaw opening is normal
options.C: Consider headache attributed to TMD after excluding other causes, with conservative management
options.D: Classify as a periapical abscess automatically
options.E: Recommend immediate occlusal equilibration of every restoration

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Consider headache attributed to TMD after excluding other causes, with conservative management

RATIONALE: Headache modified by jaw activity and reproduced in temporalis can meet criteria for headache attributed to TMD, but serious and primary headaches must still be considered. Reversible care rather than occlusal reshaping is appropriate initially.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. Diagnose trigeminal neuralgia because pain is near the eye B. Dismiss all symptoms because jaw opening is normal D. Classify as a periapical abscess automatically E. Recommend immediate occlusal equilibration of every restoration

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

EVIDENCE / SOURCE: DC/TMD classification and orofacial pain differential diagnosis

stem: An RDITN periodontal component initially receives complexity code 1. Two applicable patient-related modifying factors are identified. Under the original RDITN rules, a modifying factor may increase that component by one code increment; multiple factors do not accumulate.
lead: Which component complexity code should be entered?

options.A: 1 because modifiers cannot affect the score
options.B: 2 because modifiers are noncumulative
options.C: 3 because two modifiers must each add one point
options.D: 4 because two factors are added to the initial code
options.E: The number of modifiers is used instead of a complexity code

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — 2 because modifiers are noncumulative

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: The modifying factor can raise a component score by one code increment only, regardless of the number of applicable modifiers.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. 1 because modifiers cannot affect the score — Applicable modifiers can change a component score.
C. 3 because two modifiers must each add one point — Multiple modifiers are not added sequentially.
D. 4 because two factors are added to the initial code — The original three-level complexity scale cannot be scored as four.
E. The number of modifiers is used instead of a complexity code — Modifiers alter the relevant component score; they do not replace the coding system.

stem: A mandibular Kennedy Class I RPD has mesial occlusal rests on the terminal abutments. The distal-extension bases tend to rotate away from the tissues when sticky food is displaced.
lead: Which component function most directly resists this rotational displacement?

options.A: An indirect retainer positioned appropriately anterior to the fulcrum axis
options.B: A more flexible distal extension major connector
options.C: A deep undercut engaged by the denture base
options.D: A longer distal acrylic flange with no support check
options.E: Removal of all guiding planes

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — An indirect retainer positioned appropriately anterior to the fulcrum axis

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Indirect retention resists lifting/rotation of distal extension bases around the fulcrum line; position and support determine its effectiveness.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
B. A more flexible distal extension major connector — A flexible connector would compromise cross-arch rigidity and support.
C. A deep undercut engaged by the denture base — The tissue-supported denture base is not a retentive clasp undercut.
D. A longer distal acrylic flange with no support check — Flange length alone cannot control movement about the fulcrum.
E. Removal of all guiding planes — Guide planes contribute path control and stability rather than causing the problem.

stem: A patient has completed complex prosthodontic treatment and now needs a follow-up programme. The dentist should distinguish stable restorations requiring routine maintenance from new biological or mechanical findings requiring a focused response. stem: A laboratory asks whether a surface STL scan of the edentulous ridge can by itself show the inferior alveolar nerve canal for implant planning.
lead: What is the most accurate response?

options.A: Yes; an STL surface mesh contains all volumetric bone structures
options.B: Yes; STL contains voxel density in Hounsfield units
options.C: No; STL is surface geometry, whereas CBCT DICOM provides volumetric imaging for indicated anatomical assessment
options.D: No; DICOM contains only restoration colour
options.E: STL and DICOM are interchangeable file extensions

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — No; STL is surface geometry, whereas CBCT DICOM provides volumetric imaging for indicated anatomical assessment

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: STL describes surface mesh geometry and does not reveal internal anatomy; CBCT volumes are normally supplied as DICOM datasets.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Yes; an STL surface mesh contains all volumetric bone structures — Surface mesh geometry lacks internal nerve-canal anatomy.
B. Yes; STL contains voxel density in Hounsfield units — STL is not a volumetric voxel-density file.
D. No; DICOM contains only restoration colour — DICOM can contain volumetric CBCT anatomy, not only colour.
E. STL and DICOM are interchangeable file extensions — These formats encode different types of information.

stem: A patient is referred for specialist advice about a failing posterior restoration with uncertain root and pulpal prognosis. The history, bite testing, periodontal probing and available two-dimensional radiographs do not always distinguish fractured cusp, endodontic failure and root fracture. A root-filled tooth is persistently tender and has a growing periapical lesion, but no evidence of a fracture has yet been found.
