stem: A previously restored molar has intermittent pain on chewing. Cold sensibility, percussion, six-point periodontal probing, bite testing and an intra-oral radiograph are available. The clinician needs to distinguish a fractured cusp, pulpal disease, a vertical root fracture and non-odontogenic pain without committing prematurely to irreversible care. There is a narrow isolated 10-mm pocket next to a root-filled tooth and a J-shaped radiolucency after repeated post debonding. The dentist has checked the relevant supporting records and asks for a recommendation that avoids unnecessary intervention.
lead: Which management option is most appropriate on the information given?

options.A: Obtain targeted additional investigation because the initial tests are conflicting and the management choice would change
options.B: Treat the confirmed symptomatic irreversible pulpitis before planning definitive cuspal coverage
options.C: Reassess the occlusion and muscular pain source before removing a technically sound restoration
options.D: Assess the isolated deep periodontal defect and root-level fracture evidence before attempting reconstruction
options.E: Remove the existing restoration under magnification, assess the crack, and protect the cusp provisionally

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Assess the isolated deep periodontal defect and root-level fracture evidence before attempting reconstruction.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: There is a narrow isolated 10-mm pocket next to a root-filled tooth and a J-shaped radiolucency after repeated post debonding.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: A root fracture must be ruled out because it may make restorative treatment futile.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:

E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A sharp pain occurs specifically on release of pressure over the distolingual cusp, cold response is short and six-point probing is 2–3 mm throughout. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

options.B: Verify the intraoral framework or prosthesis fit before acceptance, especially across multiple implant supports
options.C: Specify material thickness, connector support and surface treatment based on the selected restoration
options.D: Provide a clear emergence-profile and margin prescription with photographs, shade and tissue contours
options.E: Select a retrievable screw-retained design where geometry, aesthetics and access permit

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Verify the intraoral framework or prosthesis fit before acceptance, especially across multiple implant supports.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A full-arch implant framework has a visible one-screw-test gap despite visually acceptable model fit.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Passive-fit verification is essential before loading the supporting implants.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The patient has completed several fixed units with healthy tissues but no post-treatment baseline or planned recall intervals. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A zirconia FDP has fractured at a thin connector; the remake prescription again omits dimensions and framework design. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A maxillary anterior unit requires custom tissue support and the laboratory has only a generic shade and unlabelled scan. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: An implant crown has a favourable central screw-access channel and a history of repeated cement-associated inflammation at another site. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A completely or partially edentulous patient requires a new removable prosthesis. A preliminary impression has been made, and the practitioner must select a definitive impression approach that records the denture-bearing anatomy without distorting fragile tissues or sacrificing border extension. The anterior maxillary ridge has a markedly flabby mobile segment, while the posterior palate is firm and well supported. Both a staged and a direct approach have been discussed, and neither is excluded solely by cost or operator access.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Use a copy/replica method when the existing contours and jaw relations have been successfully adapted to
options.B: Investigate and manage a pathologic mucosal condition before committing to the definitive impression
options.C: Choose a closed-mouth or functional technique when available support and muscle action warrant it
options.D: Use a selective-pressure impression with relief over mobile tissue and stable support elsewhere
options.E: Record functional borders with an appropriately extended custom tray and controlled moulding

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Use a selective-pressure impression with relief over mobile tissue and stable support elsewhere.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: The anterior maxillary ridge has a markedly flabby mobile segment, while the posterior palate is firm and well supported.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Mobile tissue should be recorded minimally displaced while maintaining support from firm anatomy.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: An older patient with Parkinson disease has successfully adapted to the old denture contours for years, but the occlusal surfaces are worn. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A severely atrophic mandible has limited conventional support and instability changes with muscular movement; controlled functional registration is feasible. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The primary cast shows an underextended lower lingual sulcus, and the old denture dislodges during functional tongue movement. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A patient scheduled for fixed prosthodontic work also reports TMJ symptoms. The dentist must determine whether the symptoms affect the restorative plan and whether irreversible occlusal reorganisation is justified. A patient has active familiar joint pain and unstable mandibular records while a full-arch occlusal change is proposed.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Delay extensive occlusal reorganisation until symptomatic TMD is assessed and stabilised
options.B: Refer for focused TMD assessment when locking or progressive limitation undermines reliable records
options.C: Avoid prophylactic occlusal adjustment when there is no established clinical indication
options.D: Use a reversible provisional scheme to test any necessary planned change in occlusal relationship
options.E: Proceed with a conformative restoration while monitoring a painless stable click

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Delay extensive occlusal reorganisation until symptomatic TMD is assessed and stabilised.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A patient has active familiar joint pain and unstable mandibular records while a full-arch occlusal change is proposed.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Active pain and inconsistent records warrant stabilisation before major irreversible reconstruction.

stem: An adult with a missing maxillary lateral incisor asks for a definitive restoration. A diagnostic wax-up, ridge assessment, smile-line record and adjacent root angulation have been reviewed. The implant position is being selected to permit a predictable cleansable crown rather than simply exploit available bone. An adequate three-dimensional restorative plan, stable tissues and a shared maintenance plan have all been confirmed. The patient understands that several technically feasible options differ in biological burden, retrievability, and long-term maintenance. The consultant is asked to prioritise the evidence that most changes prognosis.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Stage provisional soft-tissue contour development before the definitive implant crown
options.B: Correct the available ridge and inter-root restorative corridor before placing an implant
options.C: Proceed with the agreed implant restoration when prosthetic position, tissue support and patient consent are satisfactory
options.D: Re-evaluate a conservative adhesive replacement before committing to difficult implant surgery
options.E: Develop the three-dimensional implant plan from the intended crown contours and screw-access trajectory

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Proceed with the agreed implant restoration when prosthetic position, tissue support and patient consent are satisfactory.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: An adequate three-dimensional restorative plan, stable tissues and a shared maintenance plan have all been confirmed.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Definitive treatment may proceed once major constraints are resolved.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The implant is well integrated but the provisional crown has never been used to shape the thin papilla and emergence profile. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A patient has recurrent preauricular or facial pain and seeks dental treatment. The symptoms, opening pattern, joint sounds, muscular palpation, neurological signs and relation to jaw function are examined. A specialist must avoid assuming that occlusion is responsible for every pain complaint. The patient reports a dull ache increased by chewing and palpation reproduces familiar pain over the masseter. The patient wishes to preserve future options where possible but would accept a more extensive treatment if demonstrably necessary.
lead: Which course of action provides the strongest patient-specific justification among these alternatives?

options.A: Investigate a mechanical intracapsular disorder when locking or progressive limitation is prominent
options.B: Escalate unexplained progressive limitation or systemic red flags for further specialist assessment
options.C: Reassure and monitor a painless joint click without routine irreversible treatment
options.D: Treat probable myalgia conservatively with education, self-care and reversible measures
options.E: Assess neuropathic facial pain and refer appropriately when touch-triggered attacks dominate

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Treat probable myalgia conservatively with education, self-care and reversible measures.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: The patient reports a dull ache increased by chewing and palpation reproduces familiar pain over the masseter.

stem: A used disposable gown is contaminated with noninfectious body fluids. No chemicals, medicines or sharps are present, and the waste is classified as noninfectious offensive healthcare waste under the England scheme.
lead: Which segregation route best fits the stated classification?

options.A: Orange infectious waste
options.B: Yellow/black tiger-striped offensive waste
options.C: Purple cytotoxic waste
options.D: Yellow infectious-plus-chemical waste
options.E: Sharps bin

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Yellow/black tiger-striped offensive waste

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Offensive (noninfectious) contaminated protective clothing is segregated in yellow/black tiger-striped waste rather than an infectious or cytotoxic stream.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Orange infectious waste — Orange is for an infectious stream, but this waste was risk-assessed as noninfectious.
C. Purple cytotoxic waste — No cytotoxic/cytostatic contamination is described.
D. Yellow infectious-plus-chemical waste — Yellow is used for infectious waste with relevant chemical or pharmaceutical contamination; neither is present.
E. Sharps bin — Non-sharp PPE must not enter a sharps container.

The dentist evaluates denture hygiene, Candida colonisation, lip support, interocclusal rest space, nutritional and haematological history, diabetes and local irritation. Denture dimensions and support are stable, but new angular lesions follow an inhaled steroid prescription, with mucosal candidiasis and no changes in lip posture.

options.A: Assess possible loss of occlusal vertical dimension and commissural maceration alongside denture and microbial factors
options.B: Extract remaining teeth to eliminate oral Candida

stem: A restored implant is reviewed because of discomfort, bleeding, tissue change or a cosmetic complaint. Baseline probing and imaging are available or their absence is recognised; mucosal inflammation must be distinguished from progressive loss of supporting bone. A cement-retained crown has submucosal excess cement visible after careful examination and inflammation localised to that area.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Assess prosthetic contours and residual cement as removable inflammatory drivers
options.B: Improve plaque control and prosthetic cleanability, then reassess peri-implant mucositis
options.C: Return to risk-based maintenance when probing, tissues and bone are stable
options.D: Investigate peri-implantitis with baseline comparison and provide cause-focused nonsurgical care before considering further treatment
options.E: Consider increasing keratinised mucosa when brushing discomfort persists despite health and suitable hygiene measures

solution:

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A cement-retained crown has submucosal excess cement visible after careful examination and inflammation localised to that area.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: A retained foreign material should be removed and the prosthetic design reassessed.

stem: A periodontally reduced tooth has resolved inflammation and stable attachment after active treatment, with no root fracture or active mobility.
lead: Which option is the single most appropriate management or interpretation for this presentation?

options.A: Stage periodontal therapy and reassess support rather than judging prognosis from bone loss percentage alone
options.B: Gain coronal tooth structure by appropriate orthodontic extrusion before reassessing restorability
options.C: Avoid relying on a structurally hopeless root and redesign the span or replacement strategy
options.D: Preserve and restore an abutment with sound ferrule and maintainable periodontal support
options.E: Choose a removable design that allows independent replacement of future failing teeth

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Stage periodontal therapy and reassess support rather than judging prognosis from bone loss percentage alone

stem: A posterior or anterior restoration has failed and an indirect replacement is proposed. Clinical examination describes the available clearance, enamel distribution, bonding substrate, occlusal loading and aesthetic zone. A small functional cusp defect has ample sound enamel and the patient wants an inexpensive reversible treatment with future repair potential. The patient is willing to consider either a conservative or a staged approach, provided the clinician can explain the principal benefit and limitation of each.
lead: What is the most defensible recommendation at this stage?

options.A: Use additive direct composite when minimal intervention, reversibility and future repair are dominant
options.B: Choose an adhesively retained lithium disilicate partial-coverage restoration where supported by enamel and adequate clearance
options.C: Gain additional restorative clearance or revise the preparation design before choosing a material
options.D: Prefer a metal restoration where clearance and load make a thin, durable restoration advantageous
options.E: Use a monolithic zirconia restoration with manufacturer-specified thickness and suitable conditioning for a high-load site

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Use additive direct composite when minimal intervention, reversibility and future repair are dominant.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A small functional cusp defect has ample sound enamel and the patient wants an inexpensive reversible treatment with future repair potential.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Additive composite can address a limited defect without unnecessary preparation.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The vital premolar has predominantly sound enamel, adequate occlusal thickness for a bonded onlay and a moderate aesthetic requirement. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A technician and prosthodontist review an acrylic denture base that has cracked or distorted after processing. The original mould, resin mixture, curing history, occlusal loading and repair materials are known. Several processing changes might affect different failure mechanisms. A repeated midline fracture initiates at an anterior notch in a thin base, directly beneath a heavy incisal contact. Clinical and technical teams have reviewed the available evidence; the patient asks how the most important diagnostic feature should change the plan.
lead: What is the most defensible recommendation at this stage?

options.A: Reduce stress concentration through base design, thickness, contour and fit
options.B: Correct the polymer-to-monomer ratio and packing stage to limit porosity and dimensional error
options.C: Repeat processing with the specified time–temperature cycle and adequate monomer conversion
options.D: Improve bonding and material matching at a repair interface rather than relying on bulk cold-cure acrylic
options.E: Check polymerisation shrinkage and cooling procedure before assuming a jaw-relation error

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Reduce stress concentration through base design, thickness, contour and fit.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A repeated midline fracture initiates at an anterior notch in a thin base, directly beneath a heavy incisal contact.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Crack initiation is linked to geometry and repeated flexural loading.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Numerous internal voids arise when too much liquid was added and the mix was packed too early in the sandy stage. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: An old heat-cured base has been repaired with a broad cold-cure joint that repeatedly separates along the original interface. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A prosthodontist compares restorative materials for a patient with limited tooth clearance, aesthetic needs and a finite budget. Laboratory cost, biological preparation burden, repairability, strength, stiffness and long-term maintenance all matter. An upper posterior molar has low occlusal clearance and the patient accepts a visible metal restoration. The patient understands that several technically feasible options differ in biological burden, retrievability, and long-term maintenance. The consultant is asked to prioritise the evidence that most changes prognosis.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Delay definitive indirect treatment until clearance or biological prerequisites can be achieved without harm
options.B: Choose a suitably designed high-strength zirconia crown when load and adequate preparation geometry justify it
options.C: Choose direct composite for a limited repairable lesion with favourable enamel
options.D: Choose a thin cast-metal onlay when limited space and non-aesthetic posterior loading dominate
options.E: Choose an adhesively bonded glass-ceramic partial crown when enamel and thickness allow

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Choose a thin cast-metal onlay when limited space and non-aesthetic posterior loading dominate.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: An upper posterior molar has low occlusal clearance and the patient accepts a visible metal restoration.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Cast metal can preserve tissue while providing a durable thin section.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: No tested option meets its minimum thickness without exposing the pulp or compromising ferrule. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A heavily loaded molar has an adequate retentive crown preparation and manufacturer-recommended occlusal clearance. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: The patient has a small vital defect, abundant enamel and wants straightforward chairside repair. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A premolar has enamel-rich margins, suitable ceramic thickness and a moderate aesthetic requirement. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A root-filled premolar remains symptomatic. A periapical radiograph has been taken but cannot resolve whether the complex anatomy or suspected root fracture will change management. An additional 3-D assessment is under consideration.
lead: Which imaging approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Obtain routine whole-skull CBCT for every symptomatic tooth
options.B: Consider justified limited-field CBCT only if its findings are expected to change treatment
options.C: Use CT for all teeth irrespective of prior radiographs
options.D: Prescribe an implant before identifying the diagnosis
options.E: Ignore clinical tests because radiographic imaging is always definitive

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Consider justified limited-field CBCT only if its findings are expected to change treatment

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: CBCT is justified when the diagnostic question and potential management benefit outweigh radiation exposure and limitations of 2-D assessment.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Obtain routine whole-skull CBCT for every symptomatic tooth — Broad-field routine CBCT is unnecessary radiation exposure.
C. Use CT for all teeth irrespective of prior radiographs — Imaging requires individual justification and optimisation, not blanket usage.
D. Prescribe an implant before identifying the diagnosis — The diagnosis and prognosis must precede replacement planning.
E. Ignore clinical tests because radiographic imaging is always definitive — Clinical examination and sensibility tests remain complementary to radiography.

stem: A patient requests extensive fixed prosthodontic reconstruction. A charted medical history, current medication list, caries record and periodontal measurements are provided. The referring dentist asks for a definitive sequence rather than a single isolated restoration. All options might be appropriate for different patterns of disease. Oncological-dose antiresorptive treatment is current, a strategic tooth is painful but potentially restorable and extractions have been proposed solely to simplify implant planning.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Provide staged direct repairs while assessing salivary function and instituting intensive prevention
options.B: Proceed to definitive fixed restoration after documenting periodontal stability and appropriate long-term maintenance
options.C: First control active disease and modifiable risk factors, then re-evaluate the definitive restorative plan
options.D: Consider a cleansable removable or simplified treatment plan when self-care and adaptation are limiting
options.E: Coordinate with the medical team to assess medication-related surgical risk before proposing extractions or implants

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Coordinate with the medical team to assess medication-related surgical risk before proposing extractions or implants.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: Oncological-dose antiresorptive treatment is current, a strategic tooth is painful but potentially restorable and extractions have been proposed solely to simplify implant planning.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: The drug indication and invasive procedure alter jaw-osteonecrosis risk and require individualised interdisciplinary planning.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Radiotherapy has produced profound xerostomia and multiple new cervical lesions, but most teeth remain restorable and the patient has not received salivary or fluoride intervention. B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Periodontal therapy is complete, plaque scores are low, pocketing has resolved, crown margins can be cleansed and the patient accepts recalls. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A tooth requires an indirect restoration with a difficult cervical margin. Photographs, six-point probing, radiographs, caries extent and periodontal tissue phenotype have been reviewed. The treatment plan must preserve periodontal attachment and pulpal health while ensuring a cleanable and recordable margin. A posterior proximal box extends slightly below the gingival crest but has sufficient enamel/dentine for isolation and a conservative margin elevation technique. The patient understands that several technically feasible options differ in biological burden, retrievability, and long-term maintenance. The consultant is asked to prioritise the evidence that most changes prognosis.

options.B: Place or retain a supragingival margin whenever caries clearance and aesthetics allow

options.D: Reassess pulp or endodontic prognosis before undertaking deep circumferential tooth reduction
options.E: Establish a controlled equigingival or shallow intrasulcular margin with reliable tissue management

stem: A patient complains that a newly made complete denture tips during chewing. Both dentures are examined for support, borders, tooth position and centric and eccentric contacts; the clinician must avoid treating a prosthesis design problem as a simple retention deficiency. Posterior teeth are arranged far buccal to the lower support area and the denture tips with chewing even when static contacts are balanced. stem: A patient with pain-related temporomandibular disorder requests a quick definitive solution. There is no evidence of destructive joint disease, and the dentition is otherwise stable. stem: A 42-year-old has progressive palatal erosion of maxillary teeth, frequent sour taste and episodic nocturnal reflux. The patient wants porcelain veneers immediately and continues to report active symptoms.
lead: Which step is most appropriate before definitive restorative treatment?

options.A: Provide ceramic restorations before investigating the pattern
options.B: Address suspected intrinsic acid exposure, assess oral consequences and coordinate appropriate medical evaluation
options.C: Use aggressive occlusal equilibration as first-line reflux treatment
options.D: Place a lower implant overdenture
options.E: Assume attrition is the only mechanism because molars are affected

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Address suspected intrinsic acid exposure, assess oral consequences and coordinate appropriate medical evaluation

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Ongoing intrinsic acid exposure can undermine restorations; history, referral when appropriate and cause control precede irreversible rehabilitation.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Provide ceramic restorations before investigating the pattern — Continuing reflux can jeopardise newly placed restorations.
C. Use aggressive occlusal equilibration as first-line reflux treatment — Occlusal grinding does not treat gastric acid exposure.
D. Place a lower implant overdenture — No lower edentulous implant rehabilitation is indicated.
E. Assume attrition is the only mechanism because molars are affected — The palatal pattern and reflux symptoms require intrinsic-acid assessment.

stem: A patient with a partially dentate arch is considering a tooth-supported reconstruction. The candidate abutments have been charted for ferrule, clinical crown height, periodontal attachment, endodontic health and load distribution; treatment cost and possible future failure are important. A periodontally reduced tooth has resolved inflammation and stable attachment after active treatment, with no root fracture or active mobility. Both a staged and a direct approach have been discussed, and neither is excluded solely by cost or operator access.
lead: Which course of action provides the strongest patient-specific justification among these alternatives?

options.A: Gain coronal tooth structure by appropriate orthodontic extrusion before reassessing restorability
options.B: Choose a removable design that allows independent replacement of future failing teeth
options.C: Stage periodontal therapy and reassess support rather than judging prognosis from bone loss percentage alone
options.D: Avoid relying on a structurally hopeless root and redesign the span or replacement strategy
options.E: Preserve and restore an abutment with sound ferrule and maintainable periodontal support

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Stage periodontal therapy and reassess support rather than judging prognosis from bone loss percentage alone.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A periodontally reduced tooth has resolved inflammation and stable attachment after active treatment, with no root fracture or active mobility.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Healthy reduced periodontium is not synonymous with an automatically hopeless abutment.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A strategically valuable root has insufficient coronal dentine but orthodontic extrusion can create ferrule without losing necessary root support. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Several abutments have fluctuating prognosis, the patient expects future tooth losses and seeks a repairable low-cost option. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A long root-supported bridge would depend on a vertically fractured distal abutment with repeated post loosening. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A mandibular removable partial denture is planned for a Kennedy Class I pattern. stem: A patient who has worn a complete mandibular denture for over a decade seeks improved function. Clinical photographs and diagnostic casts are available; the old denture has been examined for extension, support, occlusion and polished-surface contour. The mandibular ridge is severely resorbed, the neutral zone is narrow, and both previous dentures were repeatedly dislodged during speech despite adequate static extension. options.B: Begin with a copy-denture pathway to preserve familiar tooth position and polished-surface contours
options.C: Refine the existing prosthesis with border correction and occlusal reassessment before changing its retention mechanism
options.D: Consider a two-implant mandibular overdenture after assessment of anatomy, hygiene and maintenance
options.E: Arrange evaluation of an unstable mobile ridge and a selective impression before definitive construction

stem: A patient who has worn a complete mandibular denture for over a decade seeks improved function. stem: A previously restored molar has intermittent pain on chewing. Cold sensibility, percussion, six-point periodontal probing, bite testing and an intra-oral radiograph are available. The clinician needs to distinguish a fractured cusp, pulpal disease, a vertical root fracture and non-odontogenic pain without committing prematurely to irreversible care. The tooth has no localised bite-test response and reproducible pain follows masseter loading, with matched nocturnal clenching and normal dental investigations. Two options have been discussed at the referral visit;
lead: What is the most defensible recommendation at this stage?

options.A: Assess the isolated deep periodontal defect and root-level fracture evidence before attempting reconstruction
options.B: Reassess the occlusion and muscular pain source before removing a technically sound restoration
options.C: Treat the confirmed symptomatic irreversible pulpitis before planning definitive cuspal coverage
options.D: Remove the existing restoration under magnification, assess the crack, and protect the cusp provisionally
options.E: Obtain targeted additional investigation because the initial tests are conflicting and the management choice would change

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Reassess the occlusion and muscular pain source before removing a technically sound restoration.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: The tooth has no localised bite-test response and reproducible pain follows masseter loading, with matched nocturnal clenching and normal dental investigations.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Myogenous pain should not be managed through destructive tooth treatment.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
A: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: There is a narrow isolated 10-mm pocket next to a root-filled tooth and a J-shaped radiolucency after repeated post debonding. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
C: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: Spontaneous pain lasts hours, cold provokes prolonged lingering pain, and a protected cusp no longer explains the symptoms. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
D: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A sharp pain occurs specifically on release of pressure over the distolingual cusp, cold response is short and six-point probing is 2–3 mm throughout. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.
E: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A recently traumatised tooth tests negative to cold but has normal periapical imaging, uncertain pulpal status and no swelling. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A patient who has worn a complete mandibular denture for over a decade seeks improved function. Clinical photographs and diagnostic casts are available; the old denture has been examined for extension, support, occlusion and polished-surface contour. Implant surgery is possible but not automatically the patient’s preference. The patient has Parkinsonian motor impairment, longstanding successful tooth arrangement and well tolerated polished surfaces; the teeth are worn but the bases remain acceptable.
lead: Which recommendation most appropriately balances the stated clinical findings, prognosis and long-term maintenance?

options.A: Consider a two-implant mandibular overdenture after assessment of anatomy, hygiene and maintenance
options.B: Make a new conventional denture with neutral-zone registration and functionally moulded polished surfaces
options.C: Begin with a copy-denture pathway to preserve familiar tooth position and polished-surface contours
options.D: Refine the existing prosthesis with border correction and occlusal reassessment before changing its retention mechanism
options.E: Arrange evaluation of an unstable mobile ridge and a selective impression before definitive construction

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: The patient has Parkinsonian motor impairment, longstanding successful tooth arrangement and well tolerated polished surfaces; the teeth are worn but the bases remain acceptable.

stem: A young adult with a developmental dental anomaly seeks an attractive, durable restorative solution. Orthodontic records, tooth vitality, enamel quality, jaw growth and periodontal support have been assessed. The treatment must address long-term reparability and avoid unnecessary loss of otherwise sound tissue. Hypocalcified enamel is friable and breaks down under normal use over most functional surfaces, with poor predictable bonding. The patient wishes to preserve future options where possible but would accept a more extensive treatment if demonstrably necessary.
lead: What is the single best next step before the team commits to definitive treatment?

options.A: Consider conventional full coverage only where severe structural deficiency limits reliable additive solutions
options.B: Retain a suitable primary tooth temporarily with monitoring while definitive timing is reconsidered
options.C: Offer additive direct composite with maintenance and potential later modification
options.D: Plan adhesive indirect restorations only after assessing the quality and amount of bondable enamel
options.E: Plan a multidisciplinary stage of orthodontic redistribution before selecting prosthesis form

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Consider conventional full coverage only where severe structural deficiency limits reliable additive solutions.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: Hypocalcified enamel is friable and breaks down under normal use over most functional surfaces, with poor predictable bonding.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Extensive fragile enamel may necessitate more protective indirect treatment.

WHY THE OTHER FOUR ARE LESS SUITABLE HERE:
B: This alternative would be more defensible in a case such as: A primary canine remains sound and stable with an acceptable root; the permanent successor is absent and the patient is still growing. That decisive indication differs from the findings here.

stem: A long-span fixed dental prosthesis is being redesigned after porcelain fracture, decementation or overload. The restorative team has a mounted diagnostic setup, a clinical occlusal record, guidance assessment and evidence of connector and abutment loading. options.B: Use a reversible provisional scheme to test a proposed occlusal reorganisation

options.E: Reassess abutment distribution and span length before simply selecting a stronger ceramic

stem: A mandibular molar has sharp pain on release from biting on one cusp, normal probing around most of the tooth and a vital pulp without persistent spontaneous pain. No isolated deep narrow periodontal pocket or root-fracture signs are found.
lead: Which immediate management principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Extract immediately without evaluating extent of crack
options.B: Assess and stabilise the suspected cusp crack, including cuspal coverage where indicated, while reviewing pulp status
options.C: Prescribe systemic antibiotics as the definitive treatment
options.D: Assume vertical root fracture and remove the root
options.E: Place an implant without explaining conservative alternatives

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — Assess and stabilise the suspected cusp crack, including cuspal coverage where indicated, while reviewing pulp status

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Pain on biting release and a localised cusp finding can suggest cracked-tooth syndrome; diagnostic assessment and cuspal protection may be appropriate while prognosis and pulp are monitored.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Extract immediately without evaluating extent of crack — Not every cracked vital molar has a hopeless prognosis.
C. Prescribe systemic antibiotics as the definitive treatment — Antibiotics do not stabilise an uninfected mechanical crack.
D. Assume vertical root fracture and remove the root — The narrow isolated pocket and other findings that would raise concern for vertical root fracture are absent.
E. Place an implant without explaining conservative alternatives — Conservative treatment and informed options have not been exhausted.

stem: A patient returns after delivery of a new removable prosthesis with discomfort or poor tolerance. The pattern of symptoms, mucosal findings, occlusal examination and functional movements are recorded before any intervention. A focal firm ulcer persists after adjustment and healing time, with no improvement or clear traumatic explanation. The dentist has checked the relevant supporting records and asks for a recommendation that avoids unnecessary intervention.
lead: What is the best next clinical decision?

options.A: Correct occlusal disharmony producing generalised soreness or tipping without local border trauma
options.B: Address xerostomia and low salivary lubrication as the driver of general frictional symptoms
options.C: Relieve a focal pressure spot corresponding to a clearly identified fitting-surface trauma
options.D: Refer an unexplained persistent or indurated mucosal lesion for formal assessment
options.E: Check for candida-associated inflammation and poor denture hygiene before repeated mechanical adjustment

solution:

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: A focal firm ulcer persists after adjustment and healing time, with no improvement or clear traumatic explanation.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Possible serious pathology warrants urgent evaluation.

stem: A patient receives an implant where definitive crown timing is under consideration. Bone quality, insertion stability, occlusal loading, healing conditions and the planned restoration have been assessed; the team must not confuse implant insertion with predictable osseointegration. After several weeks the implant is mobile and tender despite an apparently intact provisional crown. Two options have been discussed at the referral visit;
lead: What is the most defensible recommendation at this stage?

options.A: Stage implant placement after infection or tissue risks have been controlled
options.B: Select components and a passive prosthetic interface that avoid excessive preload or cantilever forces
options.C: Consider immediate provisionalisation only when stability, loading control and case selection support it
options.D: Delay loading when primary stability is inadequate and use a nonloading provisional replacement
options.E: Manage a suspected early failure by investigating mobility, infection and mechanical causes before definitive restoration

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: E — Manage a suspected early failure by investigating mobility, infection and mechanical causes before definitive restoration.

DECISIVE CLINICAL FEATURE: After several weeks the implant is mobile and tender despite an apparently intact provisional crown.

WHY THIS OPTION WINS: Mobility suggests failure of integration rather than a crown-only complication.

stem: A zirconia crown requires resin bonding. The laboratory confirms a zirconia-based rather than silica-based glass ceramic, with the restoration cleaned before surface conditioning.
lead: Which bonding approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Hydrofluoric acid etch followed by silane as the sole zirconia treatment
options.B: Phosphoric acid etching of the crown followed by water rinse only
options.C: Zirconia-compatible air abrasion where indicated followed by an MDP-containing system according to manufacturer instructions
options.D: Apply silane directly to polished zirconia without pretreatment
options.E: No need for any cement or retention design

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Zirconia-compatible air abrasion where indicated followed by an MDP-containing system according to manufacturer instructions

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: Zirconia is not etched like a silica-based glass ceramic; controlled abrasion and MDP chemistry are commonly used in validated zirconia protocols.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Hydrofluoric acid etch followed by silane as the sole zirconia treatment — Hydrofluoric acid is not the appropriate stand-alone conditioner for zirconia.
B. Phosphoric acid etching of the crown followed by water rinse only — Phosphoric acid rinsing alone does not establish a durable zirconia resin bond.
D. Apply silane directly to polished zirconia without pretreatment — Silane alone does not adequately bond to a non-silica zirconia substrate.
E. No need for any cement or retention design — Cementation and mechanical retention remain clinically relevant.

stem: A restored implant has suppuration, increased probing depths and confirmed progressive supporting-bone loss. The prosthesis has a non-cleansable overcontoured emergence profile. The implant remains potentially maintainable.
lead: What is the most appropriate first stage of management?

options.A: Prescribe systemic antibiotics alone and review in a year
options.B: Polish the occlusal contacts only
options.C: Begin biofilm control and appropriate non-surgical instrumentation while correcting cleansability, then reassess for possible surgery
options.D: Proceed directly to regeneration without assessing plaque control
options.E: Remove every implant with bleeding on probing

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — Begin biofilm control and appropriate non-surgical instrumentation while correcting cleansability, then reassess for possible surgery

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: The EFP S3 pathway starts with treatability assessment, biofilm/risk control, prosthesis modification where needed and non-surgical instrumentation before re-evaluation.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Prescribe systemic antibiotics alone and review in a year — Antibiotics alone cannot eliminate the prosthetic biofilm trap or replace mechanical treatment.
B. Polish the occlusal contacts only — Occlusal polishing alone does not treat the inflammatory bone-loss condition.
D. Proceed directly to regeneration without assessing plaque control — Surgery should follow treatability assessment and non-surgical management with re-evaluation.
E. Remove every implant with bleeding on probing — Bleeding does not by itself make the implant hopeless; retainability must be assessed.

stem: A specialist reviewing a referral must decide how an investigation or published estimate should influence prosthodontic management. stem: A prosthodontist is assessing discrepant clinical findings in a restoration or implant follow-up. A screening test, clinical examination and relevant imaging each have different sensitivities and potential errors; the decision should be based on a coherent synthesis, not an isolated number. options.A: Proceed with a conservative decision when investigations consistently show low risk and intervention carries greater harm

options.E: Repeat an unreliable measurement using a standardised technique before judging progression

stem: A patient takes once-daily rivaroxaban every evening. A periodontal flap operation will be performed the next morning. The patient has no additional medical complications and local haemostatic measures are planned.
lead: What is the recommended preoperative medication adjustment under SDCEP?

options.A: Do not change the evening regimen before surgery; provide haemostasis and ensure any evening dose is at least four hours after haemostasis
options.B: Omit the preceding evening rivaroxaban dose regardless of risk
options.C: Delay a morning dose that this patient never takes
options.D: Stop anticoagulation for seven days
options.E: Replace rivaroxaban with aspirin before the flap

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Do not change the evening regimen before surgery; provide haemostasis and ensure any evening dose is at least four hours after haemostasis

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: For once-daily evening rivaroxaban or edoxaban, SDCEP does not require preoperative modification; the evening dose must not be earlier than four hours after haemostasis.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
B. Omit the preceding evening rivaroxaban dose regardless of risk — The preceding evening dose does not routinely need to be omitted.
C. Delay a morning dose that this patient never takes — The patient does not take a morning dose; this advice applies to a different dosing schedule.
D. Stop anticoagulation for seven days — Prolonged interruption without medical indication may increase thrombosis risk.
E. Replace rivaroxaban with aspirin before the flap — Aspirin does not replace the prescribed anticoagulant.

stem: After several years with a maxillary complete denture opposing a mandibular bilateral distal-extension prosthesis, a patient has anterior maxillary ridge resorption, enlarged tuberosities and a reduced posterior occlusal contact scheme.
lead: Which explanation and management principle is most appropriate?

options.B: This pattern is compatible with combination syndrome; reassess posterior support, occlusal loading and prosthesis design
options.C: It proves the maxillary denture was fabricated digitally
options.D: Remove all remaining mandibular teeth immediately
options.E: Routine replacement of upper denture teeth alone addresses altered biomechanical support

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: B — This pattern is compatible with combination syndrome; reassess posterior support, occlusal loading and prosthesis design

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: The classic combination-syndrome pattern reflects unfavourable distribution of support and occlusal forces; treatment requires reassessment of the whole prosthodontic system.

A. It is simply irreversible resin shrinkage and requires only re-polishing — The characteristic tissue and occlusal changes are not explained by resin processing alone.

D. Remove all remaining mandibular teeth immediately — Extraction of remaining mandibular teeth is not a default corrective measure.
E. Routine replacement of upper denture teeth alone addresses altered biomechanical support — Replacing tooth facings alone does not address the load-distribution problem.

stem: A posterior maxillary implant can be placed at the same appointment as a minor sinus floor augmentation with adequate primary stability. The clinician is asked whether this alone justifies immediate occlusal loading.
lead: Which conclusion is best supported?

options.A: Simultaneous placement always requires immediate loading
options.B: Insertion torque alone establishes long-term osseointegration
options.C: Immediate loading is mandatory after sinus floor augmentation
options.D: Placement timing and loading timing are separate decisions; evaluate primary stability, prosthetic loading and patient factors
options.E: A high insertion torque means peri-implantitis cannot occur

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: D — Placement timing and loading timing are separate decisions; evaluate primary stability, prosthetic loading and patient factors

DECISIVE CLINICAL REASONING: The ability to place an implant simultaneously with augmentation does not automatically establish whether it can safely receive immediate functional loading.

WHY OTHER OPTIONS LOSE:
A. Simultaneous placement always requires immediate loading — Placement and loading decisions are independent.
B. Insertion torque alone establishes long-term osseointegration — Torque is only one component of stability, not proof of osseointegration.
C. Immediate loading is mandatory after sinus floor augmentation — Augmentation does not mandate immediate function.
E. A high insertion torque means peri-implantitis cannot occur — Insertion torque cannot exclude later inflammatory complications.

theme: Ferrule and post indication: anterior tooth
stem: A root-treated maxillary central incisor has a 2-mm circumferential band of sound cervical dentine and a fractured coronal restoration. After removing caries, there is insufficient coronal structure to retain a core, but an adequate root canal can accept a conservative fibre post without excessive dentine removal.
lead: What best describes the post's legitimate role?

options.A: A post should be placed into every root-filled posterior tooth
options.B: The post reinforces the root and replaces the ferrule
options.C: The post may retain a core while the remaining cervical dentine provides ferrule; assess occlusion and overall restorability
options.D: The post eliminates the need for a definitive coronal seal
options.E: Any post makes the tooth immune to fracture

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: C — The post may retain a core while the remaining cervical dentine provides ferrule; assess occlusion and overall restorability

RATIONALE: Posts mainly help retain a core when there is insufficient coronal tissue; they do not regenerate a ferrule or inherently strengthen the root. Preserving pericervical dentine and preparing a sound coronal restoration remains critical.

WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE LESS SUITABLE: A. A post should be placed into every root-filled posterior tooth B. The post reinforces the root and replaces the ferrule D. The post eliminates the need for a definitive coronal seal E. Any post makes the tooth immune to fracture

CLINICAL NOTE: Interpret the clinical details, rather than using a single keyword or a mnemonic without checking indications.

stem: A 62-year-old takes rivaroxaban in the evening. A higher-bleeding-risk periodontal flap operation is planned for the following morning. The patient has no additional bleeding or thrombotic concerns, and haemostasis will be checked before the usual evening dose.

options.B: Delay the scheduled morning rivaroxaban dose for a higher-bleeding-risk procedure
options.C: Stop rivaroxaban for several days without medical agreement
options.D: Change rivaroxaban to warfarin solely for a dental procedure
options.E: Omit all postoperative doses until every suture has been removed

solution:
PROPOSED BEST ANSWER: A — Continue the prescribed DOAC and use local haemostatic measures

CLINICAL REASONING: An evening once-daily regimen does not require a preoperative morning-dose change; take the usual evening dose at least 4 h after haemostasis.

WHY THE FOUR ALTERNATIVES ARE LESS APPROPRIATE HERE:

D. Change rivaroxaban to warfarin solely for a dental procedure — Routine conversion is not indicated; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
E. Omit all postoperative doses until every suture has been removed — Prolonged interruption is not supported by routine dental guidance; this is not the decisive priority in the stated vignette.
